Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ: MSFT ) quietly disclosed a number that changes the scale of its OpenAI relationship. In its fiscal 2026 10-K, Microsoft said it recorded $24.1 billion of revenue from commercial arrangements with OpenAI, including revenue-sharing payments. It also had $6.0 billion of accounts receivable from OpenAI at June 30. The number is huge. The missing number may be even more consequential. For investors trying to decide whether the AI buildout is producing returns or merely moving cash among strategic partners, the distinction between revenue scale and margin quality is the whole story.

Microsoft does not separately disclose the profit generated by those OpenAI commercial arrangements. The $24.1 billion should not be confused with pure Azure revenue or treated as a clean measure of AI cloud sales. It includes the economics created by the companies' broader partnership, while Microsoft also owns an around 25% interest in OpenAI on an as-converted basis and continues to receive revenue-sharing payments.

The strategic logic is still powerful, because Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT) funds and supplies infrastructure to one of the largest AI labs, gets access to OpenAI intellectual property for its products, sells cloud capacity into the relationship and participates financially in OpenAI's growth. Fiscal 2026 Microsoft Cloud growth helped push total company revenue up 18%, and Microsoft recorded $5.0 billion of net-income benefit from net gains on its OpenAI investments.

But the 10-K also shows why investors should resist treating every OpenAI dollar as high-margin software revenue. Microsoft Cloud gross margin fell to 66%, with management citing continued AI-infrastructure investment and growing AI product usage. Costs are arriving alongside the revenue through data centers, server components, depreciation and financing structures. The OpenAI relationship can be extraordinarily valuable while still carrying economics that differ sharply from Microsoft's traditional software franchise. That gap is precisely why the disclosed revenue deserves analysis instead of automatic celebration.

Insider Monkey's database showed 273 hedge funds holding MSFT as of Q2, down from 282 in Q1. Those filings precede the annual report's full-year disclosure. As of August 14, roughly 68.54 million Microsoft shares were sold short, about 0.92% of the public float, with 2.1 days to cover. The $24.1 billion figure answers whether OpenAI is already financially material to Microsoft. It does not answer the more important valuation question: how much incremental profit Microsoft keeps after paying for the infrastructure and capital required to produce it.

While we acknowledge the potential of MSFT as an investment, we believe certain other AI stocks offer greater upside potential and carry less downside risk. sources.title: OpenAI hits $10 billion in annual recurring revenue fueled by ChatGPT growth - CNBC
passages: OpenAI has hit $10 billion in annual recurring revenue, or ARR, less than three years after launching its popular ChatGPT chatbot.
WATCH: OpenAI paying business users of ChatGPT hits 3 million, up from 2 million in February
For all of last year, OpenAI had around $5.5 billion in ARR.
Reaching its meteoric growth rates requires a substantial amount of cash.
OpenAI is also targeting $125 billion in revenue by 2029, according to a person familiar with the matter who asked not to be named because the details are confidential.
The Information first reported on OpenAI's revenue ambitions.
The new revenue metrics give some context to OpenAI's monster valuation.
OpenAI closed a $40 billion funding round in March, marking the largest private tech deal on record.
At today's metrics, OpenAI is valued at about 30 times revenue, which highlights the hyper growth expectations by some of its largest investors.
OpenAI is backed by Japan's SoftBank , Microsoft , Coatue, Altimeter, Thrive and others.
The figure includes sales from the company's consumer products; ChatGPT business products; and its application programming interface, or API.
It excludes licensing revenue from Microsoft and large one-time deals, according to an OpenAI spokesperson.
OpenAI burst onto the scene with the release of the consumer version of ChatGPT in late 2022, and began launching business products the following year.
As of late March, OpenAI said it supports 500 million weekly active users.

sources.title: Microsoft recorded $10 billion in revenue from OpenAI
passages: Microsoft generated $10 billion in revenue from commercial arrangements with OpenAI, including revenue-sharing payments, in the quarter ended September 30, the company said in a regulatory filing on Wednesday.

That represents nearly 11% of Microsoft’s total quarterly revenue of $92.3 billion, highlighting the enormous financial ties that remain between the two companies even as they increasingly compete for the same customers .
For the full 2026 fiscal year, revenue from OpenAI hit $24.1 billion.
At its latest quarterly pace, Microsoft would pull in $40 billion annually from OpenAI-related arrangements.
Microsoft also reported $7.2 billion in outstanding receivables from OpenAI at the end of September, up from $6 billion at the end of June.
That money represents amounts OpenAI owes for previous transactions, not additional revenue.
TechCrunch has reached out for more information.

The companies began loosening the ties of their once-exclusive partnership in October 2025, when Microsoft relinquished its hold on OpenAI to give the startup more freedom to partner with other cloud providers.
In exchange, OpenAI committed to buying an additional $250 billion in Azure services as part of an October 2025 agreement.
Microsoft’s ownership stake in OpenAI has also declined slightly from about 25% in June to 24% in September.
That continues a gradual decline from roughly 27% following the October 2025 recapitalization.
Microsoft did not specify what caused the dilution.

extraction.body: Microsoft has announced its latest quarterly earnings, posting a record revenue of $92.3 billion, an impressive 19% growth from the same period last year. This marks the tech giant's 10th consecutive quarter of setting new revenue records. The company's net income also saw a significant increase, reaching $36.6 billion, up by 32% on a Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) basis compared to the previous year. A major contributor to Microsoft's record-breaking income this quarter is the performance of Microsoft Cloud. The segment generated $63.9 billion in revenue, a whopping 30% increase over the same period last year. However, not all of this cloud revenue can be directly linked to artificial intelligence (AI). For instance, Microsoft 365 alone accounted for nearly $28 billion in revenue during the quarter. Microsoft's cloud platform, Azure, was the biggest revenue generator for the company this quarter, bringing in $33.2 billion. Again, it's worth noting that not all of this revenue is directly tied to AI technology. Microsoft also reported $10 billion in revenue from its partnership with OpenAI. Despite expanding to Amazon Web Services (AWS), Oracle, and others, OpenAI still relies heavily on Microsoft's cloud services for many of its operations. This collaboration has significantly boosted Microsoft's bottom line and further highlights the growing importance of AI in today's tech landscape. In line with its growing revenue and future commitments, Microsoft has also ramped up its capital expenditures. The company reported a record high of $45.2 billion in capital expenditures for the quarter. This investment is aimed at preparing the company to deliver on its future revenue commitments under existing contracts with AI labs, further solidifying Microsoft's position as a leader in the tech industry.

relevantPassages.text: This marks the tech giant's 10th consecutive quarter of setting new revenue records.
Microsoft has announced its latest quarterly earnings, posting a record revenue of $92.3 billion, an impressive 19% growth from the same period last year.
For instance, Microsoft 365 alone accounted for nearly $28 billion in revenue during the quarter.
Microsoft's cloud platform, Azure, was the biggest revenue generator for the company this quarter, bringing in $33.2 billion.
In line with its growing revenue and future commitments, Microsoft has also ramped up its capital expenditures.
This collaboration has significantly boosted Microsoft's bottom line and further highlights the growing importance of AI in today's tech landscape.

coreStoryFacts.text: Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ: MSFT ) quietly disclosed a number that changes the scale of its OpenAI relationship.
In its fiscal 2026 10-K, Microsoft said it recorded $24.1 billion of revenue from commercial arrangements with OpenAI, including revenue-sharing payments.
It also had $6.0 billion of accounts receivable from OpenAI at June 30.
The missing number may be even more consequential.

For investors trying to decide whether the AI buildout is producing returns or merely moving cash among strategic partners, the distinction between revenue scale and margin quality is the whole story.
Microsoft does not separately disclose the profit generated by those OpenAI commercial arrangements.
Insider Monkey's database showed 273 hedge funds holding MSFT as of Q2, down from 282 in Q1.
Those filings precede the annual report's full-year disclosure.
As of August 14, roughly 68.54 million Microsoft shares were sold short, about 0.92% of the public float, with 2.1 days to cover.
It does not answer the more important valuation question: how much incremental profit Microsoft keeps after paying for the infrastructure and capital required to produce it.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
But the 10-K also shows why investors should resist treating every OpenAI dollar as high-margin software revenue.
The OpenAI relationship can be extraordinarily valuable while still carrying economics that differ sharply from Microsoft's traditional software franchise.
OpenAI has hit $10 billion in annual recurring revenue, or ARR, less than three years after launching its popular ChatGPT chatbot.
WATCH: OpenAI paying business users of ChatGPT hits 3 million, up from 2 million in February
For all of last year, OpenAI had around $5.5 billion in ARR.
Reaching its meteoric growth rates requires a substantial amount of cash.
OpenAI is also targeting $125 billion in revenue by 2029, according to a person familiar with the matter who asked not to be named because the details are confidential.
The Information first reported on OpenAI's revenue ambitions.
The new revenue metrics give some context to OpenAI's monster valuation.
OpenAI closed a $40 billion funding round in March, marking the largest private tech deal on record.
At today's metrics, OpenAI is valued at about 30 times revenue, which highlights the hyper growth expectations by some of its largest investors.
OpenAI is backed by Japan's SoftBank , Microsoft , Coatue, Altimeter, Thrive and others.
The figure includes sales from the company's consumer products; ChatGPT business products; and its application programming interface, or API.

sources.title: Microsoft recorded $10 billion in revenue from OpenAI
passages: Microsoft generated $10 billion in revenue from commercial arrangements with OpenAI, including revenue-sharing payments, in the quarter ended September 30, the company said in a regulatory filing on Wednesday.

That represents nearly 11% of Microsoft’s total quarterly revenue of $92.3 billion, highlighting the enormous financial ties that remain between the two companies even as they increasingly compete for the same customers .
For the full 2026 fiscal year, revenue from OpenAI hit $24.1 billion.
At its latest quarterly pace, Microsoft would pull in $40 billion annually from OpenAI-related arrangements.
Microsoft also reported $7.2 billion in outstanding receivables from OpenAI at the end of September, up from $6 billion at the end of June.
That money represents amounts OpenAI owes for previous transactions, not additional revenue.
TechCrunch has reached out for more information.

The companies began loosening the ties of their once-exclusive partnership in October 2025, when Microsoft relinquished its hold on OpenAI to give the startup more freedom to partner with other cloud providers.
In exchange, OpenAI committed to buying an additional $250 billion in Azure services as part of an October 2025 agreement.
Microsoft’s ownership stake in OpenAI has also declined slightly from about 25% in June to 24% in September.
That continues a gradual decline from roughly 27% following the October 2025 recapitalization.
Microsoft did not specify what caused the dilution.

This marks the tech giant's 10th consecutive quarter of setting new revenue records. The company's net income also saw a significant increase, reaching $36.6 billion, up by 32% on a Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) basis compared to the previous year. A major contributor to Microsoft's record-breaking income this quarter is the performance of Microsoft Cloud. The segment generated $63.9 billion in revenue, a whopping 30% increase over the same period last year. However, not all of this cloud revenue can be directly linked to artificial intelligence (AI). For instance, Microsoft 365 alone accounted for nearly $28 billion in revenue during the quarter. Microsoft's cloud platform, Azure, was the biggest revenue generator for the company this quarter, bringing in $33.2 billion. Again, it's worth noting that not all of this revenue is directly tied to AI technology. Microsoft also reported $10 billion in revenue from its partnership with OpenAI. Despite expanding to Amazon Web Services (AWS), Oracle, and others, OpenAI still relies heavily on Microsoft's cloud services for many of its operations. This collaboration has significantly boosted Microsoft's bottom line and further highlights the growing importance of AI in today's tech landscape. In line with its growing revenue and future commitments, Microsoft has also ramped up its capital expenditures. The company reported a record high of $45.2 billion in capital expenditures for the quarter. This investment is aimed at preparing the company to deliver on its future revenue commitments under existing contracts with AI labs, further solidifying Microsoft's position as a leader in the tech industry.

Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Under the terms of the agreement, ADT stockholders will receive $10.00 per share in cash, representing a 45.6% premium to ADT's closing share price of $6.87 on October 27, 2026.
The deal values ADT at $15.3 billion in enterprise value.
Thrive Holdings is a permanent capital holding company that owns and operates more than 75 businesses across accounting, IT services and the built environment.
Following the closing, ADT will form the foundation of Thrive Holdings' smart home security business.

(NYSE: ADT) (“ADT” or the “Company”), a leading provider of security, interactive and smart home solutions serving residential and small business customers in the U.S., and Thrive Holdings, a permanent capital holding company focused on investing in established businesses and advancing their capabilities through technology, today announced a definitive agreement under which Thrive Holdings will acquire ADT in an all-cash transaction. The agreement values ADT at approximately $7.6 billion in equity value and $15.3 billion in enterprise value. Under the terms of the agreement, which ADT’s Board of Directors unanimously approved, ADT stockholders will receive $10.00 per share in cash upon completion. The per share price represents a premium of 45.6% to ADT’s unaffected closing share price on October 27, 2026, and 52.1% to its 30-day volume-weighted average share price ending on October 27, 2026. The transaction would combine ADT’s more than 150 years of security experience, nationwide service network and customer trust with Thrive Holdings’ long-term capital and engineering capabilities. Thrive Holdings is a permanent capital holding company, which enables it to own and operate businesses over a long-term horizon. This ownership structure will provide ADT with greater flexibility to invest in its people and the development of new products and services. “ADT is pleased to enter into this transaction, which recognizes the value built by our more than 12,000 employees and delivers an attractive cash premium to our stockholders,” said Jim DeVries, Chairman, President and Chief Executive Officer of ADT. “Our leadership in security is based on a legacy of trust, longstanding customer relationships and the dedication of our employees. With Thrive Holdings’ long-term capital and technology expertise, ADT will gain new opportunities to accelerate innovation, enhance the customer experience and bring greater peace of mind to even more homes and businesses.” “ADT has spent generations showing up for people when it matters most,” said Kareem Zaki, Partner at Thrive Holdings. “We intend to build on that foundation by strengthening ADT’s technology and product capabilities, with the capital and patience to invest over decades. Our ambition is to help ADT’s teams better serve customers and offer a seamless service with more actionable information for the professionals responding.” Currently, more than 75 businesses across accounting, IT services and the built environment are part of Thrive Holdings. Following the closing of the transaction, ADT will form the foundation of Thrive Holdings’ smart home security business. Thrive Holdings intends to support ADT’s management in pursuing long-term growth through continued investment in the Company’s people, products and services. Thrive Holdings’ engineering teams will work alongside ADT’s professionals to identify opportunities for technology to enhance the Company’s products and services and help its teams support customers more effectively. ADT’s data and privacy policies will remain unchanged, and no new data sharing will occur without customer permission. “Protecting customers’ homes also means protecting their data. Thrive Holdings is committed to upholding the highest standards of privacy and cybersecurity to protect the information that customers entrust to ADT,” said Anuj Mehndiratta, Partner at Thrive Holdings. As previously announced, ADT’s third quarter 2026 results will be issued on November 3, 2026, prior to market opening. The Company will share a summary of its results on a 10 a.m. ET conference call. In consideration of the announced transaction, the Company will not be taking questions on the call. BOCA RATON, Fla. and NEW YORK, Oct. 29, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- ADT Inc. (NYSE: ADT) (“ADT” or the “Company”), a leading provider of security, interactive and smart home solutions serving residential and small business customers in the U.S., and Thrive Holdings, a permanent capital holding company focused on investing in established businesses and advancing their capabilities through technology, today announced a definitive agreement under which Thrive Holdings will acquire ADT in an all-cash transaction. The agreement values ADT at approximately $7.6 billion in equity value and $15.3 billion in enterprise value.

Under the terms of the agreement, which ADT’s Board of Directors unanimously approved, ADT stockholders will receive $10.00 per share in cash upon completion. The per share price represents a premium of 45.6% to ADT’s unaffected closing share price on October 27, 2026, and 52.1% to its 30-day volume-weighted average share price ending on October 27, 2026.

The transaction would combine ADT’s more than 150 years of security experience, nationwide service network and customer trust with Thrive Holdings’ long-term capital and engineering capabilities. Thrive Holdings is a permanent capital holding company, which enables it to own and operate businesses over a long-term horizon. This ownership structure will provide ADT with greater flexibility to invest in its people and the development of new products and services.

“ADT is pleased to enter into this transaction, which recognizes the value built by our more than 12,000 employees and delivers an attractive cash premium to our stockholders,” said Jim DeVries, Chairman, President and Chief Executive Officer of ADT. “Our leadership in security is based on a legacy of trust, longstanding customer relationships and the dedication of our employees. With Thrive Holdings’ long-term capital and technology expertise, ADT will gain new opportunities to accelerate innovation, enhance the customer experience and bring greater peace of mind to even more homes and businesses.”

“ADT has spent generations showing up for people when it matters most,” said Kareem Zaki, Partner at Thrive Holdings. “We intend to build on that foundation by strengthening ADT’s technology and product capabilities, with the capital and patience to invest over decades. Our ambition is to help ADT’s teams better serve customers and offer a seamless service with more actionable information for the professionals responding.”

Currently, more than 75 businesses across accounting, IT services and the built environment are part of Thrive Holdings. Following the closing of the transaction, ADT will form the foundation of Thrive Holdings’ smart home security business.

Thrive Holdings intends to support ADT’s management in pursuing long-term growth through continued investment in the Company’s people, products and services. Thrive Holdings’ engineering teams will work alongside ADT’s professionals to identify opportunities for technology to enhance the Company’s products and services and help its teams support customers more effectively.
ADT’s data and privacy policies will remain unchanged, and no new data sharing will occur without customer permission.

During Alphabet's third-quarter earnings call Wednesday, J.P. Morgan analyst Doug Anmuth asked why Search revenue growth slowed even as queries rose at their fastest pace in five years.
Philipp Schindler , Google's chief business officer, said Search revenue rose 12% year over year to $63 billion during the quarter.
Foreign exchange was the biggest factor behind the slowdown in growth compared with the second quarter, Schindler said.

He also cited retail advertising challenges linked to the EU's elimination of its de minimis exemption and normalized media and entertainment spending following an unusually strong second quarter driven by the FIFA Club World Cup.
However, AI-powered search experiences also played a role. "The strong growth in AI Overviews had an impact because of the lower monetization we were seeing in AI Mode," Schindler said.
Earlier on the call, Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai said Google's AI investments are boosting Search usage and overall query growth, including commercial searches.
"In fact, our year over year query growth rate is the highest it's been in the last five years," Pichai stated.

Google is working to improve advertising revenue from its AI search products as users increasingly turn to AI-generated answers.
Schindler said advertising experiments had produced promising results, with Google expanding ads in AI Overviews and AI Mode to more users and queries.
The tech giant is also extending these efforts into international markets and testing multi-turn ads in the U.S., which could integrate advertising into longer, conversational search experiences.
"To be clear, we feel very good about our trajectory here," Schindler said.
Separately, Pichai said increasingly capable AI models could significantly improve Google's internal productivity and accelerate product development.

He highlighted improvements in software engineering, including higher-quality code submissions and fewer rollbacks, along with opportunities to tackle bigger problems and improve consumer experiences.
Pichai said Google was rolling out a newer internal AI model, Carbon, which he described as a significant improvement over Argon.
As access expands and more computing resources become available, Pichai said he expects 2027 to be a "golden year" for productivity and innovation at Google.
Alphabet reported third-quarter revenue of about $127.58 billion, below analysts' estimates of $128.20 billion. The company reported earnings of $2.12 per share, compared with estimates of $3.02.
Looking ahead, Alphabet expects foreign exchange headwinds to weigh more heavily on fourth-quarter revenue than in the previous quarter, primarily affecting Google Search and YouTube advertising.
The company also expects tougher year-over-year comparisons as it faces the impact of Search's accelerated growth in the same quarter last year.

extraction.body: Google is expanding advertising in its AI-powered Search experience, AI Mode, to India and nine other markets. The company is looking to build new commercial opportunities around conversational search while protecting the growth of its core advertising business. The expansion, announced alongside Alphabet’s third-quarter 2026 results, will bring ads in AI Mode to Australia, Canada, India, Kenya, Malaysia, New Zealand, Nigeria, Pakistan, the Philippines and Singapore. Google plans to extend the rollout to Brazil, Mexico and the United Kingdom in the fourth quarter. In the US, it is introducing multiturn ads that can appear in follow-up queries within AI Mode. The move comes as Google Search advertising growth moderates even as usage of its AI-powered features increases. Search and other advertising revenue rose 12% year on year to $63.35 billion in the September quarter, compared with 17% growth in the previous quarter. YouTube advertising revenue increased 9.2% to $11.21 billion, while total Google advertising revenue grew 10.6% to $82.01 billion. AI Mode allows users to explore questions through longer, more conversational interactions, creating a different environment for product discovery and commercial intent than a conventional search results page. From search results to conversational discovery Google said queries in AI Mode are, on average, three times longer than traditional Search queries. The company believes AI helps it understand what users are looking for and connect them with businesses and services that match their needs. Google said its research indicates that users find ads in AI Mode relevant and that click-through rates for sponsored and organic product-list items are already similar. The expansion signals Google's intention to bring advertising into more of the AI-assisted journey, rather than limit monetisation to conventional search results. Longer queries can give the system more context about what a user wants, potentially creating opportunities for advertisers to reach consumers as they compare products, evaluate options or narrow down a purchase. However, the company has not disclosed how much revenue AI Mode advertising currently generates or how much it expects the international rollout to contribute. Pichai says AI is driving Search usage to a five-year high The advertising push comes against a broader backdrop of AI-led growth across Alphabet. On the company's Q3 earnings call, Google and Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai said Search was seeing strong momentum, with AI investments driving higher usage and growth in overall queries, including commercial queries. “Our AI investments are driving overall Search query growth, including commercial queries. In fact, our year-over-year query growth rate is the highest it’s been in the last five years,” Pichai said. He described the company's strategy as building a seamless experience across AI Overviews, AI Mode and traditional Search, as users increasingly adopt new ways of finding information. Their queries are longer, personalized, and multimodal,” he said. Pichai added that one in five AI Mode searches globally involves voice, images or documents, while Google now handles more than 50 billion visual searches a month. These shifts matter commercially because Google's advertising model has historically depended on matching search queries with relevant ads. As the interface evolves from a list of links towards AI-generated responses and more extended interactions, the company needs to determine how advertising fits into those experiences and how it can deliver value to businesses. Alphabet's growth increasingly spans advertising and AI infrastructure Alphabet reported third-quarter revenue of $127.58 billion, up 25% year on year. Google Services, which includes Search, YouTube, subscriptions and devices, generated $96.3 billion, an increase of 11%. Google Cloud revenue more than doubled to $30.71 billion, driven by demand for AI infrastructure and enterprise AI solutions. Pichai said the company was working to bring more capacity online to meet long-term demand. “We had a strong quarter and are now on a half-trillion dollar revenue run rate,” he said. “Our deep full stack approach is driving momentum across the business, with Alphabet revenues growing 25% year-over year.” The Gemini app has reached one billion users, according to Pichai, while Google's first-party model APIs are processing nearly 32 billion tokens per minute, more than four times the volume a year earlier. The company is investing heavily to support this growth. Alphabet's capital expenditure reached $51.4 billion in the quarter, primarily reflecting spending on data centres and AI infrastructure. It maintained its 2026 capital expenditure outlook of $195 billion to $205 billion and said spending would increase significantly in 2027. Net income available to common stockholders fell 25% to $26.17 billion. Alphabet attributed the decline in part to an $8.7 billion net loss on equity securities, highlighting that the profit movement was not solely a reflection of its operating performance. The next test for Google's advertising model Google's AI Mode rollout is part of a wider effort to extend its commercial ecosystem into new forms of discovery and task completion.

extraction.body: Google is expanding advertising in its AI-powered Search experience, AI Mode, to India and nine other markets. The company is looking to build new commercial opportunities around conversational search while protecting the growth of its core advertising business. The expansion, announced alongside Alphabet’s third-quarter 2026 results, will bring ads in AI Mode to Australia, Canada, India, Kenya, Malaysia, New Zealand, Nigeria, Pakistan, the Philippines and Singapore. Google plans to extend the rollout to Brazil, Mexico and the United Kingdom in the fourth quarter. In the US, it is introducing multiturn ads that can appear in follow-up queries within AI Mode. The move comes as Google Search advertising growth moderates even as usage of its AI-powered features increases. Search and other advertising revenue rose 12% year on year to $63.35 billion in the September quarter, compared with 17% growth in the previous quarter. YouTube advertising revenue increased 9.2% to $11.21 billion, while total Google advertising revenue grew 10.6% to $82.01 billion. AI Mode allows users to explore questions through longer, more conversational interactions, creating a different environment for product discovery and commercial intent than a conventional search results page. From search results to conversational discovery Google said queries in AI Mode are, on average, three times longer than traditional Search queries. The company believes AI helps it understand what users are looking for and connect them with businesses and services that match their needs. Google said its research indicates that users find ads in AI Mode relevant and that click-through rates for sponsored and organic product-list items are already similar. The expansion signals Google's intention to bring advertising into more of the AI-assisted journey, rather than limit monetisation to conventional search results. Longer queries can give the system more context about what a user wants, potentially creating opportunities for advertisers to reach consumers as they compare products, evaluate options or narrow down a purchase. However, the company has not disclosed how much revenue AI Mode advertising currently generates or how much it expects the international rollout to contribute. Pichai says AI is driving Search usage to a five-year high The advertising push comes against a broader backdrop of AI-led growth across Alphabet. On the company's Q3 earnings call, Google and Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai said Search was seeing strong momentum, with AI investments driving higher usage and growth in overall queries, including commercial queries. “Our AI investments are driving overall Search query growth, including commercial queries. In fact, our year-over-year query growth rate is the highest it’s been in the last five years,” Pichai said. He described the company's strategy as building a seamless experience across AI Overviews, AI Mode and traditional Search, as users increasingly adopt new ways of finding information. Their queries are longer, personalized, and multimodal,” he said. Pichai added that one in five AI Mode searches globally involves voice, images or documents, while Google now handles more than 50 billion visual searches a month. These shifts matter commercially because Google's advertising model has historically depended on matching search queries with relevant ads. As the interface evolves from a list of links towards AI-generated responses and more extended interactions, the company needs to determine how advertising fits into those experiences and how it can deliver value to businesses. Alphabet's growth increasingly spans advertising and AI infrastructure Alphabet reported third-quarter revenue of $127.58 billion, up 25% year on year. Google Services, which includes Search, YouTube, subscriptions and devices, generated $96.3 billion, an increase of 11%. Google Cloud revenue more than doubled to $30.71 billion, driven by demand for AI infrastructure and enterprise AI solutions. Pichai said the company was working to bring more capacity online to meet long-term demand. “We had a strong quarter and are now on a half-trillion dollar revenue run rate,” he said. “Our deep full stack approach is driving momentum across the business, with Alphabet revenues growing 25% year-over year.” The Gemini app has reached one billion users, according to Pichai, while Google's first-party model APIs are processing nearly 32 billion tokens per minute, more than four times the volume a year earlier. The company is investing heavily to support this growth. Alphabet's capital expenditure reached $51.4 billion in the quarter, primarily reflecting spending on data centres and AI infrastructure. It maintained its 2026 capital expenditure outlook of $195 billion to $205 billion and said spending would increase significantly in 2027. Net income available to common stockholders fell 25% to $26.17 billion. Alphabet attributed the decline in part to an $8.7 billion net loss on equity securities, highlighting that the profit movement was not solely a reflection of its operating performance. The next test for Google's advertising model Google's AI Mode rollout is part of a wider effort to extend its commercial ecosystem into new forms of discovery and task completion.

sources.title: Amazon updates Alexa to help you manage shopping lists and subscriptions and update delivery instructions
passages: Ahead of the holiday season, Amazon has added more than 100 new shopping-related capabilities to Alexa, including managing subscriptions and lists, updating delivery instructions, solving payment issues, and answering questions about Prime subscriptions.
The update allows you to use Alexa to create lists, register them, see what’s on them, and add or edit items.

You can also manage subscriptions with the AI bot — for example, you could ask it to change deliveries for an item to every three months instead of every month — and edit delivery instructions, such as change an address or add drop-off details.
The company said that since the start of the year, the number of people using agentic features has grown 8x, and over the last 12 months, over 400 million consumers have used Alexa for shopping.
Amazon has launched various AI-centric shopping features this year, including a shopping assistant and a way to notify users about new products and offers .

For example, if you use Amazon’s Subscribe & Save service, you can simply ask Alexa to skip your next delivery, pause a subscription, or change how frequently an item arrives. You can also find out how much money you’ve saved through Amazon Prime this year or check when your Audible subscription renews. You can tell Alexa to update your delivery instructions, check your gift card balance, find out where a refund is, or get help with an unfamiliar charge. You can access the updated assistant through the Alexa icon in the Amazon Shopping app or on Amazon’s desktop website. DoorDash has announced that it is acquiring grocery giant Instacart at an equity valuation of $17 billion, in a cash-and-stock deal. Subject to regulatory and shareholder approvals, the deal is expected to close by the end of 2027 or in the first half of 2028. DoorDash claims that, thanks to the deal, customers will have the flexibility to buy daily essentials from more stores, which also increases their chances of getting bargain deals and faster deliveries. “The combined company will offer grocers and retailers of every size DoorDash’s delivery network and Instacart’s grocery and fulfillment technology, in both apps and on stores’ own websites, along with the advertising and AI tools each company has built,” the company said in a press statement. For an average customer, there are a couple of tangible benefits emerging from this multi-billion dollar deal. AI psychic readings are available around the clock, and human practitioners are having to explain why customers should still pay to speak with them. The Guardian found psychics responding with AI-free promises and arguments that chatbots lack the human connection central to their work. Google Chrome's autofill has always been pretty handy for filling in addresses, passwords, and payment information. Now, the feature could be getting ever better thanks to better integration with Gmail. The company will soon allow the browser to dig through your Gmail inbox and pull out information you would otherwise spend several minutes hunting for. According to Google's official announcement, Chrome's enhanced autofill can now use Gemini with Personal Intelligence to retrieve order numbers, package tracking details, and flight booking information directly from Gmail. extraction.body: Personally identifiable information belonging to thousands of U.S. Department of Homeland Security employees has been published online after a hacker stole reams of data in a previously undisclosed breach at the government department earlier this year. The breach includes names, job titles, and work contact information, such as email addresses, cell phone numbers, and office locations, of more than 40,000 people who work for the federal department, including border and immigration agents, cybersecurity staffers, and senior department officials. A hacker who goes by the handle Department of Peace claimed they obtained the data from an Okta single sign-on system used by Homeland Security to allow employees and contractors across its various agencies to log in to its central network. The Okta system also contains IT and log-in records associated with the employees’ user account, including details about which systems and internal apps they are permitted to access. More than half of the dataset — some 21,000 records — relate to employees with U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), who work at airports and other ports of entry. The data also contains records associated with another 10,000 employees of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and its Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) unit, and just under a 1,000 employees who work at U.S. cybersecurity defense agency CISA. Thousands of additional records relate to staff who work at the department’s headquarters and its other agencies, including U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services and the Federal Protective Service. “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs,” said Department of Peace in a note left with the data, which TechCrunch has seen. The hacker did not respond to TechCrunch’s email requesting comment and with questions about how the breach was carried out. This is the latest data breach to hit the U.S. government in recent months, following earlier hacks involving the theft of thousands of FBI agents’ personnel records and the personal information of millions of serving and former military service personnel from the Pentagon’s human resources unit . It’s also the second breach involving Homeland Security this year, after the same hacker claimed to have taken thousands of contracts between the department and the private sector, including defense contractors and surveillance vendors. The latest batch of breached data, which appears authentic, offers a rare — albeit incomplete — view into the scale and operations of Homeland Security, whose deportations, arbitrary detentions, and killings of U.S. citizens under its leadership have become a key issue for voters ahead of the upcoming U.S. midterm elections. The stolen Homeland Security data was provided to journalist and hacker maia arson crimew, who then shared a copy with DDoSecrets , a nonprofit collective that hosts leaked datasets in the public interest. TechCrunch verified a portion of the data as authentic by matching the names of several known Homeland Security employees against an offline copy of the database. The thousands of employee directory records appear to have been exfiltrated around mid-August, according to the timestamps on each person’s record. The number of leaked records is equivalent to about one-fifth of Homeland Security’s workforce, which totals around 220,000 staff . It’s unclear whether the vulnerability that allowed the breach has been fixed or if Homeland Security is aware of the data theft. A spokesperson for Homeland Security told TechCrunch after publication: “DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively. We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected. We will update the public when more information is available.” When reached, Okta said it was aware of this report. “Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised,” a spokesperson said. While the leaked data includes identifiable information about agents and officers, the dataset also reveals more about the surveillance technologies and cybersecurity tools that Homeland Security employees may be able to access. Critics have called for investigations into tech companies that fund or provide their technology to ICE. The leaked data contains information about employees’ membership in user groups within the department’s Active Directory, a system that controls access to the department’s internal tools, services, and third-party offerings used for work. Most of the Homeland Security employees in the dataset were members of the user group that had access to Microsoft 365, the tech giant’s cloud service that hosts the agency’s emails and files, as well as user groups for accessing Adobe Acrobat, Citrix, and other typical desktop software. The data also shows that around 4,500 users, including ICE agents and deportation officers, are members of a group called “Headspace_users.” Online therapy provider Headspace previously had an $82,500 federal contract with ICE that ended in 2023 to fund “mental health software required for ERO employees,” a reference to ICE’s deportation unit. A spokesperson for Headspace said the company has not provided any services to DHS or ICE since 2023. Dozens of other user groups reference Penlink , a web surveillance company that makes technology it claims can track the location data of hundreds of millions of mobile devices. Penlink has had a contract with ICE for years. The user groups vary in size, from a handful of users in local Homeland Security offices around the country to more than 2,000 users across ICE’s HSI unit nationally. One group specifically references Penlink PLX, which the company says is used to capture and analyze “real-time intelligence” from phone calls, texts, web activity, and social media. A spokesperson for Penlink did not respond to a request for comment. One user group also includes more than 200 CBP users associated with Mobile Fortify, a facial-recognition app used by both CBP and ICE agents to identify people and verify their information and immigration status . The user groups also include several employees associated with ChatGPT access, including senior DHS officials, as well as other groups associated with investigations into the China-backed hacking groups known as Salt Typhoon and Volt Typhoon. Researchers and public information advocates say that the exposed data could provide valuable leads for investigations into alleged abuses by the Trump administration, such as identifying email addresses of agents that can be used in public records requests under the Freedom of Information Act. “Email addresses and phone numbers are indispensable tools for FOIA researchers, often making the difference between a vague records request that gets stonewalled and one that gets results,” said Ryan Shapiro, the executive director of transparency nonprofit Property of the People. “Given the Trump administration’s contempt for even basic transparency, the need for such tools is urgent,” said Shapiro. DDoSecrets co-founder and journalist Emma Best said that the exposed Homeland Security data will be a “catalyst for investigations, empowering journalists, Congressional inquiries, legal challenges, community action and Freedom of Information Act requests.” Zack Whittaker is the security editor at TechCrunch. He also authors the weekly cybersecurity newsletter, this week in security . He can be reached via encrypted message at zackwhittaker.1337 on Signal. You can also contact him by email, or to verify outreach, at [email protected] . The breach includes names, job titles, and work contact information, such as email addresses, cell phone numbers, and office locations, of more than 40,000 people who work for the federal department, including border and immigration agents, cybersecurity staffers, and senior department officials.

A hacker who goes by the handle Department of Peace claimed they obtained the data from an Okta single sign-on system used by Homeland Security to allow employees and contractors across its various agencies to log in to its central network. The Okta system also contains IT and log-in records associated with the employees’ user account, including details about which systems and internal apps they are permitted to access.
More than half of the dataset — some 21,000 records — relate to employees with U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), who work at airports and other ports of entry.

The data also contains records associated with another 10,000 employees of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and its Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) unit, and just under a 1,000 employees who work at U.S. cybersecurity defense agency CISA.

Thousands of additional records relate to staff who work at the department’s headquarters and its other agencies, including U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services and the Federal Protective Service.

“They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs,” said Department of Peace in a note left with the data, which TechCrunch has seen. The hacker did not respond to TechCrunch’s email requesting comment and with questions about how the breach was carried out.

This is the latest data breach to hit the U.S. government in recent months, following earlier hacks involving the theft of thousands of FBI agents’ personnel records and the personal information of millions of serving and former military service personnel from the Pentagon’s human resources unit . It’s also the second breach involving Homeland Security this year, after the same hacker claimed to have taken thousands of contracts between the department and the private sector, including defense contractors and surveillance vendors.

The latest batch of breached data, which appears authentic, offers a rare — albeit incomplete — view into the scale and operations of Homeland Security, whose deportations, arbitrary detentions, and killings of U.S. citizens under its leadership have become a key issue for voters ahead of the upcoming U.S. midterm elections.

The stolen Homeland Security data was provided to journalist and hacker maia arson crimew, who then shared a copy with DDoSecrets , a nonprofit collective that hosts leaked datasets in the public interest.

TechCrunch verified a portion of the data as authentic by matching the names of several known Homeland Security employees against an offline copy of the database. The thousands of employee directory records appear to have been exfiltrated around mid-August, according to the timestamps on each person’s record. The number of leaked records is equivalent to about one-fifth of Homeland Security’s workforce, which totals around 220,000 staff .
It’s unclear whether the vulnerability that allowed the breach has been fixed or if Homeland Security is aware of the data theft.

A spokesperson for Homeland Security told TechCrunch after publication: “DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively. We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected. We will update the public when more information is available.”
When reached, Okta said it was aware of this report. “Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised,” a spokesperson said.

While the leaked data includes identifiable information about agents and officers, the dataset also reveals more about the surveillance technologies and cybersecurity tools that Homeland Security employees may be able to access. Critics have called for investigations into tech companies that fund or provide their technology to ICE.

The leaked data contains information about employees’ membership in user groups within the department’s Active Directory, a system that controls access to the department’s internal tools, services, and third-party offerings used for work.

Most of the Homeland Security employees in the dataset were members of the user group that had access to Microsoft 365, the tech giant’s cloud service that hosts the agency’s emails and files, as well as user groups for accessing Adobe Acrobat, Citrix, and other typical desktop software.

The data also shows that around 4,500 users, including ICE agents and deportation officers, are members of a group called “Headspace_users.” Online therapy provider Headspace previously had an $82,500 federal contract with ICE that ended in 2023 to fund “mental health software required for ERO employees,” a reference to ICE’s deportation unit.
A spokesperson for Headspace said the company has not provided any services to DHS or ICE since 2023.

Dozens of other user groups reference Penlink , a web surveillance company that makes technology it claims can track the location data of hundreds of millions of mobile devices. Penlink has had a contract with ICE for years. The user groups vary in size, from a handful of users in local Homeland Security offices around the country to more than 2,000 users across ICE’s HSI unit nationally. One group specifically references Penlink PLX, which the company says is used to capture and analyze “real-time intelligence” from phone calls, texts, web activity, and social media.
A spokesperson for Penlink did not respond to a request for comment.

One user group also includes more than 200 CBP users associated with Mobile Fortify, a facial-recognition app used by both CBP and ICE agents to identify people and verify their information and immigration status .

The user groups also include several employees associated with ChatGPT access, including senior DHS officials, as well as other groups associated with investigations into the China-backed hacking groups known as Salt Typhoon and Volt Typhoon.

Researchers and public information advocates say that the exposed data could provide valuable leads for investigations into alleged abuses by the Trump administration, such as identifying email addresses of agents that can be used in public records requests under the Freedom of Information Act.

“Email addresses and phone numbers are indispensable tools for FOIA researchers, often making the difference between a vague records request that gets stonewalled and one that gets results,” said Ryan Shapiro, the executive director of transparency nonprofit Property of the People.
“Given the Trump administration’s contempt for even basic transparency, the need for such tools is urgent,” said Shapiro.

DDoSecrets co-founder and journalist Emma Best said that the exposed Homeland Security data will be a “catalyst for investigations, empowering journalists, Congressional inquiries, legal challenges, community action and Freedom of Information Act requests.”
Zack Whittaker is the security editor at TechCrunch. He also authors the weekly cybersecurity newsletter, this week in security .
He can be reached via encrypted message at zackwhittaker.1337 on Signal. You can also contact him by email, or to verify outreach, at [email protected] .

extraction.body: The records, which span DHS itself as well as seven component agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement and US Customs and Border Protection, were last updated on August 19, 2026. The transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets and cybersecurity researcher and journalist maia arson crimew previewed the data for WIRED, which they say they obtained from a group calling itself the Department of Peace. In a press release, DDoSecrets says the data is from DHS's Okta login system. In a note with the files, the hackers wrote, “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs.” An Okta spokesperson tells WIRED that it is unaware of any breach of its systems. Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised,” the spokesperson says. The leak comes as DHS has aggressively pursued its critics, seeking to unmask anonymous social media users, obtain customer records on protesters, and secure warrants for surveillance tools aimed at reporters. The leak follows a breach in which a group of hackers known as ShinyHunters claimed to have stolen personal information on nearly every FBI employee and their families. Law enforcement agencies have arrested several suspects and detained another who is alleged to be part of the group. The DHS records are searchable on a website crimew built. “I don't think we should let them scare us into not looking into them,” she tells WIRED. “DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively,” a Homeland Security spokesperson tells WIRED. “We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected. We will update the public when more information is available.” The DOJ did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment. According to a WIRED analysis of the data, CBP staffers account for more than half of the records. ICE accounts for about 10,000, roughly a third of them in Homeland Security Investigations, ICE’s investigative wing. Another 6,200 belong to US Citizenship and Immigration Services, and nearly 1,000 are tied to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, more than half of them contractors. Altogether, the files cover about a seventh of DHS’s workforce, revealing how DHS is structured, from senior leadership down to individual immigration agents and detention contractors. Like most large organizations, DHS uses permission groups to control access to internal systems, according to the leaked records. Nearly everyone named in the leak has access to at least some of these systems. At HSI, 39 employees across more than a dozen field offices belong to groups whose names include “CUC,” which government court filings say stands for “certified undercover operation.” Another group, apparently based in HSI's St. Paul, Minnesota, area of operations, references "Keyhole," which federal court filings describe as a certified undercover operation that recently funded HSI’s undercover surveillance of Minneapolis protest groups earlier this year. Others reference a “Communications Intercept Center TechOps (CICTO) Program,” a “Title III Intercept Program” for wiretaps, and an “Illicit Sensor Intercept Program (ISIP).” The names of the groups—there are over 55,000 in all—appear to reference tools for accessing immigration court records, pulling data from seized phones, and conducting surveillance. These include Palantir’s Falcon investigative platform and PenLink, which analyzes phone records and social media. Two permission groups, named “Executive Leadership” and “AI Access,” appear to list people given exceptions to DHS's web filter, which blocks some websites for employees. They contain the same 13 people, including former DHS head Kristi Noem; Antoine McCord, the recently departed DHS chief information officer who has returned to defense tech company Anduril; Philip Hegseth, listed as a senior adviser to the DHS secretary and the younger brother of defense secretary Pete Hegseth; and Jayce Krachenfels, listed as a policy adviser, who previously worked as a regional field director for Donald Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, according to his LinkedIn profile. Noem, McCord, Hegseth, and Krachenfels did not respond to a request for comment Other groups named in the leak reference AI tools, including OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, and Microsoft’s Copilot. One, called “Grok.com,” includes eight DHS technology officials, including the department’s former chief information officer and chief data officer. “If authentic and current, this is an extraordinarily valuable intelligence resource for those seeking to penetrate DHS,” says Alexander Leslie, a national security expert at the threat intelligence company Recorded Future. “This dataset becomes way more valuable when correlated with previously compromised information, commercial data, and other intelligence collections. An adversary could spend months exploiting these relationships to identify vulnerable personnel, develop convincing impersonation attempts, or compromise ongoing investigations.” More than 700 accounts are associated with a group apparently referencing Signal, the encrypted messaging app, nearly all belonging to CBP personnel. More than 200 CBP accounts belong to a group referencing Mobile Fortify, a face-recognition app that immigration agents use to identify people. The group includes field supervisors, special response team operators, and tactical and intelligence agents. Nearly 20 accounts appear to belong to personnel with the Department of Defense, which the administration styles as the Department of War; eight are in a group titled “ICE Tip Line DOW Surge.” About 170 accounts are listed as providing “military processing support” at ICE facilities, and 35 others explicitly identify National Guard members. Dozens of accounts have job titles like “Designated Immigration Officer” and “287(g) Officer,” which mark local law enforcement personnel authorized to carry out some immigration enforcement duties. The records also include roughly 4,400 “associates,” whose jobs range from IT developers and data scientists to nurses and detention officers. Of those, 145 are named as a “contractor” or “high risk contractor.” More than 300 records reference senior titles associated with DHS headquarters, from Noem down through deputy undersecretaries, assistant secretaries, and chiefs of staff to officials overseeing intelligence, technology, biometrics, and privacy.

extraction.body: Information released by Distributed Denial of Secrets is the third such government data disclosure in the last month Information released by Distributed Denial of Secrets is the third such government data disclosure in the last month Data identifying more than 41,000 employees and contractors for the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) was released on Wednesday in an unprecedented leak that reveals how the agency is organized. The records, which were made public by the transparency non-profit Distributed Denial of Secrets, reference operation names, surveillance programs and information on undercover initiatives. The DHS did not immediately return a message seeking comment. The leaked data unveils the ​names, phone numbers and email addresses of employees from various DHS agencies, including Immigration ‌and Customs Enforcement (ICE), Customs and Border ‌Protection (CBP), Homeland Security Investigations and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. Most of the agents in the leak – more than 21,000 – work for CBP, and about 6,600 work for ICE. The data also includes job titles, email groups and other details that show which agents were assigned to special operations, surveillance jobs, computer forensics and undercover work. It was made public at a time when the DHS, in turn, has aggressively sought to unmask critics on social media, and obtain records on protestors and journalists – even as it moves to keep its own agents anonymous, defending their right to hide their identities and faces while conducting enforcement. In a statement, Emma Best, a Distributed Denial of Secrets co-founder, said the hacktivist known as “maia arson crimew” developed a search tool for the data that would allow the public to browse it. Best said the tool would “replace anonymity with accountability” and empower journalists, guide public records requests and boost congressional oversight. The disclosure – which the ⁠non-profit data transparency group says draws ⁠on information obtained ​by an entity calling itself “the Department of Peace” – is the third government data leak to have made headlines in the past month. The Department of Peace did not immediately respond ‌to a request for comment, but in a statement included with the data, it said that DHS employees “have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs” and that it hoped the data “can ​be used to limit further harm by the DHS and supports all efforts in that direction”. In September, the hacking group ShinyHunters claimed ⁠the theft of a massive trove of data from the Federal Bureau of Investigation, including sensitive job details and medical information from thousands of bureau employees. Last week, the defense department was hit with ⁠a class action lawsuit following a breach that exposed data on millions of current and former military personnel. The Department of Peace in March claimed responsibility for hacking the DHS and posting documents related to contracts with outside vendors. Best’s statement said the Department of Peace harvested the data from the Okta sign-on service used by the DHS. Reuters could not immediately corroborate the claim. Okta said in response to a Reuters query: “Okta is ⁠secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised.” Reuters could not immediately ​verify the authenticity of the entire data ​trove but it was able to match ​personal information of about six DHS employees named in the leak to credit bureau records and breach data ​carried by the dark ‌web intelligence platform District 4 ​Labs. In other cases, ​Reuters called three DHS employees directly and was able to confirm their phone numbers and other details. One said it was the first they had heard of a breach. In several cases, the data tracked information available on DHS employees’ LinkedIn profiles. But in others, the data revealed nonpublic data about internal DHS organization charts or previously undisclosed programs or operations.

Most of the agents in the leak – more than 21,000 – work for CBP, and about 6,600 work for ICE. The data also comprised job titles, email groups and other details that show which agents were assigned to special operations, surveillance jobs, computer forensics and undercover work. What makes it concerning is the fact that the DHS has been aggressively seeking to unmask critics on social media and obtain records on protesters and journalists as it keeps its own employees' and agents' identities anonymous. Why they did it In a statement on the matter, Emma Best, a Distributed Denial of Secrets co-founder, said the hacktivist known as “maia arson crimew” developed a search tool for the data that would allow the public to browse it. Best maintained that the tool would “replace anonymity with accountability”, empower journalists, guide public records requests, and boost congressional oversight. In a statement on Wednesday, the Department of Peace noted that the DHS employees “have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs” and that it hoped the data “can ​be used to limit further harm by the DHS and supports all efforts in that direction”. It is pertinent to note that this is the third government data leak to have made headlines in the past month. In September this year, the hacking group ShinyHunters claimed ⁠the theft of a massive trove of data from the Federal Bureau of Investigation, which included sensitive job details along with medical information of thousands of bureau employees. Last week, the Department of Defence faced a major class action lawsuit following a breach that exposed data on millions of current and former military personnel. Soon after the leak, the Department of Homeland Security released a statement, insisting that it was "aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively." The agency said it was working to ensure its employees were properly protected and would update the public "when more information is available.”

coreStoryFacts.text: This is the latest data breach to hit the U.S. government in recent months, following earlier hacks involving the theft of thousands of FBI agents’ personnel records and the personal information of millions of serving and former military service personnel from the Pentagon’s human resources unit .
TechCrunch verified a portion of the data as authentic by matching the names of several known Homeland Security employees against an offline copy of the database.
The number of leaked records is equivalent to about one-fifth of Homeland Security’s workforce, which totals around 220,000 staff .
Critics have called for investigations into tech companies that fund or provide their technology to ICE.
A spokesperson for Homeland Security told TechCrunch after publication: “DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively.
We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected.
We will update the public when more information is available.”
The Okta system also contains IT and log-in records associated with the employees’ user account, including details about which systems and internal apps they are permitted to access.
Penlink has had a contract with ICE for years.
One group specifically references Penlink PLX, which the company says is used to capture and analyze “real-time intelligence” from phone calls, texts, web activity, and social media.

One user group also includes more than 200 CBP users associated with Mobile Fortify, a facial-recognition app used by both CBP and ICE agents to identify people and verify their information and immigration status .

The stolen Homeland Security data was provided to journalist and hacker maia arson crimew, who then shared a copy with DDoSecrets , a nonprofit collective that hosts leaked datasets in the public interest.
“They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs,” said Department of Peace in a note left with the data, which TechCrunch has seen.
The hacker did not respond to TechCrunch’s email requesting comment and with questions about how the breach was carried out.
Zack Whittaker is the security editor at TechCrunch.
More than half of the dataset — some 21,000 records — relate to employees with U.S.
Customs and Border Protection (CBP), who work at airports and other ports of entry.

The user groups also include several employees associated with ChatGPT access, including senior DHS officials, as well as other groups associated with investigations into the China-backed hacking groups known as Salt Typhoon and Volt Typhoon.
“DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively,” a Homeland Security spokesperson tells WIRED.
ICE accounts for about 10,000, roughly a third of them in Homeland Security Investigations, ICE’s investigative wing.

Noem, McCord, Hegseth, and Krachenfels did not respond to a request for comment Other groups named in the leak reference AI tools, including OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, and Microsoft’s Copilot.

Data identifying more than 41,000 employees and contractors for the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) was released on Wednesday in an unprecedented leak that reveals how the agency is organized.

The disclosure – which the ⁠non-profit data transparency group says draws ⁠on information obtained ​by an entity calling itself “the Department of Peace” – is the third government data leak to have made headlines in the past month.

The leaked data unveils the ​names, phone numbers and email addresses of employees from various DHS agencies, including Immigration ‌and Customs Enforcement (ICE), Customs and Border ‌Protection (CBP), Homeland Security Investigations and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.

extraction.body: Personally identifiable information belonging to thousands of U.S. Department of Homeland Security employees has been published online after a hacker stole reams of data in a previously undisclosed breach at the government department earlier this year. The breach includes names, job titles, and work contact information, such as email addresses, cell phone numbers, and office locations, of more than 40,000 people who work for the federal department, including border and immigration agents, cybersecurity staffers, and senior department officials. A hacker who goes by the handle Department of Peace claimed they obtained the data from an Okta single sign-on system used by Homeland Security to allow employees and contractors across its various agencies to log in to its central network. The Okta system also contains IT and log-in records associated with the employees’ user account, including details about which systems and internal apps they are permitted to access. More than half of the dataset — some 21,000 records — relate to employees with U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), who work at airports and other ports of entry. The data also contains records associated with another 10,000 employees of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and its Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) unit, and just under a 1,000 employees who work at U.S. cybersecurity defense agency CISA. Thousands of additional records relate to staff who work at the department’s headquarters and its other agencies, including U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services and the Federal Protective Service. “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs,” said Department of Peace in a note left with the data, which TechCrunch has seen. The hacker did not respond to TechCrunch’s email requesting comment and with questions about how the breach was carried out. This is the latest data breach to hit the U.S. government in recent months, following earlier hacks involving the theft of thousands of FBI agents’ personnel records and the personal information of millions of serving and former military service personnel from the Pentagon’s human resources unit . It’s also the second breach involving Homeland Security this year, after the same hacker claimed to have taken thousands of contracts between the department and the private sector, including defense contractors and surveillance vendors. The thousands of employee directory records appear to have been exfiltrated around mid-August, according to the timestamps on each person’s record. The number of leaked records is equivalent to about one-fifth of Homeland Security’s workforce, which totals around 220,000 staff . It’s unclear whether the vulnerability that allowed the breach has been fixed or if Homeland Security is aware of the data theft. Critics have called for investigations into tech companies that fund or provide their technology to ICE. Most of the Homeland Security employees in the dataset were members of the user group that had access to Microsoft 365, the tech giant’s cloud service that hosts the agency’s emails and files, as well as user groups for accessing Adobe Acrobat, Citrix, and other typical desktop software. A spokesperson for Headspace said the company has not provided any services to DHS or ICE since 2023. Dozens of other user groups reference Penlink , a web surveillance company that makes technology it claims can track the location data of hundreds of millions of mobile devices. Penlink has had a contract with ICE for years. One group specifically references Penlink PLX, which the company says is used to capture and analyze “real-time intelligence” from phone calls, texts, web activity, and social media. One user group also includes more than 200 CBP users associated with Mobile Fortify, a facial-recognition app used by both CBP and ICE agents to identify people and verify their information and immigration status . The user groups also include several employees associated with ChatGPT access, including senior DHS officials, as well as other groups associated with investigations into the China-backed hacking groups known as Salt Typhoon and Volt Typhoon.
