extraction.body: The records, which span DHS itself as well as seven component agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement and US Customs and Border Protection, were last updated on August 19, 2026. The transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets and cybersecurity researcher and journalist maia arson crimew previewed the data for WIRED, which they say they obtained from a group calling itself the Department of Peace. In a press release, DDoSecrets says the data is from DHS's Okta login system. In a note with the files, the hackers wrote, “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs.” An Okta spokesperson tells WIRED that it is unaware of any breach of its systems. Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised,” the spokesperson says. The leak comes as DHS has aggressively pursued its critics, seeking to unmask anonymous social media users, obtain customer records on protesters, and secure warrants for surveillance tools aimed at reporters. The leak follows a breach in which a group of hackers known as ShinyHunters claimed to have stolen personal information on nearly every FBI employee and their families. Law enforcement agencies have arrested several suspects and detained another who is alleged to be part of the group. The DHS records are searchable on a website crimew built. “I don't think we should let them scare us into not looking into them,” she tells WIRED. “DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively,” a Homeland Security spokesperson tells WIRED. “We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected. We will update the public when more information is available.” The DOJ did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment. According to a WIRED analysis of the data, CBP staffers account for more than half of the records. ICE accounts for about 10,000, roughly a third of them in Homeland Security Investigations, ICE’s investigative wing. Another 6,200 belong to US Citizenship and Immigration Services, and nearly 1,000 are tied to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, more than half of them contractors. Altogether, the files cover about a seventh of DHS’s workforce, revealing how DHS is structured, from senior leadership down to individual immigration agents and detention contractors. Like most large organizations, DHS uses permission groups to control access to internal systems, according to the leaked records. Nearly everyone named in the leak has access to at least some of these systems. At HSI, 39 employees across more than a dozen field offices belong to groups whose names include “CUC,” which government court filings say stands for “certified undercover operation.” Another group, apparently based in HSI's St. Paul, Minnesota, area of operations, references "Keyhole," which federal court filings describe as a certified undercover operation that recently funded HSI’s undercover surveillance of Minneapolis protest groups earlier this year. Others reference a “Communications Intercept Center TechOps (CICTO) Program,” a “Title III Intercept Program” for wiretaps, and an “Illicit Sensor Intercept Program (ISIP).” The names of the groups—there are over 55,000 in all—appear to reference tools for accessing immigration court records, pulling data from seized phones, and conducting surveillance. These include Palantir’s Falcon investigative platform and PenLink, which analyzes phone records and social media. Two permission groups, named “Executive Leadership” and “AI Access,” appear to list people given exceptions to DHS's web filter, which blocks some websites for employees. They contain the same 13 people, including former DHS head Kristi Noem; Antoine McCord, the recently departed DHS chief information officer who has returned to defense tech company Anduril; Philip Hegseth, listed as a senior adviser to the DHS secretary and the younger brother of defense secretary Pete Hegseth; and Jayce Krachenfels, listed as a policy adviser, who previously worked as a regional field director for Donald Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, according to his LinkedIn profile. Noem, McCord, Hegseth, and Krachenfels did not respond to a request for comment Other groups named in the leak reference AI tools, including OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, and Microsoft’s Copilot. One, called “Grok.com,” includes eight DHS technology officials, including the department’s former chief information officer and chief data officer. “If authentic and current, this is an extraordinarily valuable intelligence resource for those seeking to penetrate DHS,” says Alexander Leslie, a national security expert at the threat intelligence company Recorded Future. “This dataset becomes way more valuable when correlated with previously compromised information, commercial data, and other intelligence collections. An adversary could spend months exploiting these relationships to identify vulnerable personnel, develop convincing impersonation attempts, or compromise ongoing investigations.” More than 700 accounts are associated with a group apparently referencing Signal, the encrypted messaging app, nearly all belonging to CBP personnel. More than 200 CBP accounts belong to a group referencing Mobile Fortify, a face-recognition app that immigration agents use to identify people. The group includes field supervisors, special response team operators, and tactical and intelligence agents. Nearly 20 accounts appear to belong to personnel with the Department of Defense, which the administration styles as the Department of War; eight are in a group titled “ICE Tip Line DOW Surge.” About 170 accounts are listed as providing “military processing support” at ICE facilities, and 35 others explicitly identify National Guard members. Dozens of accounts have job titles like “Designated Immigration Officer” and “287(g) Officer,” which mark local law enforcement personnel authorized to carry out some immigration enforcement duties. The records also include roughly 4,400 “associates,” whose jobs range from IT developers and data scientists to nurses and detention officers. Of those, 145 are named as a “contractor” or “high risk contractor.” More than 300 records reference senior titles associated with DHS headquarters, from Noem down through deputy undersecretaries, assistant secretaries, and chiefs of staff to officials overseeing intelligence, technology, biometrics, and privacy.

The records, which were made public by the transparency non-profit Distributed Denial of Secrets, reference operation names, surveillance programs and information on undercover initiatives. The DHS did not immediately return a message seeking comment. The leaked data unveils the ​names, phone numbers and email addresses of employees from various DHS agencies, including Immigration ‌and Customs Enforcement (ICE), Customs and Border ‌Protection (CBP), Homeland Security Investigations and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. Most of the agents in the leak – more than 21,000 – work for CBP, and about 6,600 work for ICE. The data also includes job titles, email groups and other details that show which agents were assigned to special operations, surveillance jobs, computer forensics and undercover work. It was made public at a time when the DHS, in turn, has aggressively sought to unmask critics on social media, and obtain records on protestors and journalists – even as it moves to keep its own agents anonymous, defending their right to hide their identities and faces while conducting enforcement. In a statement, Emma Best, a Distributed Denial of Secrets co-founder, said the hacktivist known as “maia arson crimew” developed a search tool for the data that would allow the public to browse it. Best said the tool would “replace anonymity with accountability” and empower journalists, guide public records requests and boost congressional oversight. The disclosure – which the ⁠non-profit data transparency group says draws ⁠on information obtained ​by an entity calling itself “the Department of Peace” – is the third government data leak to have made headlines in the past month. The Department of Peace did not immediately respond ‌to a request for comment, but in a statement included with the data, it said that DHS employees “have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs” and that it hoped the data “can ​be used to limit further harm by the DHS and supports all efforts in that direction”. In September, the hacking group ShinyHunters claimed ⁠the theft of a massive trove of data from the Federal Bureau of Investigation, including sensitive job details and medical information from thousands of bureau employees. Last week, the defense department was hit with ⁠a class action lawsuit following a breach that exposed data on millions of current and former military personnel. The Department of Peace in March claimed responsibility for hacking the DHS and posting documents related to contracts with outside vendors. Best’s statement said the Department of Peace harvested the data from the Okta sign-on service used by the DHS. Reuters could not immediately corroborate the claim. Okta said in response to a Reuters query: “Okta is ⁠secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised.” Reuters could not immediately ​verify the authenticity of the entire data ​trove but it was able to match ​personal information of about six DHS employees named in the leak to credit bureau records and breach data ​carried by the dark ‌web intelligence platform District 4 ​Labs. In other cases, ​Reuters called three DHS employees directly and was able to confirm their phone numbers and other details. One said it was the first they had heard of a breach. In several cases, the data tracked information available on DHS employees’ LinkedIn profiles. But in others, the data revealed nonpublic data about internal DHS organization charts or previously undisclosed programs or operations.

The disclosure – which the ⁠non-profit data transparency group says draws ⁠on information obtained ​by an entity calling itself “the Department of Peace” – is the third government data leak to have made headlines in the past month.

In September, the hacking group ShinyHunters claimed ⁠the theft of a massive trove of data from the Federal Bureau of Investigation, including sensitive job details and medical information from thousands of bureau employees. Last week, the defense department was hit with ⁠a class action lawsuit following a breach that exposed data on millions of current and former military personnel.
The Department of Peace in March claimed responsibility for hacking the DHS and posting documents related to contracts with outside vendors.

In other cases, ​Reuters called three DHS employees directly and was able to confirm their phone numbers and other details. One said it was the first they had heard of a breach.

In several cases, the data tracked information available on DHS employees’ LinkedIn profiles. But in others, the data revealed nonpublic data about internal DHS organization charts or previously undisclosed programs or operations.

sources.title: Apple's Redesigned MacBook Pro Has An OLED Touchscreen, Weighs Just Three Pounds - Engadget
passages: The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR, as it's officially called, is powered by either an M5 Pro or M5 Max chip, just like the non-touch models.
And as a nice throwback to older Apple laptops, its rear Apple logo also lights up.
As part of the new design, the OLED MacBook Pro features a Dynamic Island around its webcam, and Apple claims the 14-inch model weighs just three pounds.
That's a noticeable difference from the current MacBook Pro, which clocks in at 3.4 pounds.
Apple finally announced its long-rumored redesign today, and for the most part, it seems like the company went out of its way to create its most premium laptop yet.
It's clearly not meant for a regular consumer.
And thankfully, you've still got a useful array of ports: three Thunderbolt 5 USB-C connections, MagSafe, HDMI, headphone jack and an SDXC card slot.
So what's the point of a touchscreen MacBook Pro?
It makes the simple act of casually scrolling through articles and content easier, as we've seen on touchscreen-equipped Windows PC over the last 15 years.
But in the demo video above, we can also see people swiping on media and manipulating 3D objects.
It also looks like you can interact with iOS apps just as they would with a phone, which would be particularly useful to developers.
Third-party creator apps like Notion, Canva, Powerpoint and Blender will also work with the touchscreen natively.
The ProLED XDR screen reaches up to 2,000 nits of peak brightness, according to Apple, and it features an "industry-leading" 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio.
I can only imagine the eye-searing possibilities with this screen.
It also features a 120Hz refresh rate, just like existing MacBook Pros.
Thanks to the slimmer bezels, Apple was also able to squeeze in larger 14.2-inch and 16.3-inch screens.

There's no doubt Apple is late here, but there was also a certain wisdom in completely separating its touchscreen platforms (iOS, iPadOS and watchOS) from macOS, a platform that was designed entirely around traditional computer inputs.
With Windows 8, Microsoft rushed to enable PC touchscreens as a way to compete with the potential rise of iPads.
Apple didn't have the same pressure — especially since its glass touchpads offer an incredibly smooth scrolling experience on Macs.

passages: Absurd prices aside, the launch marks a significant shift for Apple, nearly a decade after it first experimented with the Touch Bar .
The company eventually abandoned that feature, but now it’s ready to embrace a touchscreen MacBook Pro.
But if you want the absolute top-of-the-line model with every possible upgrade, prepare to cough up around $14,549.
As MacRumors first reported, Apple’s configurator prices the fully loaded 14-inch model at $14,249 and the 16-inch version at $14,549.
Both come equipped with Apple’s top-tier M5 Max chip, featuring an 18-core CPU and 40-core GPU.
For some perspective, the previous 16-inch MacBook Pro topped out at $10,149.
The new model raises that ceiling by a whopping $4,400.

These upgrades are aimed at demanding professional workloads, including video production, 3D work and other tasks involving large files or memory-intensive applications. However, their combined cost means buyers need to assess carefully whether they will use the additional capacity enough to justify the expense. Users can interact directly with content, manipulate creative projects and use touch-enabled controls in compatible applications. A redesigned hinge is intended to keep the display stable when users tap or swipe across it. The new models also bring Dynamic Island to the Mac, providing access to features including Spotlight, Live Activities and Siri AI. The launch is a notable departure for Apple, whose executives previously resisted touchscreen laptops. But the pricing raises a practical question: how many customers will pay the premium for direct screen interaction and the new display? Pre-orders opened on 28 October, with retail availability scheduled to begin on 6 November. For most buyers, the maximum configuration is unlikely to make financial sense unless their work genuinely demands that much memory and storage. The headline price nevertheless demonstrates how far Apple is willing to take its premium positioning as it adds touchscreen functionality to its professional laptop range. coreStoryFacts.text: This article Steve Jobs Thought They Were 'Ergonomically Terrible,' but Apple Is Reportedly Betting You'll Pay a Premium for the Touchscreen MacBook Pro originally appeared on Benzinga.com
Apple Inc. (NASDAQ) reportedly plans a $400 price increase for its new touch-integrated MacBook Pro models launching Wednesday at the "Pro and Tell" event.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR, as it's officially called, is powered by either an M5 Pro or M5 Max chip, just like the non-touch models.
And as a nice throwback to older Apple laptops, its rear Apple logo also lights up.
As part of the new design, the OLED MacBook Pro features a Dynamic Island around its webcam, and Apple claims the 14-inch model weighs just three pounds.
That's a noticeable difference from the current MacBook Pro, which clocks in at 3.4 pounds.
Apple finally announced its long-rumored redesign today, and for the most part, it seems like the company went out of its way to create its most premium laptop yet.
It's clearly not meant for a regular consumer.
And thankfully, you've still got a useful array of ports: three Thunderbolt 5 USB-C connections, MagSafe, HDMI, headphone jack and an SDXC card slot.
So what's the point of a touchscreen MacBook Pro?
It makes the simple act of casually scrolling through articles and content easier, as we've seen on touchscreen-equipped Windows PC over the last 15 years.
But in the demo video above, we can also see people swiping on media and manipulating 3D objects.
It also looks like you can interact with iOS apps just as they would with a phone, which would be particularly useful to developers.
Third-party creator apps like Notion, Canva, Powerpoint and Blender will also work with the touchscreen natively.
The ProLED XDR screen reaches up to 2,000 nits of peak brightness, according to Apple, and it features an "industry-leading" 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio.
I can only imagine the eye-searing possibilities with this screen.
It also features a 120Hz refresh rate, just like existing MacBook Pros.
Thanks to the slimmer bezels, Apple was also able to squeeze in larger 14.2-inch and 16.3-inch screens.

There's no doubt Apple is late here, but there was also a certain wisdom in completely separating its touchscreen platforms (iOS, iPadOS and watchOS) from macOS, a platform that was designed entirely around traditional computer inputs.
With Windows 8, Microsoft rushed to enable PC touchscreens as a way to compete with the potential rise of iPads.
Apple didn't have the same pressure — especially since its glass touchpads offer an incredibly smooth scrolling experience on Macs.
Absurd prices aside, the launch marks a significant shift for Apple, nearly a decade after it first experimented with the Touch Bar .
The company eventually abandoned that feature, but now it’s ready to embrace a touchscreen MacBook Pro.

extraction.body: Apple’s first touchscreen MacBook Pro has arrived with a price tag that pushes the company’s premium laptop strategy to a new extreme. While the new 14-inch model starts at $2,899 in the US, selecting the highest-end components for the 16-inch version can raise the total to $14,549. The figures, reported by TechCrunch following Apple’s launch on 28 October, highlight how expensive the new MacBook Pro range can become once buyers move beyond the standard configurations. The fully upgraded 14-inch model reaches $14,249, according to Apple’s online configurator pricing cited in the report. Storage is one of the biggest contributors to the final bill. According to TechCrunch, upgrading to a 4TB SSD adds $1,000, while the 8TB option costs an additional $3,000. Choosing the new 16TB maximum adds $7,000 to the configuration. The memory upgrade is similarly costly. Moving to 128GB of unified memory adds $2,000, while nano-texture glass carries a further $150 charge. These upgrades are aimed at demanding professional workloads, including video production, 3D work and other tasks involving large files or memory-intensive applications. However, their combined cost means buyers need to assess carefully whether they will use the additional capacity enough to justify the expense. The new 16-inch model’s $14,549 maximum is $4,400 higher than the previous 16-inch MacBook Pro’s reported top configuration of $10,149. That is a substantial increase for a product category that was already positioned at the premium end of the laptop market. The price increase accompanies a major change to the MacBook Pro’s display and interaction model. Apple’s new 14-inch and 16-inch machines introduce touchscreen support to the Mac for the first time, paired with a tandem OLED display marketed as PROLED XDR. Apple says the screen supports a 120Hz variable refresh rate, up to 2,000 nits of peak brightness and a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio. The display also supports both P3 and Adobe RGB colour spaces, features intended to appeal to photographers, designers and video professionals. The laptops use Apple’s M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, offer up to 128GB of unified memory and support storage configurations of up to 16TB. Apple also says the redesigned machines deliver up to 24 hours of battery life and feature a thinner, lighter enclosure. Touch input is designed to complement rather than replace the keyboard and trackpad. Users can interact directly with content, manipulate creative projects and use touch-enabled controls in compatible applications. A redesigned hinge is intended to keep the display stable when users tap or swipe across it. The new models also bring Dynamic Island to the Mac, providing access to features including Spotlight, Live Activities and Siri AI. The launch is a notable departure for Apple, whose executives previously resisted touchscreen laptops. But the pricing raises a practical question: how many customers will pay the premium for direct screen interaction and the new display? Reuters reported that PC makers shipped 33.4 million touchscreen notebooks in 2025, with an average selling price of about $1,009. That figure is far below even Apple’s entry-level touchscreen MacBook Pro price, placing the new machines in a much narrower market aimed at professionals and affluent enthusiasts. Apple’s US starting prices are $2,899 for the 14-inch M5 Pro model and $3,399 for the 16-inch M5Pro model. Higher-end M5 Max versions start at $4,499 and $4,799, respectively. Pre-orders opened on 28 October, with retail availability scheduled to begin on 6 November. For most buyers, the maximum configuration is unlikely to make financial sense unless their work genuinely demands that much memory and storage. The headline price nevertheless demonstrates how far Apple is willing to take its premium positioning as it adds touchscreen functionality to its professional laptop range. extraction.body: Additionally, the N1 chip brings Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. Apple has announced refreshes for the iMac and the entry-level, 14-inch MacBook Pro . Both machines are getting the M6 chip, which was introduced in the Mac mini several weeks ago. The M6 is split into two variants for the iMac. Picking the “M6 chip with two Thunderbolt ports” option gets you a 10-core CPU and a 10-core GPU, whereas picking “M6 chip with four Thunderbolt ports” gets you 12 cores for each, instead. The two-port variant maxes out at 24 GB of RAM and 1TB of storage, whereas the four-port one maxes out at 32GB of RAM and 2TB of storage. There’s only one M6 chip option for the MacBook Pro—the one with the 12-core GPU and CPU. It caps out at 32GB of RAM but can go to 4TB of storage. It’s a more substantial refresh for the iMac, as its previous update introduced the M4. Apple skipped the M5 and went straight to the M6 here. In terms of performance gains moving from the M4 to the M6, Apple said with the Mac mini that users can expect up to 40 percent faster CPU performance, up to double graphics performance, and nearly five times faster on-device AI. All that largely matches what we saw when we tested the M6 Mac mini last month, and users of the new iMac should expect similar numbers. The M6 iMac should see up to double SSD read/write performance compared to the M4 model, too. The previous entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pro had the M5, so that one is just stepping up a single generation. In this case, that means up to 30 percent faster graphics and up to double the Neural Engine performance. In addition to the M6 chip, both computers now have the N1 chip for wireless connectivity (that means Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6). The iMac is now configurable with up to 2.5Gb Ethernet, while the MacBook Pro still lacks an Ethernet port. There are no outward design changes to either device; they both look exactly the same as their immediate predecessors. The iMac starts at $1,499 for the two-port version, or $1,699 for the four-port version. The M6 MacBook Pro starts at $1,999. Preorders start October 28, and they ship November 6. This means the new MacBook Pro features three Thunderbolt 4 USB-C ports, a MagSafe 3 charging port, a full HDMI port, and an SD card slot.

The entry-level iMac starts at $1,500 and will be available to pre-order on October 28th, with shipping starting on November 6th.
Apple also recently revealed its A20-powered iPad mini .
At its upcoming event, the tech giant is expected to show off its long-rumored touchscreen MacBook for the first time.

The tech giant says the M6 features a 12-core CPU, paired with a 12-core GPU that delivers 30 percent faster graphics and 25 percent faster AI workload performance compared to last year's M5 chip. Interestingly, the company also compares the M6 to the M1 in its press release, highlighting that the newer, more powerful chip offers 11x faster graphics and up to 13x faster AI performance. Apple says that the M6 features a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, emphasizing that it's a powerful platform for local LLMs and that the chip is designed to take full advantage of Siri AI and Apple Intelligence. The MacBook M6 also features Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, alongside returning features like the 12-megapixel Center Stage camera and Liquid Retina XDR display with optional nano-texture. Beyond the bump up to the M6 chip, the entry-level 14-inch MacBook features the same overall design and port layout as last year's M5 upgrade and, in fact, the year prior's M4 refresh. This means the new MacBook Pro features three Thunderbolt 4 USB-C ports, a MagSafe 3 charging port, a full HDMI port, and an SD card slot. While this isn't exactly surprising, given Apple's MacBook Pro design has been around for several years now, it would have been nice to see it evolve in some way. Pricing for the 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro starts at $2,000 for the 16GB version, which matches last year's pricing. Pre-orders start on October 28th, with shipping beginning on November 6th. Apple also refreshed its all-in-one iMac with the M6 chip . This update comes two years after the colorful computer got the M4 chip (the iMac skipped the M5 series entirely). The base M6 configuration in the iMac features a 10-core CPU and a 10-core GPU, a step up from the 8-core M4 CPU in the last-generation iMac. There's also a more expensive 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU configuration Beyond the chip upgrade, there isn't much else new. The refreshed iMac features Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 like the new 14-inch MacBook Pro. It also has the same Thunderbolt ports as the M4 iMac — two on the 10-core and four on the 12-core. The colors are all the same too: Blue, Purple, Pink, Orange, Yellow, Green, and Silver. At the very least, it would have been great to see an iMac color refresh and a port selection that made a bit more sense. The entry-level iMac starts at $1,500 and will be available to pre-order on October 28th, with shipping starting on November 6th. The M6 MacBook Pro and iMac follow the M6 Mac Mini that Apple revealed earlier this year, which the company somewhat confusingly showed off alongside the M5 Max and M5 Ultra Mac Studio. The M6 is Apple's first 2nm chip and bumps up to a 12-core CPU from the M5's 10 cores. Apple also recently revealed its A20-powered iPad mini . At its upcoming event, the tech giant is expected to show off its long-rumored touchscreen MacBook for the first time. The redesigned tablet also features a thinner and lighter design. Usually the speed of the internet and connection at the time you are using it. Nobody really focuses on that. I'm sure my Antigravity work sessions would be improved greatly by a much better and consistent internet connection than a slightly faster processor in my Mac. Just food for thought.

Usually the speed of the internet and connection at the time you are using it. Nobody really focuses on that. extraction.body: Additionally, the N1 chip brings Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. Apple has announced refreshes for the iMac and the entry-level, 14-inch MacBook Pro . Both machines are getting the M6 chip, which was introduced in the Mac mini several weeks ago. The M6 is split into two variants for the iMac. Picking the “M6 chip with two Thunderbolt ports” option gets you a 10-core CPU and a 10-core GPU, whereas picking “M6 chip with four Thunderbolt ports” gets you 12 cores for each, instead. The two-port variant maxes out at 24 GB of RAM and 1TB of storage, whereas the four-port one maxes out at 32GB of RAM and 2TB of storage. There’s only one M6 chip option for the MacBook Pro—the one with the 12-core GPU and CPU. It caps out at 32GB of RAM but can go to 4TB of storage. It’s a more substantial refresh for the iMac, as its previous update introduced the M4. Apple skipped the M5 and went straight to the M6 here. In terms of performance gains moving from the M4 to the M6, Apple said with the Mac mini that users can expect up to 40 percent faster CPU performance, up to double graphics performance, and nearly five times faster on-device AI. All that largely matches what we saw when we tested the M6 Mac mini last month, and users of the new iMac should expect similar numbers. The M6 iMac should see up to double SSD read/write performance compared to the M4 model, too. The previous entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pro had the M5, so that one is just stepping up a single generation. In this case, that means up to 30 percent faster graphics and up to double the Neural Engine performance. In addition to the M6 chip, both computers now have the N1 chip for wireless connectivity (that means Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6). The iMac is now configurable with up to 2.5Gb Ethernet, while the MacBook Pro still lacks an Ethernet port. There are no outward design changes to either device; they both look exactly the same as their immediate predecessors. The iMac starts at $1,499 for the two-port version, or $1,699 for the four-port version. The M6 MacBook Pro starts at $1,999. Preorders start October 28, and they ship November 6. In addition to the M6 chip, both computers now have the N1 chip for wireless connectivity (that means Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6). The iMac is now configurable with up to 2.5Gb Ethernet, while the MacBook Pro still lacks an Ethernet port.

There are no outward design changes to either device; they both look exactly the same as their immediate predecessors. The iMac starts at $1,499 for the two-port version, or $1,699 for the four-port version. The M6 MacBook Pro starts at $1,999.
Preorders start October 28, and they ship November 6.

While this isn't exactly surprising, given Apple's MacBook Pro design has been around for several years now, it would have been nice to see it evolve in some way. At the very least, it would have been great to see an iMac color refresh and a port selection that made a bit more sense. The M6 MacBook Pro and iMac follow the M6 Mac Mini that Apple revealed earlier this year, which the company somewhat confusingly showed off alongside the M5 Max and M5 Ultra Mac Studio. I love my MacBook Pro M5 and hope it lasts me as long as my M1 did. What confuses me is why so much emphasis is put on the device's bigger, better performance, but most people are running most things online now, so the performance is surely about the weakest link... Usually the speed of the internet and connection at the time you are using it. Nobody really focuses on that. I'm sure my Antigravity work sessions would be improved greatly by a much better and consistent internet connection than a slightly faster processor in my Mac. Just food for thought.

sources.title: Apple launches M6 iMac, entry-level MacBook Pro ahead of touchscreen laptop - The Straits Times
passages: Apple has rolled out a new 24-inch iMac and an entry-level MacBook Pro with a 14-inch screen, marking key updates in an end-to-end overhaul of the company’s computer line.
Apple said the M6 chip makes the iMac five times faster than the prior model from 2024 for artificial intelligence, while the new MacBook Pro is 30% speedier than its predecessor for graphics.
Beyond the push into touchscreen displays, Apple is preparing a refreshed MacBook Neo and MacBook Air for the first half of 2027 .
It is planning an M7 Ultra and a new Mac Studio in 2028.
The company continues to sell higher-end M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pros, which have more advanced main processing and graphics cores compared with the entry M6 machines.

extraction.body: The updated iMac and low-end MacBook Pro become available for pre-ordering on Oct 28 and arrive beginning Nov 6. Apple has rolled out a new 24-inch iMac and an entry-level MacBook Pro with a 14-inch screen, marking key updates in an end-to-end overhaul of the company’s computer line. The new iMac and MacBook Pro, unveiled on Oct 27 , are visually similar to their predecessors – with the main changes happening internally. Both machines now include the M6 chip, which debuted in the Mac mini in September. The iMac is moving from an M4 processor, while the MacBook Pro received the M5 in 2025 . The updates represent a second day of Apple announcements this week, with the company rolling out a revamped iPad mini on Oct 26 with a new screen and water resistance. Apple will cap the launches on Oct 28 with its first MacBook Pro with a touchscreen, Bloomberg News has reported. The updated iMac and low-end MacBook Pro become available for pre-orders on Oct 28 and will arrive beginning Nov 6, Apple said, matching the new iPad mini. The new iMac starts at US$1,499 (S$1,920), while the MacBook Pro begins at US$1,999. Apple said the M6 chip makes the iMac five times faster than the prior model from 2024 for artificial intelligence, while the new MacBook Pro is 30% speedier than its predecessor for graphics. The company continues to sell higher-end M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pros, which have more advanced main processing and graphics cores compared with the entry M6 machines. The updated 14-inch MacBook Pro and iMac also include Bluetooth 6 and Wi-Fi 7, while the laptop gets faster charging. Both machines go on sale Nov. 6 after pre-orders open on Oct 28 . The new Macs come as part of a slew of changes to the company’s computer line. Beyond the push into touchscreen displays, Apple is preparing a refreshed MacBook Neo and MacBook Air for the first half of 2027 . The company is also working on a redesigned low-end MacBook Pro and the release of its first M7, M7 Pro and M7 Max chips in 2027. It is planning an M7 Ultra and a new Mac Studio in 2028. Apple’s overhauled MacBook Pro with a touchscreen – coming on Oct 28 – will include a lighter and slightly thinner design, slimmer bezels around the display and OLED technology, Bloomberg reported.

Concerns have been mounting everywhere about the environmental impact of data centers, with alarms ringing at various environmental think tanks. The Sierra Club, one of the oldest environmental preservation organizations in the U.S., has now put forth an estimate that by 2030, U.S. data center buildouts will be outputting as much carbon dioxide as the entirety of Mexico, pushing back progress on greenhouse gas reduction by 15 years, Bloomberg reports. The Club's principal advisor for climate and energy, Jeremy Fusher, puts it plainly: "the numbers continue to sort of boggle our minds." He's referring to an estimate that with the output from pending data center builds, the output from the U.S. power sector is set to put 2.1 billion metric tons of CO2 in the atmosphere by the end of the decade, an uptick of 42% compared to 2025 figures. The researchers' previous estimates were between a quarter and half of the current projections. An increasing number of countries and states are enacting laws demanding that new data center builds have a large portion of their power generated by green sources. However, those laws rarely apply retroactively, and oftentimes have a phase-in period. Even the Irish law on the matter demanding that new data centers be fed by 80% of renewable power only requires that that happens six years after they're powered up. In the current AI-driven market, speed of construction is king. Roughly 40% of U.S. data centers are fed by natural gas turbines , and the situation doesn't look like it'll be changing much. It'll likely get worse, as the addition of green sources almost assuredly won't keep up with demand. Much like RAM, GPUs, and storage, turbines were all slurped up by data centers. Their prices have risen by 50%, and production is backlogged for years, with one maker stating it's opening slots for production in 2032 . Having said all that, Brendan Pierpont from Energy Innovation, another climate-concerned organization, points out that although the current path looks dangerous for the environment, it's hard to make a hard prediction of how the situation will play out. He justifies his position with common data center roadblocks: the availability of turbines, delays in grid connections, and other delay factors. Truth be told, at this point it's hard to predict how many data centers will actually reach completion, given that requests for permits far exceed available grid capacity across the U.S., and a sizable number of buildouts are encountering strong opposition . Plus, although the AI bubble is still alive and well, concerns started to arise about the economics of hyperscalers, indicating some may go the way of the dodo — and their projects along with them. extraction.body: The US power sector could release 42 percent more planet-heating carbon dioxide pollution by 2030 than it did in 2025 as it builds out more fossil fuel infrastructure to meet data center electricity demand, according to a new analysis by the Sierra Club. CO2 emissions from electricity generation would increase by 618 million tons by the end of the decade if planned AI projects are constructed. That’s roughly equivalent to carbon pollution from the electricity use of 128,788,523 homes in a year. The Sierra Club’s estimate is higher than some previous projections from other groups. Another study published by academic researchers in June forecast that electricity demand from data centers and crypto mines could push up power sector emissions by 28 percent by 2030 when compared to a scenario with no data center growth. The outcome depends on how many planned data center projects actually come to fruition, as well as on what type of technology is used to power those facilities. Net US greenhouse gas emission have fallen from a peak of about 6.58 billion metric tons in 2007 to about 5.35 billion metric tons in 2025. But that pollution started ticking back up last year as data centers drove up electricity demand. The Trump administration is incentivising the buildout of fossil fuel infrastructure for data centers while simultaneously rolling back pollution regulations and stalling renewable energy projects. The US is now planning to build more fossil fuel capacity than it has in a decade, according to a separate report published this month by the Environmental Defense Fund.

extraction.body: Electricity prices in the U.S. are rising sharply, but the burden of rising bills isn’t evenly distributed. A Yale Climate Connections analysis of electricity prices has found that data centers and other commercial electricity users are consuming more kilowatts than ever, but the price they pay for that electricity has risen only a little. And industrial users of electricity are actually paying lower prices, on average, than they were two years ago. But between 2020 and 2024, residential electricity prices in the U.S. increased by 25%. In other words, people using their toasters, laptops, and electric heating and cooking at home are paying ever-increasing prices, while the data centers that are driving rapid growth in electricity demand are scoring handsome discounts. You'll receive the latest climate change news, tips, and inspiring stories twice a week. Sign up to be part of the solution today A word of warning: this analysis might make you mad, but hopefully in a productive way. Electricity customers are sorted into use types: residential for homes, commercial for businesses and data centers, and industrial for facilities like factories or refineries. The graph below shows how the prices paid by these three sectors have shifted over time. From 1997 through 2007, electricity prices for all three categories of users rose and fell at a similar pace. In 2008, that trend stopped. That year, electricity prices went up for residences but down for businesses and industries. Over the next decade, home uses of electricity became more expensive, while electricity prices for businesses stayed nearly flat. In 2021, the trend shifted again. Electricity prices for all three sectors began to rise steeply, but unequally. The gap between home energy use and business/industrial energy use became even larger. In the last two years, these differences became especially stark, as shown in the chart below. In just two years, starting in 2022, residential electricity prices rose by 10%, while commercial prices increased by only 3%, and industrial electricity prices fell by 2%. This is an example of the “ K-shaped economy ,” where things improve for some groups while getting worse for others. The lines on a K-shaped graph head off in different directions, illustrating an ever-larger gap between those benefiting and those left out. If any one sector is driving the growth in electricity usage, it would make sense for that sector to foot the bill for the power plants and power lines needed to serve their demand. So let’s look at how electricity use is growing in each sector. The chart below shows how the amount of electricity used by each sector has changed since 1997. Industrial use has stayed relatively flat, while commercial and residential use both grew at fairly similar rates and are now consuming about 40% more power than they were in 1997. But a new pattern emerged in the last three years, as seen in the chart below. Commercial demand for electricity rose sharply and steadily, using 9% more power over just a three-year span. Glenn McGrath, an electricity data analyst at the U.S. Energy Information Administration, wrote in an email that the growing energy needs of data centers “are likely a significant factor” behind increasing electricity use in the commercial sector. To sum up the situation in recent years, household electricity use has grown the least of the three sectors, but that’s where prices have gone up the most. The data illustrates how residential users are subsidizing the energy bills of A.I. and data centers, a perspective backed up by other recent analyses . A report by the Harvard Law School Environmental and Energy Law Program, Extracting Profits from the Public , lays out some of the reasons why Big Tech is able to off-load its costs onto the public and outlines specific steps policymakers can take to restore balance. We help millions of people better understand climate change and what to do about it. Help us reach even more people like you. But for individual consumers, the situation is the opposite. In many states, people have no choice in their energy provider or their energy prices, and they can’t look elsewhere for a better deal. In the parlance of the energy industry, everyday people are often called “captive ratepayers” because we have little choice but to be the ever-faithful customers of a monopoly utility. Rising electricity bills can trigger a host of negative consequences. High energy costs may prevent people from adequately heating or cooling their homes, which can contribute to both physical and mental health problems. Expensive energy can also lead people to forego necessities in other areas of their lives in order to keep up with rising bills and avoid having their service shut off. These burdens fall disproportionately on low-income, Black, Hispanic, and disadvantaged households, who spend a large portion of their income on energy bills. Higher electricity prices could also slow the adoption of modern, climate-friendly technology such as electric vehicles, heat pumps, and induction stoves that rely on electricity. That said, electric cars and appliances are more efficient than their fossil-fuel counterparts, so the trade-off is often still worth it. And in some cases, expensive electricity can spur faster adoption of climate solutions. Home solar panels pay for themselves more quickly, and energy conservation measures make even more financial sense than before. The electricity system in the U.S. is undergoing multiple stresses at once. Data centers seem to have an unquenchable thirst for energy, as extreme weather – often made worse by our warming climate – destabilizes the grid and causes spikes in electricity demand. At the same time, electricity generation is slowly transitioning from large, centralized power plants to numerous, distributed forms of electricity generation. But at the root of it all, the data suggests that everyday people are footing the bill while companies that consume ever more power are paying less. At a time when corporations seem to enjoy many structural advantages over consumers, from lower tax rates to relaxed pollution requirements , the burden of rising energy bills can make one feel powerless. And yes, the pun was intentional. Decisions about electricity rates are made by public utility commissions , which don’t usually get much attention – but that may be changing. In the November 2025 elections in Georgia, two incumbent public utility commissioners were resoundingly defeated after residential electricity prices climbed by 41% in just four years. Commissions are increasingly criticized for rubber-stamping price hikes and not protecting ratepayers who are caught inside a monopolistic system. If you’re interested in learning more about the electricity decision-making process near you, here’s a directory of public utility commissions in every state , and Canary Media wrote a user-friendly guide to engaging with your electricity regulators. In other words, people using their toasters, laptops, and electric heating and cooking at home are paying ever-increasing prices, while the data centers that are driving rapid growth in electricity demand are scoring handsome discounts.

In just two years, starting in 2022, residential electricity prices rose by 10%, while commercial prices increased by only 3%, and industrial electricity prices fell by 2%.

This is an example of the “ K-shaped economy ,” where things improve for some groups while getting worse for others. The lines on a K-shaped graph head off in different directions, illustrating an ever-larger gap between those benefiting and those left out.

If any one sector is driving the growth in electricity usage, it would make sense for that sector to foot the bill for the power plants and power lines needed to serve their demand. So let’s look at how electricity use is growing in each sector.

But a new pattern emerged in the last three years, as seen in the chart below. Commercial demand for electricity rose sharply and steadily, using 9% more power over just a three-year span.

Glenn McGrath, an electricity data analyst at the U.S. Energy Information Administration, wrote in an email that the growing energy needs of data centers “are likely a significant factor” behind increasing electricity use in the commercial sector.
To sum up the situation in recent years, household electricity use has grown the least of the three sectors, but that’s where prices have gone up the most.

The data illustrates how residential users are subsidizing the energy bills of A.I. and data centers, a perspective backed up by other recent analyses . A report by the Harvard Law School Environmental and Energy Law Program, Extracting Profits from the Public , lays out some of the reasons why Big Tech is able to off-load its costs onto the public and outlines specific steps policymakers can take to restore balance.

In the parlance of the energy industry, everyday people are often called “captive ratepayers” because we have little choice but to be the ever-faithful customers of a monopoly utility.

Expensive energy can also lead people to forego necessities in other areas of their lives in order to keep up with rising bills and avoid having their service shut off. These burdens fall disproportionately on low-income, Black, Hispanic, and disadvantaged households, who spend a large portion of their income on energy bills.

Higher electricity prices could also slow the adoption of modern, climate-friendly technology such as electric vehicles, heat pumps, and induction stoves that rely on electricity. That said, electric cars and appliances are more efficient than their fossil-fuel counterparts, so the trade-off is often still worth it.

And in some cases, expensive electricity can spur faster adoption of climate solutions. Home solar panels pay for themselves more quickly, and energy conservation measures make even more financial sense than before.

The electricity system in the U.S. is undergoing multiple stresses at once. Data centers seem to have an unquenchable thirst for energy, as extreme weather – often made worse by our warming climate – destabilizes the grid and causes spikes in electricity demand. At the same time, electricity generation is slowly transitioning from large, centralized power plants to numerous, distributed forms of electricity generation.

But at the root of it all, the data suggests that everyday people are footing the bill while companies that consume ever more power are paying less. At a time when corporations seem to enjoy many structural advantages over consumers, from lower tax rates to relaxed pollution requirements , the burden of rising energy bills can make one feel powerless. SAINT LOUIS, Mo. — Late yesterday, Ameren Missouri filed a proposed long-range energy plan with its regulators at the Missouri Public Service Commission (PSC).

If approved as proposed, Ameren Missouri would significantly increase its reliance on fossil fuels, including a large increase in gas-burning power plants and extended coal-burning at its Labadie and Sioux plants.
Ironically, Ameren cites recent extreme weather as a justification for its gas-heavy investments, a plan that will exacerbate local climate disasters.
Extreme weather can also quickly send the price of gas skyrocketing, as was the case during Winter Storm Uri.

If approved as proposed, Ameren Missouri would significantly increase its reliance on fossil fuels, including a large increase in gas-burning power plants and extended coal-burning at its Labadie and Sioux plants. Labadie is the deadliest coal plant in the country. Ameren’s significant investment in new gas and continued coal burning coincides with the utility dropping its carbon dioxide emissions reduction goals from the promotional materials for its latest energy plan. Ironically, Ameren cites recent extreme weather as a justification for its gas-heavy investments, a plan that will exacerbate local climate disasters. Extreme weather can also quickly send the price of gas skyrocketing, as was the case during Winter Storm Uri. The Sierra Club actively intervenes when Ameren files its energy plans before the PSC. In previous years, Ameren admitted that it does not consider the public health impacts of the energy generation investments it makes, including new gas plants and coal plant extensions. Additionally, Ameren does not consider the climate impact of fugitive emissions from the extraction and transportation of natural gas, which is predominantly methane, a potent greenhouse gas. Ameren released its new energy plan against the backdrop of the Trump administration’s proposal to repeal the Endangerment Finding , the basis for regulating greenhouse gas emissions under the Clean Air Act. SAINT LOUIS, Mo. — Late yesterday, Ameren Missouri filed a proposed long-range energy plan with its regulators at the Missouri Public Service Commission (PSC). If approved as proposed, Ameren Missouri would significantly increase its reliance on fossil fuels, including a large increase in gas-burning power plants and extended coal-burning at its Labadie and Sioux plants. Labadie is the deadliest coal plant in the country.

Ameren’s significant investment in new gas and continued coal burning coincides with the utility dropping its carbon dioxide emissions reduction goals from the promotional materials for its latest energy plan. Ironically, Ameren cites recent extreme weather as a justification for its gas-heavy investments, a plan that will exacerbate local climate disasters. Extreme weather can also quickly send the price of gas skyrocketing, as was the case during Winter Storm Uri.

The Sierra Club actively intervenes when Ameren files its energy plans before the PSC. In previous years, Ameren admitted that it does not consider the public health impacts of the energy generation investments it makes, including new gas plants and coal plant extensions. Additionally, Ameren does not consider the climate impact of fugitive emissions from the extraction and transportation of natural gas, which is predominantly methane, a potent greenhouse gas.

Ameren released its new energy plan against the backdrop of the Trump administration’s proposal to repeal the Endangerment Finding , the basis for regulating greenhouse gas emissions under the Clean Air Act.
Significant and concerning changes to Ameren’s energy plan from last year include:
Statement from Jenn DeRose, Sierra Club’s Beyond Coal Campaign Strategist in Missouri:

“The saying goes to stop digging if you’re in a hole, but Ameren is still digging with its pollution-heavy plan even though it admits extreme weather events are increasing. Burning more coal and gas will only increase the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events like heatwaves, droughts, and floods. Ameren and tech companies are gambling with the future of humanity as they power data centers with coal and gas. We need Ameren to stop making bad investments for families and small businesses, and this plan is full of them. Concerns have been mounting everywhere about the environmental impact of data centers, with alarms ringing at various environmental think tanks. The Sierra Club, one of the oldest environmental preservation organizations in the U.S., has now put forth an estimate that by 2030, U.S. data center buildouts will be outputting as much carbon dioxide as the entirety of Mexico, pushing back progress on greenhouse gas reduction by 15 years, Bloomberg reports. The Club's principal advisor for climate and energy, Jeremy Fusher, puts it plainly: "the numbers continue to sort of boggle our minds." He's referring to an estimate that with the output from pending data center builds, the output from the U.S. power sector is set to put 2.1 billion metric tons of CO2 in the atmosphere by the end of the decade, an uptick of 42% compared to 2025 figures. The researchers' previous estimates were between a quarter and half of the current projections. An increasing number of countries and states are enacting laws demanding that new data center builds have a large portion of their power generated by green sources. However, those laws rarely apply retroactively, and oftentimes have a phase-in period. Even the Irish law on the matter demanding that new data centers be fed by 80% of renewable power only requires that that happens six years after they're powered up. In the current AI-driven market, speed of construction is king. Roughly 40% of U.S. data centers are fed by natural gas turbines , and the situation doesn't look like it'll be changing much. It'll likely get worse, as the addition of green sources almost assuredly won't keep up with demand. Much like RAM, GPUs, and storage, turbines were all slurped up by data centers. Their prices have risen by 50%, and production is backlogged for years, with one maker stating it's opening slots for production in 2032 . Having said all that, Brendan Pierpont from Energy Innovation, another climate-concerned organization, points out that although the current path looks dangerous for the environment, it's hard to make a hard prediction of how the situation will play out. He justifies his position with common data center roadblocks: the availability of turbines, delays in grid connections, and other delay factors. Truth be told, at this point it's hard to predict how many data centers will actually reach completion, given that requests for permits far exceed available grid capacity across the U.S., and a sizable number of buildouts are encountering strong opposition . Plus, although the AI bubble is still alive and well, concerns started to arise about the economics of hyperscalers, indicating some may go the way of the dodo — and their projects along with them. extraction.body: The US power sector could release 42 percent more planet-heating carbon dioxide pollution by 2030 than it did in 2025 as it builds out more fossil fuel infrastructure to meet data center electricity demand, according to a new analysis by the Sierra Club. CO2 emissions from electricity generation would increase by 618 million tons by the end of the decade if planned AI projects are constructed. That’s roughly equivalent to carbon pollution from the electricity use of 128,788,523 homes in a year. The Sierra Club’s estimate is higher than some previous projections from other groups. Another study published by academic researchers in June forecast that electricity demand from data centers and crypto mines could push up power sector emissions by 28 percent by 2030 when compared to a scenario with no data center growth. The outcome depends on how many planned data center projects actually come to fruition, as well as on what type of technology is used to power those facilities. Net US greenhouse gas emission have fallen from a peak of about 6.58 billion metric tons in 2007 to about 5.35 billion metric tons in 2025. But that pollution started ticking back up last year as data centers drove up electricity demand. The Trump administration is incentivising the buildout of fossil fuel infrastructure for data centers while simultaneously rolling back pollution regulations and stalling renewable energy projects. The US is now planning to build more fossil fuel capacity than it has in a decade, according to a separate report published this month by the Environmental Defense Fund.

extraction.body: Electricity prices in the U.S. are rising sharply, but the burden of rising bills isn’t evenly distributed. A Yale Climate Connections analysis of electricity prices has found that data centers and other commercial electricity users are consuming more kilowatts than ever, but the price they pay for that electricity has risen only a little. And industrial users of electricity are actually paying lower prices, on average, than they were two years ago. But between 2020 and 2024, residential electricity prices in the U.S. increased by 25%. In other words, people using their toasters, laptops, and electric heating and cooking at home are paying ever-increasing prices, while the data centers that are driving rapid growth in electricity demand are scoring handsome discounts. You'll receive the latest climate change news, tips, and inspiring stories twice a week. Sign up to be part of the solution today A word of warning: this analysis might make you mad, but hopefully in a productive way. Electricity customers are sorted into use types: residential for homes, commercial for businesses and data centers, and industrial for facilities like factories or refineries. The graph below shows how the prices paid by these three sectors have shifted over time. From 1997 through 2007, electricity prices for all three categories of users rose and fell at a similar pace. In 2008, that trend stopped. That year, electricity prices went up for residences but down for businesses and industries. Over the next decade, home uses of electricity became more expensive, while electricity prices for businesses stayed nearly flat. In 2021, the trend shifted again. Electricity prices for all three sectors began to rise steeply, but unequally. The gap between home energy use and business/industrial energy use became even larger. In the last two years, these differences became especially stark, as shown in the chart below. In just two years, starting in 2022, residential electricity prices rose by 10%, while commercial prices increased by only 3%, and industrial electricity prices fell by 2%. This is an example of the “ K-shaped economy ,” where things improve for some groups while getting worse for others. The lines on a K-shaped graph head off in different directions, illustrating an ever-larger gap between those benefiting and those left out. If any one sector is driving the growth in electricity usage, it would make sense for that sector to foot the bill for the power plants and power lines needed to serve their demand. So let’s look at how electricity use is growing in each sector. The chart below shows how the amount of electricity used by each sector has changed since 1997. Industrial use has stayed relatively flat, while commercial and residential use both grew at fairly similar rates and are now consuming about 40% more power than they were in 1997. But a new pattern emerged in the last three years, as seen in the chart below. Commercial demand for electricity rose sharply and steadily, using 9% more power over just a three-year span. Glenn McGrath, an electricity data analyst at the U.S. Energy Information Administration, wrote in an email that the growing energy needs of data centers “are likely a significant factor” behind increasing electricity use in the commercial sector. To sum up the situation in recent years, household electricity use has grown the least of the three sectors, but that’s where prices have gone up the most. The data illustrates how residential users are subsidizing the energy bills of A.I. and data centers, a perspective backed up by other recent analyses . A report by the Harvard Law School Environmental and Energy Law Program, Extracting Profits from the Public , lays out some of the reasons why Big Tech is able to off-load its costs onto the public and outlines specific steps policymakers can take to restore balance. We help millions of people better understand climate change and what to do about it. Help us reach even more people like you. But for individual consumers, the situation is the opposite. In many states, people have no choice in their energy provider or their energy prices, and they can’t look elsewhere for a better deal. In the parlance of the energy industry, everyday people are often called “captive ratepayers” because we have little choice but to be the ever-faithful customers of a monopoly utility. Rising electricity bills can trigger a host of negative consequences. High energy costs may prevent people from adequately heating or cooling their homes, which can contribute to both physical and mental health problems. Expensive energy can also lead people to forego necessities in other areas of their lives in order to keep up with rising bills and avoid having their service shut off. These burdens fall disproportionately on low-income, Black, Hispanic, and disadvantaged households, who spend a large portion of their income on energy bills. Higher electricity prices could also slow the adoption of modern, climate-friendly technology such as electric vehicles, heat pumps, and induction stoves that rely on electricity. That said, electric cars and appliances are more efficient than their fossil-fuel counterparts, so the trade-off is often still worth it. And in some cases, expensive electricity can spur faster adoption of climate solutions. Home solar panels pay for themselves more quickly, and energy conservation measures make even more financial sense than before. The electricity system in the U.S. is undergoing multiple stresses at once. Data centers seem to have an unquenchable thirst for energy, as extreme weather – often made worse by our warming climate – destabilizes the grid and causes spikes in electricity demand. At the same time, electricity generation is slowly transitioning from large, centralized power plants to numerous, distributed forms of electricity generation. But at the root of it all, the data suggests that everyday people are footing the bill while companies that consume ever more power are paying less. At a time when corporations seem to enjoy many structural advantages over consumers, from lower tax rates to relaxed pollution requirements , the burden of rising energy bills can make one feel powerless. And yes, the pun was intentional. Decisions about electricity rates are made by public utility commissions , which don’t usually get much attention – but that may be changing. In the November 2025 elections in Georgia, two incumbent public utility commissioners were resoundingly defeated after residential electricity prices climbed by 41% in just four years. Commissions are increasingly criticized for rubber-stamping price hikes and not protecting ratepayers who are caught inside a monopolistic system. If you’re interested in learning more about the electricity decision-making process near you, here’s a directory of public utility commissions in every state , and Canary Media wrote a user-friendly guide to engaging with your electricity regulators. SAINT LOUIS, Mo. — Late yesterday, Ameren Missouri filed a proposed long-range energy plan with its regulators at the Missouri Public Service Commission (PSC). If approved as proposed, Ameren Missouri would significantly increase its reliance on fossil fuels, including a large increase in gas-burning power plants and extended coal-burning at its Labadie and Sioux plants. Labadie is the deadliest coal plant in the country. Ameren’s significant investment in new gas and continued coal burning coincides with the utility dropping its carbon dioxide emissions reduction goals from the promotional materials for its latest energy plan. Ironically, Ameren cites recent extreme weather as a justification for its gas-heavy investments, a plan that will exacerbate local climate disasters. Extreme weather can also quickly send the price of gas skyrocketing, as was the case during Winter Storm Uri. The Sierra Club actively intervenes when Ameren files its energy plans before the PSC. In previous years, Ameren admitted that it does not consider the public health impacts of the energy generation investments it makes, including new gas plants and coal plant extensions. Additionally, Ameren does not consider the climate impact of fugitive emissions from the extraction and transportation of natural gas, which is predominantly methane, a potent greenhouse gas. Ameren released its new energy plan against the backdrop of the Trump administration’s proposal to repeal the Endangerment Finding , the basis for regulating greenhouse gas emissions under the Clean Air Act. Significant and concerning changes to Ameren’s energy plan from last year include: Statement from Jenn DeRose, Sierra Club’s Beyond Coal Campaign Strategist in Missouri: “The saying goes to stop digging if you’re in a hole, but Ameren is still digging with its pollution-heavy plan even though it admits extreme weather events are increasing. Burning more coal and gas will only increase the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events like heatwaves, droughts, and floods. Ameren and tech companies are gambling with the future of humanity as they power data centers with coal and gas. We need Ameren to stop making bad investments for families and small businesses, and this plan is full of them. Unless elected officials, business owners and every customer start holding Ameren accountable, we’ll be stuck with an expensive and polluting electric grid that benefits billionaires and harms struggling families.” The Sierra Club is America’s largest and most influential grassroots environmental organization, with millions of members and supporters. It is made with 45 percent recycled content overall, 6 including 100 percent recycled aluminum in the enclosure, 100 percent recycled cobalt in the battery, and, in a first for Apple, 100 percent recycled tantalum in multiple capacitors.
It is manufactured with 60 percent renewable electricity, such as wind and solar, across the supply chain.
As with all Apple products, its paper packaging is 100 percent fiber-based 7 and designed to be recycled.
M6 features an advanced 12-core CPU with the world’s fastest CPU core, so everything from productivity tasks to more demanding pro workflows feels incredibly fast and responsive.
And with phenomenal battery life of up to 24 hours, it delivers the same remarkable performance whether plugged in or on battery, so users can work, create, and pursue their passions from anywhere.

3 It also offers the advanced features users love, including the stunning Liquid Retina XDR display with a nano-texture option, a 12MP Center Stage camera, an immersive six-speaker sound system, and a wide array of ports.
Available in space black and silver, it can be pre-ordered beginning tomorrow, October 28, with availability starting Friday, November 6.
The 12-core GPU, also with two additional cores, delivers up to 30 percent faster graphics performance when compared to M5.

Siri AI can draw on personal context to help users find what they need in the moment across messages, emails, photos, and more; answer questions about virtually any topic; and get things done across apps — all with groundbreaking privacy protections.
Siri AI is integrated into Spotlight and systemwide context menus, and users can ask Siri about what’s on their display with Visual Intelligence using a dedicated keyboard shortcut.
Users can also write and edit with Siri almost anywhere they type.
Additionally, Apple Intelligence makes apps smarter and more useful.

In Safari, it powers new tools that automatically organize a user’s tabs into topics; notify them of website changes, like product restocks or price drops; and enable the creation of custom extensions based on a description.
Updates to Liquid Glass deliver an even more focused and approachable experience.

A new slider in Settings gives users the option to personalize Liquid Glass, adjusting it anywhere from ultraclear to fully tinted to match their preference, and app icons are sharper and more defined.
Apple revolutionized personal technology with the introduction of the Macintosh in 1984.
Today, Apple leads the world in innovation with iPhone, iPad, Mac, AirPods, Apple Watch, and Apple Vision Pro.

Apple’s six software platforms — iOS, iPadOS, macOS, watchOS, visionOS, and tvOS — provide seamless experiences across all Apple devices and empower people with breakthrough services including the App Store, Apple Music, Apple Pay, iCloud, and Apple TV.
Apple’s more than 150,000 employees are dedicated to making the best products on earth and to leaving the world better than we found it.
The latest news and updates, direct from Apple.

Owners of aging machines get another replacement option, while recent Mac buyers need evidence that the changes address an actual limitation.
Preorders began October 28, with availability scheduled for November 6.
Apple claims up to 30 percent faster graphics and up to 25 percent faster AI workloads than M5.
That combination gives the product a broader purpose than running AI demonstrations.
A professional laptop still has to support ordinary work between demanding tasks.
The useful next step is to connect that direction to a task you actually perform.
Identify the delay, capacity limit, or reliability problem behind your interest in replacing a laptop.
Then compare reviews and application tests against that specific need.
Keep conventional work in the evaluation alongside AI features, especially when the computer must support a full working day.
If your current machine already handles those tasks comfortably, wait for evidence of a meaningful improvement.
If it does not, use the shipping product’s measured behavior to judge the replacement.
Which recurring constraint would the new laptop need to remove for the upgrade to make sense?
Apple is extending its local AI strategy through a familiar laptop format.
That makes this announcement easier to evaluate through workloads than through appearance.

Apple advertises up to 24 hours of battery life.
Neither specification establishes how long a demanding local AI session will last.

The central question is how much additional work those improvements let a laptop handle locally.

The CPU, the processor responsible for general computing, and GPU, the processor used for graphics and parallel calculations, both gain additional cores.

The specifications describe more computing resources, although applications determine how effectively those resources get used.
This is where Apple’s own product history becomes useful.
Its M5 GPU architecture already included a Neural Accelerator in each GPU core.
Apple also described support through its software frameworks and development interfaces.
Apple’s performance figures describe selected workloads and comparison systems.

Some server-based features have daily limits.
The important change is therefore cumulative.

extraction.body: Apple on Tuesday unveiled its new 14-inch MacBook Pro, powered by its latest M6 chip. The new MacBook Pro has 24 hours of battery life and now supports Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 connectivity. The laptop starts at $1,999 and is available in space black and silver. Apple also announced its latest iMac , which is also powered by the M6 chip. The tech giant revealed the new devices just a day before its “Pro and Tell” event scheduled for Wednesday. On Monday, Apple announced its new iPad mini . The tech giant says the M6 chip features a 12-core CPU with the world’s fastest CPU core and a 12-core GPU that delivers more responsive performance, up to 30% faster graphics, and up to 25% faster AI workloads compared with the M5 chip. The M6 delivers up to 13 times the LLM prompt-processing speed of the M1 MacBook Pro and up to 1.3 times faster performance than the M5 model, Apple says. The M6 MacBook Pro starts with 16GB of unified memory, configurable up to 32GB, and has memory bandwidth of up to 170GB/s, up from the 153GB/s on the M5 chip. It includes HDMI, MagSafe 3, three Thunderbolt 4 ports, an SDXC card slot, and a headphone jack. Like previous models, the laptop features a 12-megapixel camera. The M6 MacBook Pro supports fast charging, reaching up to 50% charge in 30 minutes with a compatible high-wattage USB-C power adapter. As for the new M6-powered iMac, it features a faster CPU and GPU, with Neural Accelerators built into every core. Apple says the M6 delivers smooth multitasking and powerful performance for everyday apps, photo editing, and video production. The new iMac starts at $1,499 and comes in blue, green, pink, yellow, purple, orange, and silver. The company also notes that the new iMac delivers up to five times faster on-device AI performance than the M4 model. It features a 24-inch 4.5K Retina display, an advanced camera and audio system, up to four Thunderbolt 4 ports, color-matched accessories, and macOS 27. Both the new MacBook Pro and iMac can be preordered starting October 28 and will be available starting November 6. Aisha is a consumer news reporter at TechCrunch. Apple is extending its local AI strategy through a familiar laptop format. That makes this announcement easier to evaluate through workloads than through appearance.

Apple also lists a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, its dedicated AI processing hardware. A faster processor cannot automatically make an oversized workload practical. Conversely, a smaller model that already fits can still benefit from reduced waiting. Those distinctions matter when reading a launch announcement organized around performance improvements.

The laptop also adds Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, the latest wireless generations listed for this model. Apple advertises up to 24 hours of battery life. Neither specification establishes how long a demanding local AI session will last.

sources.title: Amazon adds delivery tracking, last-minute adds, gift ideas to Alexa+ - TechCrunch
passages: Another new feature rolling out now will allow Alexa device owners to add items to an upcoming delivery at any time until the item leaves the warehouse.
This builds on a similar feature recently added to Amazon’s retail website and app, so it isn’t necessarily an Alexa+ exclusive, but the feature wasn’t live on Alexa devices so far.
Amazon says Alexa+ is now available to “tens of millions” of customers, and these new features are live for users in the U.S. and Canada.
While not everyone has been happy with Alexa+, the company says the percentage of users who downgraded back to the AI-free interface remains in the “very low single digits.”
Amazon has long had to deal with the reality that owners of its Echo smart speakers weren’t using its voice-controlled assistant, Alexa, to buy things, as it had hoped.
To access the new experience, Amazon users can say “Alexa, where’s my stuff?” or “Open Shopping Essentials.” Soon, a shopping widget will be available to add to the Echo device’s home screen, too.

From this dashboard, Amazon shoppers can track deliveries in real time, see information about recent orders, get reminders about household essentials they need to reorder, and view their shopping list and saved items.
The company has already been working on features that make Alexa+ more of a shopping assistant with abilities like automated deal tracking and automatic purchases.
The former feature lets you set Alexa to alert you when items in your cart or list drop below a certain price point.
If you also have automatic purchases set up, Alexa can immediately order an item when it reaches that target price.
Alexa+ is also gaining the ability to recommend gifts.
You’ll be able to describe who you’re shopping for, or the occasion, and Alexa+ will display product suggestions on the screen, organized into categories.

passages: Amazon is adding several new features to its AI shopping assistant, including ways to create, edit, and move items between shopping lists and gift registries.

Alexa for Shopping lives next to the search bar across Amazon’s app and website, and can do things like set price alerts, compare items, and automatically purchase products when they drop below a set price.
