extraction.body: Personally identifiable information belonging to thousands of U.S. Department of Homeland Security employees has been published online after a hacker stole reams of data in a previously undisclosed breach at the government department earlier this year. The breach includes names, job titles, and work contact information, such as email addresses, cell phone numbers, and office locations, of more than 40,000 people who work for the federal department, including border and immigration agents, cybersecurity staffers, and senior department officials. A hacker who goes by the handle Department of Peace claimed they obtained the data from an Okta single sign-on system used by Homeland Security to allow employees and contractors across its various agencies to log in to its central network. The Okta system also contains IT and log-in records associated with the employees’ user account, including details about which systems and internal apps they are permitted to access. More than half of the dataset — some 21,000 records — relate to employees with U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), who work at airports and other ports of entry. The data also contains records associated with another 10,000 employees of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and its Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) unit, and just under a 1,000 employees who work at U.S. cybersecurity defense agency CISA. Thousands of additional records relate to staff who work at the department’s headquarters and its other agencies, including U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services and the Federal Protective Service. “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs,” said Department of Peace in a note left with the data, which TechCrunch has seen. The hacker did not respond to TechCrunch’s email requesting comment and with questions about how the breach was carried out. This is the latest data breach to hit the U.S. government in recent months, following earlier hacks involving the theft of thousands of FBI agents’ personnel records and the personal information of millions of serving and former military service personnel from the Pentagon’s human resources unit . It’s also the second breach involving Homeland Security this year, after the same hacker claimed to have taken thousands of contracts between the department and the private sector, including defense contractors and surveillance vendors. The latest batch of breached data, which appears authentic, offers a rare — albeit incomplete — view into the scale and operations of Homeland Security, whose deportations, arbitrary detentions, and killings of U.S. citizens under its leadership have become a key issue for voters ahead of the upcoming U.S. midterm elections. The stolen Homeland Security data was provided to journalist and hacker maia arson crimew, who then shared a copy with DDoSecrets , a nonprofit collective that hosts leaked datasets in the public interest. TechCrunch verified a portion of the data as authentic by matching the names of several known Homeland Security employees against an offline copy of the database. The thousands of employee directory records appear to have been exfiltrated around mid-August, according to the timestamps on each person’s record. The number of leaked records is equivalent to about one-fifth of Homeland Security’s workforce, which totals around 220,000 staff . It’s unclear whether the vulnerability that allowed the breach has been fixed or if Homeland Security is aware of the data theft. A spokesperson for Homeland Security told TechCrunch after publication: “DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively. We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected. We will update the public when more information is available.” When reached, Okta said it was aware of this report. “Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised,” a spokesperson said. While the leaked data includes identifiable information about agents and officers, the dataset also reveals more about the surveillance technologies and cybersecurity tools that Homeland Security employees may be able to access. Critics have called for investigations into tech companies that fund or provide their technology to ICE. The leaked data contains information about employees’ membership in user groups within the department’s Active Directory, a system that controls access to the department’s internal tools, services, and third-party offerings used for work. Most of the Homeland Security employees in the dataset were members of the user group that had access to Microsoft 365, the tech giant’s cloud service that hosts the agency’s emails and files, as well as user groups for accessing Adobe Acrobat, Citrix, and other typical desktop software. The data also shows that around 4,500 users, including ICE agents and deportation officers, are members of a group called “Headspace_users.” Online therapy provider Headspace previously had an $82,500 federal contract with ICE that ended in 2023 to fund “mental health software required for ERO employees,” a reference to ICE’s deportation unit. A spokesperson for Headspace said the company has not provided any services to DHS or ICE since 2023. Dozens of other user groups reference Penlink , a web surveillance company that makes technology it claims can track the location data of hundreds of millions of mobile devices. Penlink has had a contract with ICE for years. The user groups vary in size, from a handful of users in local Homeland Security offices around the country to more than 2,000 users across ICE’s HSI unit nationally. One group specifically references Penlink PLX, which the company says is used to capture and analyze “real-time intelligence” from phone calls, texts, web activity, and social media. A spokesperson for Penlink did not respond to a request for comment. One user group also includes more than 200 CBP users associated with Mobile Fortify, a facial-recognition app used by both CBP and ICE agents to identify people and verify their information and immigration status . The user groups also include several employees associated with ChatGPT access, including senior DHS officials, as well as other groups associated with investigations into the China-backed hacking groups known as Salt Typhoon and Volt Typhoon. Researchers and public information advocates say that the exposed data could provide valuable leads for investigations into alleged abuses by the Trump administration, such as identifying email addresses of agents that can be used in public records requests under the Freedom of Information Act. “Email addresses and phone numbers are indispensable tools for FOIA researchers, often making the difference between a vague records request that gets stonewalled and one that gets results,” said Ryan Shapiro, the executive director of transparency nonprofit Property of the People. “Given the Trump administration’s contempt for even basic transparency, the need for such tools is urgent,” said Shapiro. DDoSecrets co-founder and journalist Emma Best said that the exposed Homeland Security data will be a “catalyst for investigations, empowering journalists, Congressional inquiries, legal challenges, community action and Freedom of Information Act requests.” Zack Whittaker is the security editor at TechCrunch. He also authors the weekly cybersecurity newsletter, this week in security . He can be reached via encrypted message at zackwhittaker.1337 on Signal. You can also contact him by email, or to verify outreach, at [email protected] .

sources.title: The NYT Cooking app is testing AI recipe modifications
passages: The New York Times is testing a new AI feature for its Cooking app that helps users to modify recipes, and it has sparked some drama among users.

Last Friday, NYT Cooking senior editor Genevieve Ko announced the feature, which can be used to recommend substitutions for ingredients and cooking equipment, scale recipes to any number of servings, and “generally make our recipes work for what a cook needs at that moment.” One of the examples given in the article shows a user asking to use baby spinach instead of kale, with the Cooking app feature advising that because baby spinach wilts faster, it should be added during a later step of the recipe.

The AI modification feature is being rolled out gradually while the NYT monitors how it performs — it’s currently available to all Cooking subscribers on the iOS app, and it will be more broadly available “soon.” Some NYT readers have pushed back against the feature, citing concerns in the article’s comment section around the environmental impact of widespread AI adoption and the general impact that AI features may have on the user experience.

extraction.body: The New York Times is testing a new AI feature for its Cooking app that helps users to modify recipes, and it has sparked some drama among users. Last Friday, NYT Cooking senior editor Genevieve Ko announced the feature, which can be used to recommend substitutions for ingredients and cooking equipment, scale recipes to any number of servings, and “generally make our recipes work for what a cook needs at that moment.” One of the examples given in the article shows a user asking to use baby spinach instead of kale, with the Cooking app feature advising that because baby spinach wilts faster, it should be added during a later step of the recipe. Ko says it can also change the recipes around different pans and tools. Customized recipes are private and can’t be published or shared through the app. The AI modification feature is being rolled out gradually while the NYT monitors how it performs — it’s currently available to all Cooking subscribers on the iOS app, and it will be more broadly available “soon.” Some NYT readers have pushed back against the feature, citing concerns in the article’s comment section around the environmental impact of widespread AI adoption and the general impact that AI features may have on the user experience. “I’ve always loved NYT Cooking and it pains me that the AI mandate has reached what used to be a wonderful and simple collection of recipes and notes from all sorts of different people.” This isn’t the first time that AI has been used by the NYT Cooking app. Ko says it was used to convert imperial volume measurements to metric weight measurements in recipes two years ago, and a feature was added last year that converts recipes to halve or double the original serving size. The comments on the new AI feature announcement post have since been closed, but NYT spokesperson Jordan Cohen tells The Verge that this is standard practice: “Comments on this article remained open for four days, with editors from Cooking taking care to answer questions, address concerns and engage directly with readers. We kept that conversation open to give readers a meaningful opportunity to share feedback and hear from the team. Closing comments on older articles is standard practice at The Times so that our moderators can focus on new discussions. We’re pleased to see that many members of our Cooking community are interested in exploring this tool and are already trying it out on our iOS app; they’re reporting good results.”

sources.title: The New York Times Cooking is letting readers taste test recipes over text to drive subscriptions - Digiday
passages: Despite recent reports that subscriptions to news organizations have stalled in the past year, The New York Times Company has continued to grow its subscriber base, adding 190,000 digital-only subscribers in the first quarter of this year.
With a simple text featuring an emoji, the publisher is dishing out 150 recipes for free.
Velasquez said it’s a “fast” and “playful” way to communicate with NYT Cooking and to simplify the process of finding summer recipes.
Once readers get a recipe, they can text that same emoji up to five times to get different recipes featuring that same ingredient.
And they want to get more free and simple recipes in front of readers — such as with free seven-day and 14-day trials, and now with the emoji text line.
The hope is to ultimately convert newly introduced readers into paid subscribers, who pay $5 a month or $40 a year for a subscription to NYT Cooking.
However, it will also require “significant outreach” to introduce audiences to this initiative, he added.
This text line is part of a broader strategy at NYT Cooking.

The team was hearing from readers that Cooking recipes were too hard to make and had inaccessible ingredients, Velasquez explained, so it became clear that they had to highlight easier recipes to both draw new subscribers in and retain those who are already paying.
The Times is not providing any additional special subscription offer or messaging to texters.

Texting as an audience engagement channel historically hasn’t been successful in driving subscriber acquisitions, according Tchivzhel, based on his experience working with publishers at Mather Economics.
“But it is perhaps a deeper level of engagement that can drive more meaningful connections between [the] audience and the Cooking product,” he said in an email.

“If a user voluntarily texts NYT Cooking, this is a strong signal of propensity to engage [and or] pay and reduces friction for the user getting the recipe they are after,” said Arvid Tchivzhel, svp of product at subscription management and customer data analytics firm Mather Economics.

extraction.body: Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit The New York Times is trying out a new way to boost subscriptions and engagement to its paywalled NYT Cooking recipe platform. With a simple text featuring an emoji, the publisher is dishing out 150 recipes for free. From June 21 through August 15, people in the U.S. can text one fruit or vegetable emoji — like a strawberry, tomato, coconut or corn on the cob — to “361-COOK-NYT” and receive a link to a recipe for free featuring that food item. They will also get early access to special NYT Cooking events starting this July, such as cherry picking in Michigan. Normally, it would cost a subscriber $5 a month to access these features. Once readers get a recipe, they can text that same emoji up to five times to get different recipes featuring that same ingredient. The recipes come from a pool of them that the Times team deemed popular, are easy to make and highlighted summer produce, said Camilla Velasquez, general manager of New York Times Cooking. The Times hopes that giving away recipes for free via text message will help people who are familiar with the NYT Cooking product but aren’t paying subscribers to see the value of a subscription. The Times is not providing any additional special subscription offer or messaging to texters. “It’s [for] people who are curious about [NYT Cooking], but haven’t really been able to take the plunge because they haven’t been able to experience enough of the recipes and this is their opportunity to do so,” Velasquez said. Why emojis? Velasquez said it’s a “fast” and “playful” way to communicate with NYT Cooking and to simplify the process of finding summer recipes. It’s also a way to appeal to the younger audiences NYT Cooking is trying to target, such as millennials. For the text line, The New York Times is working with text messaging platform Subtext, which also works with other publishers like Condé Nast and USA Today Network. This text line is part of a broader strategy at NYT Cooking. The focus for NYT Cooking’s team this year has been “easy to find, easy to make,” Velasquez said. The team was hearing from readers that Cooking recipes were too hard to make and had inaccessible ingredients, Velasquez explained, so it became clear that they had to highlight easier recipes to both draw new subscribers in and retain those who are already paying. There are a couple of ways NYT Cooking is responding. The overarching goal is to “simplify [NYT Cooking] as much as we can,” Velasquez said. The team is working on cutting down the number of ingredients and steps in some recipes. And they want to get more free and simple recipes in front of readers — such as with free seven-day and 14-day trials, and now with the emoji text line. The hope is to ultimately convert newly introduced readers into paid subscribers, who pay $5 a month or $40 a year for a subscription to NYT Cooking. “If a user voluntarily texts NYT Cooking, this is a strong signal of propensity to engage [and or] pay and reduces friction for the user getting the recipe they are after,” said Arvid Tchivzhel, svp of product at subscription management and customer data analytics firm Mather Economics. However, it will also require “significant outreach” to introduce audiences to this initiative, he added. The New York Times is marketing its new emoji text line with billboards in states like Michigan and Washington (for in-season cherries and corn, respectively), events and posts on its social accounts. Despite recent reports that subscriptions to news organizations have stalled in the past year, The New York Times Company has continued to grow its subscriber base, adding 190,000 digital-only subscribers in the first quarter of this year. The company now has over 9 million digital-only subscribers, though it does not break out data on how many subscribers are specifically subscribed to Cooking. In Q1 2023, The New York Times Company surpassed 3 million subscribers who were paying for a bundle (which includes access to the Times’ core news and standalone Cooking, Games, Wirecutter and The Athletic products) or multi-product subscription plan, thanks to about 520,000 new digital-only bundle and multi-product subscribers in the quarter. Velasquez said the main drivers of subscriber conversions are NYT Cooking app usage, videos on social media and newsletters. She declined to share how many NYT Cooking subscribers there are, or how many are converting through these platforms. Texting as an audience engagement channel historically hasn’t been successful in driving subscriber acquisitions, according Tchivzhel, based on his experience working with publishers at Mather Economics. “But it is perhaps a deeper level of engagement that can drive more meaningful connections between [the] audience and the Cooking product,” he said in an email. Other companies are also using text messaging as a marketing tactic, such as KBP Brands, a KFC franchisee , which recently expanded SMS marketing across its 847 U.S. locations. The Times has a plan for readers who don’t want to subscribe. extraction.body: The New York Times is testing a new AI feature for its Cooking app that helps users to modify recipes, and it has sparked some drama among users. Last Friday, NYT Cooking senior editor Genevieve Ko announced the feature, which can be used to recommend substitutions for ingredients and cooking equipment, scale recipes to any number of servings, and “generally make our recipes work for what a cook needs at that moment.” One of the examples given in the article shows a user asking to use baby spinach instead of kale, with the Cooking app feature advising that because baby spinach wilts faster, it should be added during a later step of the recipe. Ko says it can also change the recipes around different pans and tools. Customized recipes are private and can’t be published or shared through the app. The AI modification feature is being rolled out gradually while the NYT monitors how it performs — it’s currently available to all Cooking subscribers on the iOS app, and it will be more broadly available “soon.” Some NYT readers have pushed back against the feature, citing concerns in the article’s comment section around the environmental impact of widespread AI adoption and the general impact that AI features may have on the user experience. “I’ve always loved NYT Cooking and it pains me that the AI mandate has reached what used to be a wonderful and simple collection of recipes and notes from all sorts of different people.” This isn’t the first time that AI has been used by the NYT Cooking app. Ko says it was used to convert imperial volume measurements to metric weight measurements in recipes two years ago, and a feature was added last year that converts recipes to halve or double the original serving size. The comments on the new AI feature announcement post have since been closed, but NYT spokesperson Jordan Cohen tells The Verge that this is standard practice: “Comments on this article remained open for four days, with editors from Cooking taking care to answer questions, address concerns and engage directly with readers. We kept that conversation open to give readers a meaningful opportunity to share feedback and hear from the team. Closing comments on older articles is standard practice at The Times so that our moderators can focus on new discussions. We’re pleased to see that many members of our Cooking community are interested in exploring this tool and are already trying it out on our iOS app; they’re reporting good results.”

extraction.body: Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit The New York Times is trying out a new way to boost subscriptions and engagement to its paywalled NYT Cooking recipe platform. With a simple text featuring an emoji, the publisher is dishing out 150 recipes for free. From June 21 through August 15, people in the U.S. can text one fruit or vegetable emoji — like a strawberry, tomato, coconut or corn on the cob — to “361-COOK-NYT” and receive a link to a recipe for free featuring that food item. They will also get early access to special NYT Cooking events starting this July, such as cherry picking in Michigan. Normally, it would cost a subscriber $5 a month to access these features. Once readers get a recipe, they can text that same emoji up to five times to get different recipes featuring that same ingredient. The recipes come from a pool of them that the Times team deemed popular, are easy to make and highlighted summer produce, said Camilla Velasquez, general manager of New York Times Cooking. The Times hopes that giving away recipes for free via text message will help people who are familiar with the NYT Cooking product but aren’t paying subscribers to see the value of a subscription. The Times is not providing any additional special subscription offer or messaging to texters. “It’s [for] people who are curious about [NYT Cooking], but haven’t really been able to take the plunge because they haven’t been able to experience enough of the recipes and this is their opportunity to do so,” Velasquez said. Why emojis? Velasquez said it’s a “fast” and “playful” way to communicate with NYT Cooking and to simplify the process of finding summer recipes. It’s also a way to appeal to the younger audiences NYT Cooking is trying to target, such as millennials. For the text line, The New York Times is working with text messaging platform Subtext, which also works with other publishers like Condé Nast and USA Today Network. This text line is part of a broader strategy at NYT Cooking. The focus for NYT Cooking’s team this year has been “easy to find, easy to make,” Velasquez said. The team was hearing from readers that Cooking recipes were too hard to make and had inaccessible ingredients, Velasquez explained, so it became clear that they had to highlight easier recipes to both draw new subscribers in and retain those who are already paying. There are a couple of ways NYT Cooking is responding. The overarching goal is to “simplify [NYT Cooking] as much as we can,” Velasquez said. The team is working on cutting down the number of ingredients and steps in some recipes. And they want to get more free and simple recipes in front of readers — such as with free seven-day and 14-day trials, and now with the emoji text line. The hope is to ultimately convert newly introduced readers into paid subscribers, who pay $5 a month or $40 a year for a subscription to NYT Cooking. “If a user voluntarily texts NYT Cooking, this is a strong signal of propensity to engage [and or] pay and reduces friction for the user getting the recipe they are after,” said Arvid Tchivzhel, svp of product at subscription management and customer data analytics firm Mather Economics. However, it will also require “significant outreach” to introduce audiences to this initiative, he added. The New York Times is marketing its new emoji text line with billboards in states like Michigan and Washington (for in-season cherries and corn, respectively), events and posts on its social accounts. Despite recent reports that subscriptions to news organizations have stalled in the past year, The New York Times Company has continued to grow its subscriber base, adding 190,000 digital-only subscribers in the first quarter of this year. The company now has over 9 million digital-only subscribers, though it does not break out data on how many subscribers are specifically subscribed to Cooking. In Q1 2023, The New York Times Company surpassed 3 million subscribers who were paying for a bundle (which includes access to the Times’ core news and standalone Cooking, Games, Wirecutter and The Athletic products) or multi-product subscription plan, thanks to about 520,000 new digital-only bundle and multi-product subscribers in the quarter. Velasquez said the main drivers of subscriber conversions are NYT Cooking app usage, videos on social media and newsletters. She declined to share how many NYT Cooking subscribers there are, or how many are converting through these platforms. Texting as an audience engagement channel historically hasn’t been successful in driving subscriber acquisitions, according Tchivzhel, based on his experience working with publishers at Mather Economics. “But it is perhaps a deeper level of engagement that can drive more meaningful connections between [the] audience and the Cooking product,” he said in an email. Other companies are also using text messaging as a marketing tactic, such as KBP Brands, a KFC franchisee , which recently expanded SMS marketing across its 847 U.S. locations. The Times has a plan for readers who don’t want to subscribe. The team was hearing from readers that Cooking recipes were too hard to make and had inaccessible ingredients, Velasquez explained, so it became clear that they had to highlight easier recipes to both draw new subscribers in and retain those who are already paying.

There are a couple of ways NYT Cooking is responding. The overarching goal is to “simplify [NYT Cooking] as much as we can,” Velasquez said. The team is working on cutting down the number of ingredients and steps in some recipes. And they want to get more free and simple recipes in front of readers — such as with free seven-day and 14-day trials, and now with the emoji text line. The hope is to ultimately convert newly introduced readers into paid subscribers, who pay $5 a month or $40 a year for a subscription to NYT Cooking.

“If a user voluntarily texts NYT Cooking, this is a strong signal of propensity to engage [and or] pay and reduces friction for the user getting the recipe they are after,” said Arvid Tchivzhel, svp of product at subscription management and customer data analytics firm Mather Economics.

However, it will also require “significant outreach” to introduce audiences to this initiative, he added. The New York Times is marketing its new emoji text line with billboards in states like Michigan and Washington (for in-season cherries and corn, respectively), events and posts on its social accounts.

Despite recent reports that subscriptions to news organizations have stalled in the past year, The New York Times Company has continued to grow its subscriber base, adding 190,000 digital-only subscribers in the first quarter of this year. The company now has over 9 million digital-only subscribers, though it does not break out data on how many subscribers are specifically subscribed to Cooking.

In Q1 2023, The New York Times Company surpassed 3 million subscribers who were paying for a bundle (which includes access to the Times’ core news and standalone Cooking, Games, Wirecutter and The Athletic products) or multi-product subscription plan, thanks to about 520,000 new digital-only bundle and multi-product subscribers in the quarter.

Velasquez said the main drivers of subscriber conversions are NYT Cooking app usage, videos on social media and newsletters. She declined to share how many NYT Cooking subscribers there are, or how many are converting through these platforms.

Texting as an audience engagement channel historically hasn’t been successful in driving subscriber acquisitions, according Tchivzhel, based on his experience working with publishers at Mather Economics. “But it is perhaps a deeper level of engagement that can drive more meaningful connections between [the] audience and the Cooking product,” he said in an email.
Other companies are also using text messaging as a marketing tactic, such as KBP Brands, a KFC franchisee , which recently expanded SMS marketing across its 847 U.S. locations.
The Times has a plan for readers who don’t want to subscribe.

Smart health hardware these days has increasingly leaned on recurring software subscriptions to further monetize the user base, but Withings’ latest move is now crossing a line. If you pick up a Withings smart scale or hybrid smartwatch today hoping to route your health metrics into Apple Health or Google Health Connect for broader health tracking , you’re in for an unpleasant surprise: seamless data syncing to these platforms is no longer free. Withings responded to a customer complaint thread, announcing that the company has officially moved automatic third-party app syncing behind its paid Withings Plus subscription tier for any accounts created on or after October 13, 2026. While the initial outrage from customers was around Apple Health sync, the change also applies to Android users relying on Google Health Connect . From now on, automatically pushing weight, body composition, sleep metrics, or heart rates collected from Withings devices into Google Health Connect or Apple Health requires coughing up for Withings Plus, which costs around $99.50 a year or $9.95 per month. As Withings clarified, existing users are grandfathered in and retain free automatic sync to third-party services. This exemption is tied to your Withings account rather than any physical device, so you can purchase new hardware without triggering the paywall. However, such a move erodes customer confidence in the product ecosystem and casts doubt on the future. As an owner of a Withings Body Smart scale myself, I’d think twice about a new Withings purchase despite the grandfathering. Newly registered users receive a standard trial period to test Withings Plus features. However, once the trial lapses, automatic syncing will pause. The silver lining for new and future Withings users is that their data isn’t completely held hostage (yet). All users can still manually export their historical health records as CSV or PDF without a subscription. All users can continue to import data from other services into the Withings app and share clinical health reports with physicians. Withings isn’t the first smart health brand to try and monetize its ecosystem beyond the hardware. However, in terms of monetization, other smart health brands monetize predictive analytics and AI-based coaching features rather than holding data hostage. Automatic syncing to wider Apple and Google platforms feels like a core feature to me — my daily weight check-ins through my Withings Body Smart scale come right after the daily workouts that are tracked through an Apple Watch and are read together with my daily sleep scores to give me a holistic overview of how my body has progressed over the months. Without (free) automatic syncing back into the wider platform, I have a harder time recommending the smart scale to new users. User sentiment in Withings’ support thread echoes my own, as expected.

sources.title: This open-source project lets you sync Withings data to other apps without a subscription
passages: Anthony’s solution was to create an open-source project called YourOwnWeigh that reroutes your data away from Withings’ servers so it can be wirelessly synced to other apps and platforms for free.

When it was revealed earlier this month that Withings would require new users to subscribe to a Withings Plus subscription to sync heath data from the company’s devices to third-party apps, Tom Anthony, who was already fed up with the Withings mobile app which they describe as a “bloated mess,” became motivated to “free” their scales.
The YourOwnWeigh web app handles several tasks, including using Bluetooth to update Withings scales with alternate firmware so they upload data to a non-Withings server you’ve configured.
YourOwnWeigh is also currently limited to just two older models of Withings’ scales.
Instead of hosting a copy of Withings’ firmware, it’s downloaded and patched as needed.

extraction.body: When it was revealed earlier this month that Withings would require new users to subscribe to a Withings Plus subscription to sync heath data from the company’s devices to third-party apps, Tom Anthony, who was already fed up with the Withings mobile app which they describe as a “bloated mess,” became motivated to “free” their scales. Anthony’s solution was to create an open-source project called YourOwnWeigh that reroutes your data away from Withings’ servers so it can be wirelessly synced to other apps and platforms for free. You can read more about the project on GitHub, where you’ll also find quick-start guides on how to get YourOwnWeigh set up, but it mostly consists of a web app running on a server of your choice. If you don’t already operate your own, Anthony says YourOwnWeigh can run entirely on a free CloudFlare account given how little data it’s moving around. The YourOwnWeigh web app handles several tasks, including using Bluetooth to update Withings scales with alternate firmware so they upload data to a non-Withings server you’ve configured. Instead of hosting a copy of Withings’ firmware, it’s downloaded and patched as needed. The web app also imports the scale’s current settings and existing user profiles, and downloads the health data generated by regular weigh-ins. To get that data into Apple Health, Anthony used Apple Shortcuts to create a scheduled automation that pulls the Withings data off the alternate server and imports it into the app, but they’re hoping the community can come up with ways to expand the compatibility to other apps, including Google Health. YourOwnWeigh is also currently limited to just two older models of Withings’ scales. But assuming the firmware on newer models can be patched in a similar manner, expanding the project’s compatibility should be possible.

extraction.body: Affiliate links on Android Authority may earn us a commission. Learn more. Smart health hardware these days has increasingly leaned on recurring software subscriptions to further monetize the user base, but Withings’ latest move is now crossing a line. If you pick up a Withings smart scale or hybrid smartwatch today hoping to route your health metrics into Apple Health or Google Health Connect for broader health tracking , you’re in for an unpleasant surprise: seamless data syncing to these platforms is no longer free. Withings responded to a customer complaint thread, announcing that the company has officially moved automatic third-party app syncing behind its paid Withings Plus subscription tier for any accounts created on or after October 13, 2026. While the initial outrage from customers was around Apple Health sync, the change also applies to Android users relying on Google Health Connect . From now on, automatically pushing weight, body composition, sleep metrics, or heart rates collected from Withings devices into Google Health Connect or Apple Health requires coughing up for Withings Plus, which costs around $99.50 a year or $9.95 per month. As Withings clarified, existing users are grandfathered in and retain free automatic sync to third-party services. This exemption is tied to your Withings account rather than any physical device, so you can purchase new hardware without triggering the paywall. However, such a move erodes customer confidence in the product ecosystem and casts doubt on the future. As an owner of a Withings Body Smart scale myself, I’d think twice about a new Withings purchase despite the grandfathering. Newly registered users receive a standard trial period to test Withings Plus features. However, once the trial lapses, automatic syncing will pause. The silver lining for new and future Withings users is that their data isn’t completely held hostage (yet). All users can still manually export their historical health records as CSV or PDF without a subscription. All users can continue to import data from other services into the Withings app and share clinical health reports with physicians. Withings isn’t the first smart health brand to try and monetize its ecosystem beyond the hardware. However, in terms of monetization, other smart health brands monetize predictive analytics and AI-based coaching features rather than holding data hostage. Automatic syncing to wider Apple and Google platforms feels like a core feature to me — my daily weight check-ins through my Withings Body Smart scale come right after the daily workouts that are tracked through an Apple Watch and are read together with my daily sleep scores to give me a holistic overview of how my body has progressed over the months. Without (free) automatic syncing back into the wider platform, I have a harder time recommending the smart scale to new users. User sentiment in Withings’ support thread echoes my own, as expected.

extraction.body: When it was revealed earlier this month that Withings would require new users to subscribe to a Withings Plus subscription to sync heath data from the company’s devices to third-party apps, Tom Anthony, who was already fed up with the Withings mobile app which they describe as a “bloated mess,” became motivated to “free” their scales. Anthony’s solution was to create an open-source project called YourOwnWeigh that reroutes your data away from Withings’ servers so it can be wirelessly synced to other apps and platforms for free. You can read more about the project on GitHub, where you’ll also find quick-start guides on how to get YourOwnWeigh set up, but it mostly consists of a web app running on a server of your choice. If you don’t already operate your own, Anthony says YourOwnWeigh can run entirely on a free CloudFlare account given how little data it’s moving around. The YourOwnWeigh web app handles several tasks, including using Bluetooth to update Withings scales with alternate firmware so they upload data to a non-Withings server you’ve configured. Instead of hosting a copy of Withings’ firmware, it’s downloaded and patched as needed. The web app also imports the scale’s current settings and existing user profiles, and downloads the health data generated by regular weigh-ins. To get that data into Apple Health, Anthony used Apple Shortcuts to create a scheduled automation that pulls the Withings data off the alternate server and imports it into the app, but they’re hoping the community can come up with ways to expand the compatibility to other apps, including Google Health. YourOwnWeigh is also currently limited to just two older models of Withings’ scales. But assuming the firmware on newer models can be patched in a similar manner, expanding the project’s compatibility should be possible.

sources.title: Google tells platforms to noindex link-shared pages by default - PPC Land
passages: Google today revised its Search Central guide on preventing user-generated spam , widening it beyond comment forms and hosting services to "tools that let users publish shared pages, generated content, or web apps." The page gains a new section, "Only index content meant for Search," which says pages created for direct sharing, collaboration or utility should carry a noindex rule or be blocked from crawling by default, and it adds Search Console alerts and platform-level metrics to its monitoring checklist.
The change is logged in an entry posted today on Google's documentation changelog , and the page carries a "Last updated 2026-10-26 UTC" stamp.
Marketing teams use many of the kinds of services the guide now describes.
Campaign microsites, prototype landing pages, hosted forms, interactive calculators, AI-generated reports and shared chat outputs are often built on third-party platforms and passed around by link.
Google's guidance does not describe what that opt-in should look like.

When DuckDuckGo launched share links for its Duck.ai assistant on October 7, 2026, it said that shared conversations from ChatGPT and Claude had appeared in search results over the previous year, sometimes with names and personal details attached.

Security firm Claroc has cited 2025 cases in which more than 370,000 Grok conversations were indexed, figures it gave when Meta paused sharing in its Muse AI agent on October 20 after more than 6,800 share hostnames surfaced in passive DNS records.
Claroc said that exposure did not involve search engines, and that Muse's robots.txt asked crawlers to stay off its share paths.
It is filed as an update to a guide, not as a change to Google's spam policies, which live in a separate document.
That distinction carries particular weight for link-shared content.

A share link exists to be pasted elsewhere - into social posts, forums, messaging apps and emails - which is precisely the kind of external linking that can lead Google to index a blocked URL without its content.
The new section does not discuss the interaction.
Google's own products fall within the categories as well.
Neither product's coverage establishes whether its shared pages are indexed by search engines.
Google has not said whether enforcement will follow, and the guide describes no consequence for a platform that leaves shared pages indexable.

What the page does say is that spammers "may create a large number of pages or sites that violate our spam policies." Those policies include scaled content abuse , which covers mass-produced pages that add little value for users, and Google stated in May 2026 that its spam policies apply to AI Overviews and AI Mode as well as to traditional results.
Those pages can end up in Google Search even when they were only meant for the few people holding the link, which lets spammers fill results with junk hosted on someone else's trusted website.
Google names no products, companies or technologies.
The words "artificial intelligence" appear nowhere on the page.
A robots.txt disallow rule works at a different stage.
It stops a crawler from fetching a URL but does not, on its own, keep that URL out of the index.
The two methods therefore do not stack, and combining them can defeat the noindex rule.
Google does not say which services prompted the change.
PPC Land's coverage over the past year has documented several types of product that match the guide's new language.
The change also concerns publishers, SEO teams and marketers who build on those platforms or compete with pages hosted on them.

Research by security firm RedAccess, reported in May 2026, found more than 5,000 apps built with vibe coding tools such as Lovable, Replit, Base44 and Netlify that had essentially no authentication, along with phishing sites impersonating Bank of America, Costco, FedEx, Trader Joe's and McDonald's on Lovable's domain .
RedAccess located the apps by searching Google and Bing for the platforms' default domains.
The UGC Fresh Data Program offers a contrast with today's change.

Within one month, then, Google has documented a faster route into its systems for moderated public discussion, and a default route out of its index for user-created pages that were never meant to be searched.
For platform operators, the monitoring additions carry a cost.

Verifying subdomains, watching Page Indexing reports for unexplained growth, and building internal alerts for concentrated URL creation by a handful of accounts all require engineering and moderation time.
The guide acknowledges this kind of trade-off elsewhere, noting that moderation "adds overhead" to daily workflows.
It does not quantify what Google expects of smaller services.
The "Monitor your service for abuse" list gained two items, both placed at the top.
The first asks operators to verify their site or subdomain in Search Console so that Google can email them if it issues a manual action against the site or detects security issues.

It also names two Search Console reports, Page Indexing and Search performance, to be checked regularly for "unexpected spikes in indexed pages, impressions, or queries" that do not match what the platform is for.
According to Search Engine Roundtable, consultant Marie Haynes asked on X whether the update means new manual actions are coming for AI tools and app-building platforms.

Another clue from Google about new types of spam they are dealing with (likely at a big enough scale to warrant changing their documentation) and ... another clue about what they'll be targeting in the future?"
The question of manual actions has been live for weeks.
The evidence was anecdotal, and Google did not comment.
That update was the fourth spam update of the year, following rollouts on March 24, June 24 and August 18 .

It still suggests applying a noindex robots meta tag to posts from new users who have no reputation on a platform, lifting it once they earn one, and adding a "nofollow or ugc rel attribute" to links in untrusted content.
Pages published on trusted platform domains can compete in results with original sites, and since May those same spam policies have applied to the AI answers that sit above the links.
Platforms that tighten indexing defaults reduce one source of that competition.
Those signals remain, now from third place down.
Will those platforms switch their indexing defaults?
The monitoring section still cites the site: search operator, Google Alerts, web server logs, the Google Safe Browsing API and language detection tools, including the Google Translate API v2.

extraction.body: Web app builders and generated-content tools now sit in the spam guide, next to new Search Console alerts. Will those platforms switch their indexing defaults? Google today revised its Search Central guide on preventing user-generated spam , widening it beyond comment forms and hosting services to "tools that let users publish shared pages, generated content, or web apps." The page gains a new section, "Only index content meant for Search," which says pages created for direct sharing, collaboration or utility should carry a noindex rule or be blocked from crawling by default, and it adds Search Console alerts and platform-level metrics to its monitoring checklist. The change is logged in an entry posted today on Google's documentation changelog , and the page carries a "Last updated 2026-10-26 UTC" stamp. Google has a help page for websites that let the public post things, and today it said that tools where people make pages, apps or automatically generated content to share by link can be abused by spammers too. Those pages can end up in Google Search even when they were only meant for the few people holding the link, which lets spammers fill results with junk hosted on someone else's trusted website. Google now says pages like that should be hidden from search by default, and that the companies running these tools should watch Search Console and their own numbers for sudden jumps in new public pages. The page is titled "Prevent user-generated spam on your site and platform." It sits in the "Preventing and monitoring abuse" part of Search Central's monitoring and debugging documentation, alongside guides on malware, phishing and deceptive sites, and the Google Safe Browsing Repeat Offenders Policy. Three passages are new or rewritten. Every other paragraph, from the reputation system for new accounts to an example about overnight traffic from Italian IP addresses on a site aimed at Japan, is unchanged word for word. The introduction previously warned that spammers exploit open comment forms, and that "hosting platforms may be similarly open to abuse," with spammers creating large numbers of sites that break Google's spam policies. The revised sentence reads: "Hosting platforms and tools that let users publish shared pages, generated content, or web apps may be similarly open to abuse; spammers may create a large number of pages or sites that violate our spam policies and add little or no value to the web." Two edits sit inside that sentence. The first adds a category of service defined by what its users can publish - shared pages, generated content and web apps - rather than by whether it sells hosting. The second changes the unit of abuse from "sites" to "pages or sites," which brings individual URLs, not just whole sites, within the scope of the warning. Google names no products, companies or technologies. The words "artificial intelligence" appear nowhere on the page. The new section, "Only index content meant for Search," is placed after the advice on identifying spammy accounts and before the passage on manual approval. It runs to two short paragraphs. The first asks services whose users create "shareable pages, generated outputs, or interactive tools" to consider whether that content is meant to be found through search engines or "only accessed directly by people with a link." "When pages are created for direct sharing, collaboration, or utility rather than public search discovery, apply the noindex rule (using a robots meta tag or X-Robots-Tag HTTP response header) or block crawling in robots.txt by default." Everything turns on the final two words. The guide does not tell platforms to keep shared content out of Search permanently, nor does it describe what should happen when a user wants a shared page to be found. Exclusion is the starting position. How, or whether, a page later moves into the index is left unaddressed. The "Monitor your service for abuse" list gained two items, both placed at the top. The first asks operators to verify their site or subdomain in Search Console so that Google can email them if it issues a manual action against the site or detects security issues. It also names two Search Console reports, Page Indexing and Search performance, to be checked regularly for "unexpected spikes in indexed pages, impressions, or queries" that do not match what the platform is for. The reference to subdomains is specific. Many hosting and app-building services give each user project its own subdomain, and a subdomain can be verified as a separate Search Console property. Neither item comes with a threshold. Google does not say what size of spike warrants attention, or what share of indexable URLs counts as "large." The page is titled "Prevent user-generated spam on your site and platform." It sits in the "Preventing and monitoring abuse" part of Search Central's monitoring and debugging documentation, alongside guides on malware, phishing and deceptive sites, and the Google Safe Browsing Repeat Offenders Policy. The introduction previously warned that spammers exploit open comment forms, and that "hosting platforms may be similarly open to abuse," with spammers creating large numbers of sites that break Google's spam policies. The first adds a category of service defined by what its users can publish - shared pages, generated content and web apps - rather than by whether it sells hosting. The second changes the unit of abuse from "sites" to "pages or sites," which brings individual URLs, not just whole sites, within the scope of the warning. Google names no products, companies or technologies. The words "artificial intelligence" appear nowhere on the page.

The new section, "Only index content meant for Search," is placed after the advice on identifying spammy accounts and before the passage on manual approval. It runs to two short paragraphs. The first asks services whose users create "shareable pages, generated outputs, or interactive tools" to consider whether that content is meant to be found through search engines or "only accessed directly by people with a link."

"When pages are created for direct sharing, collaboration, or utility rather than public search discovery, apply the noindex rule (using a robots meta tag or X-Robots-Tag HTTP response header) or block crawling in robots.txt by default."

Everything turns on the final two words. sources.title: Google's New AI Spam Detector Judges Networks, Not Pages — High-AI Sites Are Already Slipping - CMSWire
passages: The timing matters because the traffic data is already moving.

Over the past month I've watched websites with heavy concentrations of AI-generated content, the kind Ahrefs now flags as "Very high" on its AI Content Level metric, begin sliding in Google organic search.
This also lines up with the rollout of Google’s latest June 2026 spam update that recently finished rolling out.
But when declines cluster around a specific site profile right as Google publishes both an algorithm update and research on detecting that exact profile, it deserves attention.
Google's 2023 guidance rewards content for quality regardless of production method; enforcement targets scaled content abuse, meaning high-volume, low-value pages built mainly to manipulate rankings.
A content classifier scans for repetitive, templated narratives and for high-frequency publishing behavior that no human schedule produces.
An infrastructure component ties accounts back to a common source.
When enough accounts in a cluster show the same AI-generated templates, Google removes the whole cluster at once rather than penalizing individual pages.
Automation has been part of publishing for decades, from sports scores to weather forecasts.
The risk calculus for AI-heavy SEO & AEO has changed shape.
The question used to be whether a single page looked low quality.
The question now includes whether your templates, publishing cadence, infrastructure and content similarities make your operation resemble a coordinated spam network.
Gabe's read: Google will not let companies spam their way into AI search , and marketers should expect stronger automated systems plus manual actions.
Traditional quality filters evaluate one piece of content at a time.
Google's researchers acknowledge that generative AI broke that model.
Spammers can now produce endless variations of what the paper calls functionally identical content: every page technically unique, every page effectively the same.
At volume, that flood is built to swamp content-level filters.
SBERT has existed since 2019, and Montti points out the SEO industry has rarely discussed it as a spam-detection mechanism.
Its appearance in a Google paper about catching synthetic spam suggests it may have been put to that use only recently.
One more detail worth knowing: speed of adaptation.
The paper describes using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and Automatic Prompt Optimization (APO) to retune classifiers when spammers move to new generative models.
That means days of adjustment instead of months of retraining.
When the next model ships and spam operations migrate, Google can follow almost immediately.
The paper, covered by Roger Montti at Search Engine Journal and shared widely by Glenn Gabe on X , describes the Scalable Cluster Termination System.

coreStoryFacts.text: Google today revised its Search Central guide on preventing user-generated spam , widening it beyond comment forms and hosting services to "tools that let users publish shared pages, generated content, or web apps." The page gains a new section, "Only index content meant for Search," which says pages created for direct sharing, collaboration or utility should carry a noindex rule or be blocked from crawling by default, and it adds Search Console alerts and platform-level metrics to its monitoring checklist.
The change is logged in an entry posted today on Google's documentation changelog , and the page carries a "Last updated 2026-10-26 UTC" stamp.
Marketing teams use many of the kinds of services the guide now describes.
Campaign microsites, prototype landing pages, hosted forms, interactive calculators, AI-generated reports and shared chat outputs are often built on third-party platforms and passed around by link.
Google's guidance does not describe what that opt-in should look like.

When DuckDuckGo launched share links for its Duck.ai assistant on October 7, 2026, it said that shared conversations from ChatGPT and Claude had appeared in search results over the previous year, sometimes with names and personal details attached.

Security firm Claroc has cited 2025 cases in which more than 370,000 Grok conversations were indexed, figures it gave when Meta paused sharing in its Muse AI agent on October 20 after more than 6,800 share hostnames surfaced in passive DNS records.
Claroc said that exposure did not involve search engines, and that Muse's robots.txt asked crawlers to stay off its share paths.
It is filed as an update to a guide, not as a change to Google's spam policies, which live in a separate document.
That distinction carries particular weight for link-shared content.

A share link exists to be pasted elsewhere - into social posts, forums, messaging apps and emails - which is precisely the kind of external linking that can lead Google to index a blocked URL without its content.
The new section does not discuss the interaction.
Google's own products fall within the categories as well.
Neither product's coverage establishes whether its shared pages are indexed by search engines.
Google has not said whether enforcement will follow, and the guide describes no consequence for a platform that leaves shared pages indexable.

What the page does say is that spammers "may create a large number of pages or sites that violate our spam policies." Those policies include scaled content abuse , which covers mass-produced pages that add little value for users, and Google stated in May 2026 that its spam policies apply to AI Overviews and AI Mode as well as to traditional results.
Those pages can end up in Google Search even when they were only meant for the few people holding the link, which lets spammers fill results with junk hosted on someone else's trusted website.
Google names no products, companies or technologies.
The words "artificial intelligence" appear nowhere on the page.
A robots.txt disallow rule works at a different stage.
It stops a crawler from fetching a URL but does not, on its own, keep that URL out of the index.
The two methods therefore do not stack, and combining them can defeat the noindex rule.
Google does not say which services prompted the change.
PPC Land's coverage over the past year has documented several types of product that match the guide's new language.

extraction.body: Web app builders and generated-content tools now sit in the spam guide, next to new Search Console alerts. Will those platforms switch their indexing defaults? Google today revised its Search Central guide on preventing user-generated spam , widening it beyond comment forms and hosting services to "tools that let users publish shared pages, generated content, or web apps." The page gains a new section, "Only index content meant for Search," which says pages created for direct sharing, collaboration or utility should carry a noindex rule or be blocked from crawling by default, and it adds Search Console alerts and platform-level metrics to its monitoring checklist. The change is logged in an entry posted today on Google's documentation changelog , and the page carries a "Last updated 2026-10-26 UTC" stamp. Google has a help page for websites that let the public post things, and today it said that tools where people make pages, apps or automatically generated content to share by link can be abused by spammers too. Those pages can end up in Google Search even when they were only meant for the few people holding the link, which lets spammers fill results with junk hosted on someone else's trusted website. Google now says pages like that should be hidden from search by default, and that the companies running these tools should watch Search Console and their own numbers for sudden jumps in new public pages. The page is titled "Prevent user-generated spam on your site and platform." It sits in the "Preventing and monitoring abuse" part of Search Central's monitoring and debugging documentation, alongside guides on malware, phishing and deceptive sites, and the Google Safe Browsing Repeat Offenders Policy. Three passages are new or rewritten. Every other paragraph, from the reputation system for new accounts to an example about overnight traffic from Italian IP addresses on a site aimed at Japan, is unchanged word for word. The introduction previously warned that spammers exploit open comment forms, and that "hosting platforms may be similarly open to abuse," with spammers creating large numbers of sites that break Google's spam policies. The revised sentence reads: "Hosting platforms and tools that let users publish shared pages, generated content, or web apps may be similarly open to abuse; spammers may create a large number of pages or sites that violate our spam policies and add little or no value to the web." Two edits sit inside that sentence. The first adds a category of service defined by what its users can publish - shared pages, generated content and web apps - rather than by whether it sells hosting. The second changes the unit of abuse from "sites" to "pages or sites," which brings individual URLs, not just whole sites, within the scope of the warning. Google names no products, companies or technologies. The words "artificial intelligence" appear nowhere on the page. The new section, "Only index content meant for Search," is placed after the advice on identifying spammy accounts and before the passage on manual approval. It runs to two short paragraphs. The first asks services whose users create "shareable pages, generated outputs, or interactive tools" to consider whether that content is meant to be found through search engines or "only accessed directly by people with a link." "When pages are created for direct sharing, collaboration, or utility rather than public search discovery, apply the noindex rule (using a robots meta tag or X-Robots-Tag HTTP response header) or block crawling in robots.txt by default." Everything turns on the final two words. The guide does not tell platforms to keep shared content out of Search permanently, nor does it describe what should happen when a user wants a shared page to be found. Exclusion is the starting position. How, or whether, a page later moves into the index is left unaddressed. The "Monitor your service for abuse" list gained two items, both placed at the top. The first asks operators to verify their site or subdomain in Search Console so that Google can email them if it issues a manual action against the site or detects security issues. It also names two Search Console reports, Page Indexing and Search performance, to be checked regularly for "unexpected spikes in indexed pages, impressions, or queries" that do not match what the platform is for. The reference to subdomains is specific. Many hosting and app-building services give each user project its own subdomain, and a subdomain can be verified as a separate Search Console property. Neither item comes with a threshold. Google does not say what size of spike warrants attention, or what share of indexable URLs counts as "large." In the previous version, the monitoring list opened with spam signals such as redirects, large numbers of ad sections, spammy keywords and large blocks of encoded JavaScript, and Search Console was not mentioned anywhere on the page. Those signals remain, now from third place down. The changelog entry is brief. Under "What," Google wrote that it "Updated the user-generated spam prevention guide with guidance on blocking indexing of link-shared content and monitoring abuse in Search Console." The "Why" line says the change was made "To help platforms keep user-created pages that aren't meant for Search out of the index and detect spam earlier." The phrase "link-shared content" appears in the changelog but not on the guide itself, which speaks of "shareable pages" and "direct sharing." The entry offers no figures on the scale of the abuse, no examples and no date for any related enforcement. It is filed as an update to a guide, not as a change to Google's spam policies, which live in a separate document. The page remains a set of recommendations addressed to site and platform operators. The new section gives platforms two mechanisms, and they are not interchangeable. A robots.txt disallow rule works at a different stage. It stops a crawler from fetching a URL but does not, on its own, keep that URL out of the index. Google's John Mueller explained in September 2024 that pages blocked by robots.txt can still be indexed when other pages link to them, and that a crawler shut out by robots.txt never sees a noindex tag on the blocked page. The two methods therefore do not stack, and combining them can defeat the noindex rule. That distinction carries particular weight for link-shared content. A share link exists to be pasted elsewhere - into social posts, forums, messaging apps and emails - which is precisely the kind of external linking that can lead Google to index a blocked URL without its content. The new section does not discuss the interaction. It also differs in emphasis from another Search Central page revised five days earlier: on October 21, Google's "Control what you share with Google Search" page listed robots.txt as a blocking method only for images and videos , not as a way to keep web pages out of results. The remainder of the guide predates today's revision. It still suggests applying a noindex robots meta tag to posts from new users who have no reputation on a platform, lifting it once they earn one, and adding a "nofollow or ugc rel attribute" to links in untrusted content. The concern is the use of a platform's domain to publish spam rather than ranking damage to the host: in January, Mueller said that spam links in blog comments have no effect on a host site's rankings . Other recommendations are untouched: a published abuse policy communicated at sign-up; records of signup patterns such as form completion time, request volumes from one IP address range, user agents and chosen user names; manual approval of suspicious interactions; IP blocklists and firewall deny lists, with Akismet named as an option for WordPress; and reCAPTCHA or similar verification at sign-up to keep automated scripts from generating large numbers of sites. The monitoring section still cites the site: search operator, Google Alerts, web server logs, the Google Safe Browsing API and language detection tools, including the Google Translate API v2. Google does not say which services prompted the change. PPC Land's coverage over the past year has documented several types of product that match the guide's new language. Chat transcripts are one. When DuckDuckGo launched share links for its Duck.ai assistant on October 7, 2026, it said that shared conversations from ChatGPT and Claude had appeared in search results over the previous year, sometimes with names and personal details attached. Duck.ai's share pages instruct search engines not to index them in both the page markup and the server response, the two noindex methods that Google's new section lists, and they expire after 48 hours by default. Security firm Claroc has cited 2025 cases in which more than 370,000 Grok conversations were indexed, figures it gave when Meta paused sharing in its Muse AI agent on October 20 after more than 6,800 share hostnames surfaced in passive DNS records. Claroc said that exposure did not involve search engines, and that Muse's robots.txt asked crawlers to stay off its share paths. App builders are another. Research by security firm RedAccess, reported in May 2026, found more than 5,000 apps built with vibe coding tools such as Lovable, Replit, Base44 and Netlify that had essentially no authentication, along with phishing sites impersonating Bank of America, Costco, FedEx, Trader Joe's and McDonald's on Lovable's domain . RedAccess located the apps by searching Google and Bing for the platforms' default domains. Google's own products fall within the categories as well. Opal, its no-code app builder, expanded from 15 to more than 160 countries in November 2025 , drawing criticism from independent publisher advocate Nate Hake, who argued that promoting mass-generated blog and marketing content conflicted with Google's own Search guidance. Playground, the game builder Google opened to US adults on October 7, 2026, lets creators share games by link or publish them to a public gallery . Neither product's coverage establishes whether its shared pages are indexed by search engines. Search Engine Roundtable , which reported the change today, described the new section as a significant addition that tells platforms to distinguish between content intended for public discovery and content intended only for direct access. According to Search Engine Roundtable, consultant Marie Haynes asked on X whether the update means new manual actions are coming for AI tools and app-building platforms. SEO consultant Lily Ray wrote on X : "My first thought was Claude artifacts, ChatGPT pages/sites, FB posts, and other social/AI tools that make it easy to churn out indexable UGC at scale. Another clue from Google about new types of spam they are dealing with (likely at a big enough scale to warrant changing their documentation) and ... another clue about what they'll be targeting in the future?" Both readings remain speculation. Google has not said whether enforcement will follow, and the guide describes no consequence for a platform that leaves shared pages indexable. What the page does say is that spammers "may create a large number of pages or sites that violate our spam policies." Those policies include scaled content abuse , which covers mass-produced pages that add little value for users, and Google stated in May 2026 that its spam policies apply to AI Overviews and AI Mode as well as to traditional results. The question of manual actions has been live for weeks. On October 7, Haynes reported a sharp rise in requests for help with manual actions, from essentially none to several a week, as Google's September 2026 spam update ran for 13 days and 16 hours before finishing on October 8. The evidence was anecdotal, and Google did not comment. That update was the fourth spam update of the year, following rollouts on March 24, June 24 and August 18 . The UGC Fresh Data Program offers a contrast with today's change. It gives approved forum and social platforms a dedicated pipeline to send new public posts and engagement signals to Google, on condition that they run active moderation and a user reporting mechanism, and that every post is tied to a creator with a public profile. Within one month, then, Google has documented a faster route into its systems for moderated public discussion, and a default route out of its index for user-created pages that were never meant to be searched. Marketing teams use many of the kinds of services the guide now describes. Campaign microsites, prototype landing pages, hosted forms, interactive calculators, AI-generated reports and shared chat outputs are often built on third-party platforms and passed around by link. If platforms adopt noindex as the default for such pages, content created there will not enter Google's index unless the platform provides, and the user selects, a way to make it public. Google's guidance does not describe what that opt-in should look like. For publishers and SEO teams, the change concerns the supply side of search spam. Pages published on trusted platform domains can compete in results with original sites, and since May those same spam policies have applied to the AI answers that sit above the links. Platforms that tighten indexing defaults reduce one source of that competition. The guide's warning applies to every such service, whatever its current defaults. For platform operators, the monitoring additions carry a cost. Verifying subdomains, watching Page Indexing reports for unexplained growth, and building internal alerts for concentrated URL creation by a handful of accounts all require engineering and moderation time. The guide acknowledges this kind of trade-off elsewhere, noting that moderation "adds overhead" to daily workflows. It does not quantify what Google expects of smaller services. And it leaves a commercial tension unexamined: many platforms have grown in part through user pages that rank in Google, and the line between a page "meant for Search" and one made "for direct sharing" is drawn by the platform, not by Google. The change also concerns publishers, SEO teams and marketers who build on those platforms or compete with pages hosted on them. What: Google revised its guide to preventing user-generated spam. It now names tools for shared pages, generated content and web apps as open to abuse, adds an "Only index content meant for Search" section recommending noindex (via robots meta tag or X-Robots-Tag) or a robots.txt block by default for pages made for direct sharing, collaboration or utility, and adds Search Console verification, report checks and platform-level creation and indexing alerts to its monitoring advice. When: Today, October 26, 2026, according to Google's documentation changelog and the page's "Last updated" stamp. Where: On the "Prevent user-generated spam on your site and platform" page in the Search Central documentation, under monitoring and debugging, with the monitoring tools located in Search Console.
