It sits in the "Preventing and monitoring abuse" part of Search Central's monitoring and debugging documentation, alongside guides on malware, phishing and deceptive sites, and the Google Safe Browsing Repeat Offenders Policy. Three passages are new or rewritten. Every other paragraph, from the reputation system for new accounts to an example about overnight traffic from Italian IP addresses on a site aimed at Japan, is unchanged word for word.

The introduction previously warned that spammers exploit open comment forms, and that "hosting platforms may be similarly open to abuse," with spammers creating large numbers of sites that break Google's spam policies. The revised sentence reads: "Hosting platforms and tools that let users publish shared pages, generated content, or web apps may be similarly open to abuse; spammers may create a large number of pages or sites that violate our spam policies and add little or no value to the web."

Two edits sit inside that sentence. The first adds a category of service defined by what its users can publish - shared pages, generated content and web apps - rather than by whether it sells hosting. The second changes the unit of abuse from "sites" to "pages or sites," which brings individual URLs, not just whole sites, within the scope of the warning. Google names no products, companies or technologies. The words "artificial intelligence" appear nowhere on the page.

The new section, "Only index content meant for Search," is placed after the advice on identifying spammy accounts and before the passage on manual approval. It runs to two short paragraphs. The first asks services whose users create "shareable pages, generated outputs, or interactive tools" to consider whether that content is meant to be found through search engines or "only accessed directly by people with a link."

"When pages are created for direct sharing, collaboration, or utility rather than public search discovery, apply the noindex rule (using a robots meta tag or X-Robots-Tag HTTP response header) or block crawling in robots.txt by default."

Everything turns on the final two words. The guide does not tell platforms to keep shared content out of Search permanently, nor does it describe what should happen when a user wants a shared page to be found. Exclusion is the starting position. How, or whether, a page later moves into the index is left unaddressed.

The "Monitor your service for abuse" list gained two items, both placed at the top. The first asks operators to verify their site or subdomain in Search Console so that Google can email them if it issues a manual action against the site or detects security issues. It also names two Search Console reports, Page Indexing and Search performance, to be checked regularly for "unexpected spikes in indexed pages, impressions, or queries" that do not match what the platform is for. The reference to subdomains is specific. Many hosting and app-building services give each user project its own subdomain, and a subdomain can be verified as a separate Search Console property.

Neither item comes with a threshold. Google does not say what size of spike warrants attention, or what share of indexable URLs counts as "large." In the previous version, the monitoring list opened with spam signals such as redirects, large numbers of ad sections, spammy keywords and large blocks of encoded JavaScript, and Search Console was not mentioned anywhere on the page. Those signals remain, now from third place down.

The changelog entry is brief. Under "What," Google wrote that it "Updated the user-generated spam prevention guide with guidance on blocking indexing of link-shared content and monitoring abuse in Search Console." The "Why" line says the change was made "To help platforms keep user-created pages that aren't meant for Search out of the index and detect spam earlier."

The phrase "link-shared content" appears in the changelog but not on the guide itself, which speaks of "shareable pages" and "direct sharing." The entry offers no figures on the scale of the abuse, no examples and no date for any related enforcement. It is filed as an update to a guide, not as a change to Google's spam policies, which live in a separate document. The page remains a set of recommendations addressed to site and platform operators.
The new section gives platforms two mechanisms, and they are not interchangeable.

A robots.txt disallow rule works at a different stage. It stops a crawler from fetching a URL but does not, on its own, keep that URL out of the index. Google's John Mueller explained in September 2024 that pages blocked by robots.txt can still be indexed when other pages link to them, and that a crawler shut out by robots.txt never sees a noindex tag on the blocked page. The two methods therefore do not stack, and combining them can defeat the noindex rule.

That distinction carries particular weight for link-shared content. A share link exists to be pasted elsewhere - into social posts, forums, messaging apps and emails - which is precisely the kind of external linking that can lead Google to index a blocked URL without its content. The new section does not discuss the interaction. It also differs in emphasis from another Search Central page revised five days earlier: on October 21, Google's "Control what you share with Google Search" page listed robots.txt as a blocking method only for images and videos , not as a way to keep web pages out of results.

The remainder of the guide predates today's revision. It still suggests applying a noindex robots meta tag to posts from new users who have no reputation on a platform, lifting it once they earn one, and adding a "nofollow or ugc rel attribute" to links in untrusted content. The concern is the use of a platform's domain to publish spam rather than ranking damage to the host: in January, Mueller said that spam links in blog comments have no effect on a host site's rankings .

Other recommendations are untouched: a published abuse policy communicated at sign-up; records of signup patterns such as form completion time, request volumes from one IP address range, user agents and chosen user names; manual approval of suspicious interactions; IP blocklists and firewall deny lists, with Akismet named as an option for WordPress; and reCAPTCHA or similar verification at sign-up to keep automated scripts from generating large numbers of sites. The monitoring section still cites the site: search operator, Google Alerts, web server logs, the Google Safe Browsing API and language detection tools, including the Google Translate API v2.
Google does not say which services prompted the change. PPC Land's coverage over the past year has documented several types of product that match the guide's new language.

Chat transcripts are one. When DuckDuckGo launched share links for its Duck.ai assistant on October 7, 2026, it said that shared conversations from ChatGPT and Claude had appeared in search results over the previous year, sometimes with names and personal details attached. Duck.ai's share pages instruct search engines not to index them in both the page markup and the server response, the two noindex methods that Google's new section lists, and they expire after 48 hours by default. Security firm Claroc has cited 2025 cases in which more than 370,000 Grok conversations were indexed, figures it gave when Meta paused sharing in its Muse AI agent on October 20 after more than 6,800 share hostnames surfaced in passive DNS records. Claroc said that exposure did not involve search engines, and that Muse's robots.txt asked crawlers to stay off its share paths.

App builders are another. Research by security firm RedAccess, reported in May 2026, found more than 5,000 apps built with vibe coding tools such as Lovable, Replit, Base44 and Netlify that had essentially no authentication, along with phishing sites impersonating Bank of America, Costco, FedEx, Trader Joe's and McDonald's on Lovable's domain . RedAccess located the apps by searching Google and Bing for the platforms' default domains.

Google's own products fall within the categories as well. Opal, its no-code app builder, expanded from 15 to more than 160 countries in November 2025 , drawing criticism from independent publisher advocate Nate Hake, who argued that promoting mass-generated blog and marketing content conflicted with Google's own Search guidance. Playground, the game builder Google opened to US adults on October 7, 2026, lets creators share games by link or publish them to a public gallery . Neither product's coverage establishes whether its shared pages are indexed by search engines.

Search Engine Roundtable , which reported the change today, described the new section as a significant addition that tells platforms to distinguish between content intended for public discovery and content intended only for direct access. According to Search Engine Roundtable, consultant Marie Haynes asked on X whether the update means new manual actions are coming for AI tools and app-building platforms.

SEO consultant Lily Ray wrote on X : "My first thought was Claude artifacts, ChatGPT pages/sites, FB posts, and other social/AI tools that make it easy to churn out indexable UGC at scale. Another clue from Google about new types of spam they are dealing with (likely at a big enough scale to warrant changing their documentation) and ... another clue about what they'll be targeting in the future?"

Both readings remain speculation. Google has not said whether enforcement will follow, and the guide describes no consequence for a platform that leaves shared pages indexable. What the page does say is that spammers "may create a large number of pages or sites that violate our spam policies." Those policies include scaled content abuse , which covers mass-produced pages that add little value for users, and Google stated in May 2026 that its spam policies apply to AI Overviews and AI Mode as well as to traditional results.

The question of manual actions has been live for weeks. On October 7, Haynes reported a sharp rise in requests for help with manual actions, from essentially none to several a week, as Google's September 2026 spam update ran for 13 days and 16 hours before finishing on October 8. The evidence was anecdotal, and Google did not comment. That update was the fourth spam update of the year, following rollouts on March 24, June 24 and August 18 .

The UGC Fresh Data Program offers a contrast with today's change. It gives approved forum and social platforms a dedicated pipeline to send new public posts and engagement signals to Google, on condition that they run active moderation and a user reporting mechanism, and that every post is tied to a creator with a public profile. Within one month, then, Google has documented a faster route into its systems for moderated public discussion, and a default route out of its index for user-created pages that were never meant to be searched.

Marketing teams use many of the kinds of services the guide now describes. Campaign microsites, prototype landing pages, hosted forms, interactive calculators, AI-generated reports and shared chat outputs are often built on third-party platforms and passed around by link. If platforms adopt noindex as the default for such pages, content created there will not enter Google's index unless the platform provides, and the user selects, a way to make it public. Google's guidance does not describe what that opt-in should look like.

For publishers and SEO teams, the change concerns the supply side of search spam. Pages published on trusted platform domains can compete in results with original sites, and since May those same spam policies have applied to the AI answers that sit above the links. Platforms that tighten indexing defaults reduce one source of that competition. The guide's warning applies to every such service, whatever its current defaults.

For platform operators, the monitoring additions carry a cost. Verifying subdomains, watching Page Indexing reports for unexplained growth, and building internal alerts for concentrated URL creation by a handful of accounts all require engineering and moderation time. The guide acknowledges this kind of trade-off elsewhere, noting that moderation "adds overhead" to daily workflows. It does not quantify what Google expects of smaller services. And it leaves a commercial tension unexamined: many platforms have grown in part through user pages that rank in Google, and the line between a page "meant for Search" and one made "for direct sharing" is drawn by the platform, not by Google.

Who: Google, through its Search Central documentation, addressing operators of hosting platforms and tools that let users publish shared pages, generated content or web apps. The change also concerns publishers, SEO teams and marketers who build on those platforms or compete with pages hosted on them.

What: Google revised its guide to preventing user-generated spam. It now names tools for shared pages, generated content and web apps as open to abuse, adds an "Only index content meant for Search" section recommending noindex (via robots meta tag or X-Robots-Tag) or a robots.txt block by default for pages made for direct sharing, collaboration or utility, and adds Search Console verification, report checks and platform-level creation and indexing alerts to its monitoring advice.
When: Today, October 26, 2026, according to Google's documentation changelog and the page's "Last updated" stamp.
Where: On the "Prevent user-generated spam on your site and platform" page in the Search Central documentation, under monitoring and debugging, with the monitoring tools located in Search Console.

Why: According to Google, "To help platforms keep user-created pages that aren't meant for Search out of the index and detect spam earlier." Google has not said which services prompted the change or whether enforcement will follow.

passages: The timing matters because the traffic data is already moving.

Over the past month I've watched websites with heavy concentrations of AI-generated content, the kind Ahrefs now flags as "Very high" on its AI Content Level metric, begin sliding in Google organic search.
This also lines up with the rollout of Google’s latest June 2026 spam update that recently finished rolling out.
But when declines cluster around a specific site profile right as Google publishes both an algorithm update and research on detecting that exact profile, it deserves attention.
Google's 2023 guidance rewards content for quality regardless of production method; enforcement targets scaled content abuse, meaning high-volume, low-value pages built mainly to manipulate rankings.
A content classifier scans for repetitive, templated narratives and for high-frequency publishing behavior that no human schedule produces.
An infrastructure component ties accounts back to a common source.
When enough accounts in a cluster show the same AI-generated templates, Google removes the whole cluster at once rather than penalizing individual pages.
Automation has been part of publishing for decades, from sports scores to weather forecasts.
The risk calculus for AI-heavy SEO & AEO has changed shape.
The question used to be whether a single page looked low quality.
The question now includes whether your templates, publishing cadence, infrastructure and content similarities make your operation resemble a coordinated spam network.
Gabe's read: Google will not let companies spam their way into AI search , and marketers should expect stronger automated systems plus manual actions.
Traditional quality filters evaluate one piece of content at a time.
Google's researchers acknowledge that generative AI broke that model.
Spammers can now produce endless variations of what the paper calls functionally identical content: every page technically unique, every page effectively the same.
At volume, that flood is built to swamp content-level filters.
SBERT has existed since 2019, and Montti points out the SEO industry has rarely discussed it as a spam-detection mechanism.
Its appearance in a Google paper about catching synthetic spam suggests it may have been put to that use only recently.
One more detail worth knowing: speed of adaptation.
The paper describes using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and Automatic Prompt Optimization (APO) to retune classifiers when spammers move to new generative models.
That means days of adjustment instead of months of retraining.
When the next model ships and spam operations migrate, Google can follow almost immediately.
The paper, covered by Roger Montti at Search Engine Journal and shared widely by Glenn Gabe on X , describes the Scalable Cluster Termination System.

extraction.body: CMSWire's Marketing & Customer Experience Leadership channel is the go-to hub for actionable research, editorial and opinion for CMOs, aspiring CMOs and today's customer experience innovators. Our dedicated editorial and research teams focus on bringing you the data and information you need to navigate today's complex customer, organizational and technical landscapes. We've got you covered. For two years the AI content debate has circled one question: can Google actually tell? A newly published Google research paper suggests the answer is yes, just not in the way most marketers expected. The paper, covered by Roger Montti at Search Engine Journal and shared widely by Glenn Gabe on X , describes the Scalable Cluster Termination System. Google built it to fight AI-generated video spam on its platforms, but the methods it describes (text embeddings, template detection, publishing-behavior analysis) apply just as cleanly to web content. Gabe's read: Google will not let companies spam their way into AI search , and marketers should expect stronger automated systems plus manual actions. The timing matters because the traffic data is already moving. Over the past month I've watched websites with heavy concentrations of AI-generated content, the kind Ahrefs now flags as "Very high" on its AI Content Level metric, begin sliding in Google organic search. This also lines up with the rollout of Google’s latest June 2026 spam update that recently finished rolling out. Correlation is not causation. But when declines cluster around a specific site profile right as Google publishes both an algorithm update and research on detecting that exact profile, it deserves attention. Traditional quality filters evaluate one piece of content at a time. Is this page thin? Does it satisfy intent? Google's researchers acknowledge that generative AI broke that model. Spammers can now produce endless variations of what the paper calls functionally identical content: every page technically unique, every page effectively the same. At volume, that flood is built to swamp content-level filters. S-CTS works from a wider angle. It looks for the organizational structure of a spam operation, meaning the mass reuse of a semantic narrative template across many accounts, combined with infrastructure signals suggesting those accounts share an operator. The system groups related accounts into what the researchers call Generation Clusters, networks statistically likely to be running the same script, API or automation stack. Two components do the work. A content classifier scans for repetitive, templated narratives and for high-frequency publishing behavior that no human schedule produces. An infrastructure component ties accounts back to a common source. When enough accounts in a cluster show the same AI-generated templates, Google removes the whole cluster at once rather than penalizing individual pages. Now swap "accounts" for "domains" and "videos" for "articles." A network of sites publishing 30 templated posts a day from the same prompt stack fits this detection model exactly. S-CTS groups accounts that share templated content and infrastructure signals into Generation Clusters, then removes the entire cluster at once instead of penalizing individual pages. For SEO practitioners, the most useful detail sits in the methodology: Sentence-BERT. The researchers cite SBERT, a model that converts sentences into embeddings comparable by cosine similarity, to support the paper's core assumption that automated AI text leaves a distinct mathematical footprint. When thousands of pages come from the same prompts and the same tools, they land close together in embedding space no matter how different they look to a human reader. SBERT has existed since 2019, and Montti points out the SEO industry has rarely discussed it as a spam-detection mechanism. Its appearance in a Google paper about catching synthetic spam suggests it may have been put to that use only recently. One more detail worth knowing: speed of adaptation. The paper describes using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and Automatic Prompt Optimization (APO) to retune classifiers when spammers move to new generative models. That means days of adjustment instead of months of retraining. When the next model ships and spam operations migrate, Google can follow almost immediately. Sentence-BERT converts text into embeddings, and pages generated from the same prompts and tools cluster together in embedding space even when their wording looks unique to a human reader. The loudest reaction to this research has also been the least accurate one, so the distinction is worth stating plainly. Google's official guidance from 2023 still stands: content gets rewarded for quality and helpfulness regardless of how it was produced. Automation has been part of publishing for decades, from sports scores to weather forecasts. What Google targets falls under its spam policies , specifically scaled content abuse: producing large volumes of pages mainly to manipulate rankings rather than help people. The March 2024 core update already wiped out networks of AI-heavy sites under that policy. This research shows the enforcement machinery getting sharper. The practical line is velocity and intent. A brand publishing four edited, AI-assisted articles a week that answer real customer questions looks nothing like a site pushing 30 posts a day from one prompt template. The second pattern is a fingerprint, and fingerprints are what cluster-level detection finds. When a skeptic in Gabe's replies asked whether these systems would sweep up all AI-generated content, his answer was direct: Google uses multiple signals, AI usage alone does not equal spam and anyone scaling thin content with AI should consider themselves warned. No. Google's 2023 guidance rewards content for quality regardless of production method; enforcement targets scaled content abuse, meaning high-volume, low-value pages built mainly to manipulate rankings. The following table highlights the most important lessons, actions and strategic considerations emerging from these five recommended content moves. Prioritizing human-led writing, stripping templated AI phrasing, cutting padding, adding real point of view and publishing at least some content for readers rather than rankings all reduce the templated-content fingerprint S-CTS looks for. The risk calculus for AI-heavy SEO & AEO has changed shape. The question used to be whether a single page looked low quality. The question now includes whether your templates, publishing cadence, infrastructure and content similarities make your operation resemble a coordinated spam network. That is a much harder problem to solve with a plugin or a prompt, and based on the traffic declines of the past month, Google may already be grading the exam. My own strategy stays the same: build a strong brand on a strong domain, publish content that serves real search intent and treat AI as a tool rather than an identity. The sites getting removed at the cluster level made themselves look like machines. Do not be one of them. Learn how you can join our contributor community. This also lines up with the rollout of Google’s latest June 2026 spam update that recently finished rolling out. Correlation is not causation. But when declines cluster around a specific site profile right as Google publishes both an algorithm update and research on detecting that exact profile, it deserves attention.

Traditional quality filters evaluate one piece of content at a time. Is this page thin? Does it satisfy intent? Google's researchers acknowledge that generative AI broke that model. Spammers can now produce endless variations of what the paper calls functionally identical content: every page technically unique, every page effectively the same. At volume, that flood is built to swamp content-level filters.

S-CTS works from a wider angle. It looks for the organizational structure of a spam operation, meaning the mass reuse of a semantic narrative template across many accounts, combined with infrastructure signals suggesting those accounts share an operator. The system groups related accounts into what the researchers call Generation Clusters, networks statistically likely to be running the same script, API or automation stack.

Two components do the work. A content classifier scans for repetitive, templated narratives and for high-frequency publishing behavior that no human schedule produces. An infrastructure component ties accounts back to a common source. When enough accounts in a cluster show the same AI-generated templates, Google removes the whole cluster at once rather than penalizing individual pages.
Now swap "accounts" for "domains" and "videos" for "articles." A network of sites publishing 30 templated posts a day from the same prompt stack fits this detection model exactly.
S-CTS groups accounts that share templated content and infrastructure signals into Generation Clusters, then removes the entire cluster at once instead of penalizing individual pages.
For SEO practitioners, the most useful detail sits in the methodology: Sentence-BERT.

The researchers cite SBERT, a model that converts sentences into embeddings comparable by cosine similarity, to support the paper's core assumption that automated AI text leaves a distinct mathematical footprint. When thousands of pages come from the same prompts and the same tools, they land close together in embedding space no matter how different they look to a human reader.

SBERT has existed since 2019, and Montti points out the SEO industry has rarely discussed it as a spam-detection mechanism. Its appearance in a Google paper about catching synthetic spam suggests it may have been put to that use only recently.

One more detail worth knowing: speed of adaptation. The paper describes using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and Automatic Prompt Optimization (APO) to retune classifiers when spammers move to new generative models. That means days of adjustment instead of months of retraining. When the next model ships and spam operations migrate, Google can follow almost immediately.
Sentence-BERT converts text into embeddings, and pages generated from the same prompts and tools cluster together in embedding space even when their wording looks unique to a human reader.
The loudest reaction to this research has also been the least accurate one, so the distinction is worth stating plainly.

Google's official guidance from 2023 still stands: content gets rewarded for quality and helpfulness regardless of how it was produced. Automation has been part of publishing for decades, from sports scores to weather forecasts.
What Google targets falls under its spam policies , specifically scaled content abuse: producing large volumes of pages mainly to manipulate rankings rather than help people.
The March 2024 core update already wiped out networks of AI-heavy sites under that policy. This research shows the enforcement machinery getting sharper.

The practical line is velocity and intent. A brand publishing four edited, AI-assisted articles a week that answer real customer questions looks nothing like a site pushing 30 posts a day from one prompt template. The second pattern is a fingerprint, and fingerprints are what cluster-level detection finds.

When a skeptic in Gabe's replies asked whether these systems would sweep up all AI-generated content, his answer was direct: Google uses multiple signals, AI usage alone does not equal spam and anyone scaling thin content with AI should consider themselves warned.

No. Google's 2023 guidance rewards content for quality regardless of production method; enforcement targets scaled content abuse, meaning high-volume, low-value pages built mainly to manipulate rankings.
The following table highlights the most important lessons, actions and strategic considerations emerging from these five recommended content moves.

Prioritizing human-led writing, stripping templated AI phrasing, cutting padding, adding real point of view and publishing at least some content for readers rather than rankings all reduce the templated-content fingerprint S-CTS looks for.

The risk calculus for AI-heavy SEO & AEO has changed shape. The question used to be whether a single page looked low quality. The question now includes whether your templates, publishing cadence, infrastructure and content similarities make your operation resemble a coordinated spam network. That is a much harder problem to solve with a plugin or a prompt, and based on the traffic declines of the past month, Google may already be grading the exam.

My own strategy stays the same: build a strong brand on a strong domain, publish content that serves real search intent and treat AI as a tool rather than an identity. The sites getting removed at the cluster level made themselves look like machines. Do not be one of them.

The new section advises websites with pages made for direct sharing, collaboration or utility to set a noindex tag or use a robots.txt directive to block crawlers by default for those pages. According to Google’s changelog this is an addition relating to “blocking indexing of link-shared content.” The new section includes a link to the introductory page about robots.txt , and according to that introductory page the robots.txt file “is not a mechanism for keeping a web page out of Google.” Google’s new “Only index content meant for Search” section follows the guide’s advice on spotting spammy accounts and reads: “If your service lets users create shareable pages, generated outputs, or interactive tools, consider whether that content is meant to be found through search engines or only accessed directly by people with a link.” “When pages are created for direct sharing, collaboration, or utility rather than public search discovery, apply the noindex rule (using a robots meta tag or X-Robots-Tag HTTP response header) or block crawling in robots.txt by default.” The guide’s opening paragraph said hosting platforms “may be similarly open to abuse.” The updated sentence adds “tools that let users publish shared pages, generated content, or web apps,” and says spammers may create a large number of “pages or sites” where it used to say sites. The previous version, last updated Dec. 10, 2025, already suggested noindex on posts from new users until they build a reputation on the platform. That advice is unchanged. Google’s robots.txt introduction says a page “that’s disallowed in robots.txt can still be indexed if linked to from other sites.” Google won’t crawl the blocked content in that case, but the URL and possibly the anchor text of links pointing to it can appear in results, without a description. Google’s page on noindex says the rule only works when robots.txt isn’t blocking the page, because otherwise “the crawler will never see the noindex rule.” Google’s “Control what you share” page , updated Oct. 21, lists robots.txt as applicable to “images and video” and noindex as applicable to “all content types.” On July 27, I confirmed that Claude’s share path was blocked by a “Disallow” directive in robots.txt. In addition, the share pages also returned a “none” value for the X-Robots-Tag HTTP response header. Google treats “none” as equal to both noindex and nofollow according to its documentation of robots meta tags . I have been unable to determine what Google saw when it initially found those links. The new spam guide from Google states you should be verifying your website or subdomain through Search Console for your platform to receive emails when it gets a manual action or has a security issue. It further suggests you check the Page Indexing report and Search performance report on an ongoing basis for “unexpected spikes” of indexed pages, impressions or queries which do not align with your platform’s intent. A new bullet under the guide’s monitoring advice suggests tracking creation and indexing at the platform level, with alerts for spikes in newly published public pages or “a small number of users generating a large share of indexable URLs.” Google’s changelog says its Oct. 26 update to the spam guide aims to help platforms “keep user-created pages that aren’t meant for Search out of the index and detect spam earlier.” For share links, generated outputs, and app pages, check that any noindex can reach Googlebot. A robots.txt rule that blocks Googlebot from those pages means Google never reads it. The Page Indexing report that Google’s new monitoring advice points to has a status called “Indexed, though blocked by robots.txt.” Google’s help for that status says to remove the block and use noindex. Share URLs that Google indexes despite a robots.txt block can appear under that status in Search Console. Follow on YouTube. Matt G. extraction.body: The identities of over 41,000 officials from the Department of Homeland Security have allegedly been exposed in a massive data breach by a hacktivist group calling itself the Department of Peace. Late Wednesday stateside, the database was posted on Distributed Denial of Secrets, a nonprofit dedicated to news leaks, with claims that it was obtained from an Okta single sign-on service used by the DHS. Okta didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. DDoS said that "this is not a comprehensive list of all DHS employees," quoting cofounder Emma Best saying, "Rather than an indiscriminate directory of every DHS employee, Icepick identifies many of the architects and drivers of DHS policy and operations." DHS didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. The agency told the Washington Post that it was "aware of a potential breach" and was "working to address the situation swiftly and effectively." The searchable database appears to include employees from Immigration and Customs Enforcement, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, Customs and Border Protection and the DHS headquarters. The hacker group said the leak was carried out in response to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin reportedly saying on July 17 that ICE will be "turning up the heat on the streets" by intensifying immigration arrests and traffic stops. In U.S. President Donald Trump's second term, the backlash to his efforts to intensify arrests and deportations of suspected illegal immigrants has increased as ICE agents have been documented using physical force during operations. Records involve personnel from several federal agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). When those records are exposed, attackers may be able to identify accounts with sensitive permissions or use internal details to develop more convincing phishing attempts. Late Wednesday stateside, the database was posted on Distributed Denial of Secrets, a nonprofit dedicated to news leaks, with claims that it was obtained from an Okta single sign-on service used by the DHS. Okta didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. DDoS said that "this is not a comprehensive list of all DHS employees," quoting cofounder Emma Best saying, "Rather than an indiscriminate directory of every DHS employee, Icepick identifies many of the architects and drivers of DHS policy and operations." DHS didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. The agency told the Washington Post that it was "aware of a potential breach" and was "working to address the situation swiftly and effectively." The searchable database appears to include employees from Immigration and Customs Enforcement, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, Customs and Border Protection and the DHS headquarters. coreStoryFacts.text: "We make the world's best touch computer on an iPad," Ternus, then Apple's senior VP of hardware engineering, told The Wall Street Journal in 2021.
And the Mac is totally optimized for indirect input.
We haven't really felt a reason to change that."
"Yes, for the very first time, we are bringing touch to the Mac," Ternus said in live remarks to media and analysts in Los Angeles.
The launch signifies the growing strategic importance of the Mac to Apple, despite it generating less revenue than the iPhone.
In the most recent quarter, Apple reported $10.35 billion in Mac sales, or just under 10% of the company's total revenue.

Hardware technology hasn't been the limiting factor for Apple merging its desktop and mobile interfaces, he added, and Apple could have been waiting to launch a touchscreen laptop until it could present a good user experience and perfect its software after attempts to make its iPad more like a laptop.
Apple has had a historical resistance to touchscreen laptops.
Software chief Craig Federighi said in 2018 that the ergonomics would fatigue users.
Apple on Wednesday announced its first laptop with a touchscreen, which it's calling MacBook Pro with ProLED XDR Display.
This is Apple's third major product launch under new CEO John Ternus, signaling a faster cadence for hardware releases.
It's also a major reversal for Apple, which has resisted putting touchscreens on its laptops for decades as some Windows machines gained the feature.
Apple also introduced new iMac and MacBook Pro models with M6 chips this week, after price hikes to the lineup totaling several hundred dollars in June.
Apple introduced an iPad Mini on Monday that starts at $699, $100 more than its predecessor.
But many software developers swear by the Mac, and it remains the only supported platform to develop iPhone apps.
And in recent months, Apple has highlighted its chips and memory architecture to make the case that its computers are the best fit for local or edge AI that runs on a device, instead of the cloud.
Apple's own shipments fell 11% during the quarter, according to the estimate.
Ternus has been working on Macs since he joined the company and was credited along with silicon chief Johny Srouji as the leader of Apple's effort to get Macs running on Apple's chips, not Intel's.
Apple credited Ternus' work on Mac in its official CEO transition statement .
Apple said the laptop has a new display, using OLED technology, that offers more brightness, better colors and wider viewing angles.
It's using Apple's M5 Pro or Max chips, and Apple said Wednesday that it's lighter than Apple's current Pro laptops.
In a video, Apple showed users swiping on the screen to manipulate videos or images.
In September, Apple released new iPhones, including its first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo.
It also revealed a new smart speaker with a display called HomeView that uses a redesigned version of Siri to answer a broader range of questions.

extraction.body: Apple has revealed its first touch screen Macbook. It is targeted at graphic designers, photographers, musicians and other creative types. More than a decade after touch-screen Windows laptops first hit the market, Apple has taken the wraps off its first touch-screen Macbook Pro. The Cupertino-based company announced the new laptop on Wednesday during its “Pro and Tell” in Los Angeles, a special event to launch the new product. It marks a turning point for the company, which for years said it would not develop a touch-screen laptop. Apple users interested in a touch-first device should buy an iPad instead, the company has long argued. In fact, Apple co-founder and former CEO Steve Jobs once famously said that touch-screen laptops were “ergonomically terrible ” during a keynote in 2010 promoting the Macbook Air, the company’s light and ultraportable laptop. Alex DePaoli, a marketing professor in the D’Amore-McKim School of Business said the company likely has pivoted on its stance against making a totally touch-friendly Mac out of the desire to entice the higher end market and creative professionals. “Apple has made itself the go-to brand for people who do drawing and drafting as part of their work,” he said. That is how the company is marketing it. In a press release announcing the laptop, the company touted its new features, specifically to that crowd. Graphic designers no longer have to rely on the computer’s trackpad to move and orient their 3D models or sketches, musicians can use their hands to play keys on a virtual piano, and photographers can easily pinch and zoom on images using their fingers, it highlighted. And it is certainly high end. The computer, which comes in 14-inch and 16-inch variants, starts at $2,899. Customers can pre-order the device now. It launches on Nov. 6. DePaoli said Apple is following its signature playbook with the touch-screen Macbook, as the company has a habit of entering established consumer electronic categories with its own premium line of products. It waits for others to work out the kinks with the underlying technology and then introduces its own more “polished” device, he said. A great example is the iPhone Duo, the company’s first folding phone that hit store shelves last week, he said. Apple wasn’t the first to enter the folding phone market, but early reception of the device has been positive. Analysts at Counterpoint Research , a marketing research firm, estimated that by the end of the year the company is expected to sell more than six million units. It hasn’t been completely rosey, however. Some users have reported that their phone’s inner folding displays are already breaking under normal use. Apple issued a statement acknowledging the defect was “impacting a small number of iPhone units” and that anyone who is experiencing the issue should contact the company for a replacement. The launch of the Macbook Pro is likely to bring less fanfare than Duo as many users likely assumed Apple already offered a touch-screen Macbook, DePaoli said. “This is a technology that is not going to surprise or delight people,” he said. “It’s going to confuse people that Apple didn’t already offer this.” The company has flirted with adding touch inputs on its laptops before. In 2016, it introduced the Touch Bar to the Macbook Pro, a touch-screen display that replaced the laptop’s function key row. But it was phased out a few years later. Apple never acknowledged why it removed the Touch Bar, but the feature had poor software support from outside developers, and many Mac users prefer traditional function row keys, according to tech industry experts. Mark Miller, a computer science professor in Northeastern’s Silicon Valley campus and a former Apple employee, believes the company is adding a touch screen to the Macbook as a way to stand out in a sea of touch-screen Windows laptops. “No doubt Apple feels some pressure to ‘check the box’ since the competition touts it as a Windows-only feature,” he said. But will Apple entering this long established market have a big impact and make touch-screen laptops cool? Maybe for diehard Apple enthusiasts. But for other consumers, DePaoli is skeptical. “I don’t think you are going to move a lot of units by saying, ‘Hey, that thing you’ve been trying to do for ten years, you can actually do it now,” he said. Apple wasn’t the first to enter the folding phone market, but early reception of the device has been positive. Analysts at Counterpoint Research , a marketing research firm, estimated that by the end of the year the company is expected to sell more than six million units.

It hasn’t been completely rosey, however. Some users have reported that their phone’s inner folding displays are already breaking under normal use. Apple issued a statement acknowledging the defect was “impacting a small number of iPhone units” and that anyone who is experiencing the issue should contact the company for a replacement.
The launch of the Macbook Pro is likely to bring less fanfare than Duo as many users likely assumed Apple already offered a touch-screen Macbook, DePaoli said.
“This is a technology that is not going to surprise or delight people,” he said. “It’s going to confuse people that Apple didn’t already offer this.”
The company has flirted with adding touch inputs on its laptops before. In 2016, it introduced the Touch Bar to the Macbook Pro, a touch-screen display that replaced the laptop’s function key row.

But it was phased out a few years later. Apple never acknowledged why it removed the Touch Bar, but the feature had poor software support from outside developers, and many Mac users prefer traditional function row keys, according to tech industry experts.

Mark Miller, a computer science professor in Northeastern’s Silicon Valley campus and a former Apple employee, believes the company is adding a touch screen to the Macbook as a way to stand out in a sea of touch-screen Windows laptops.
“No doubt Apple feels some pressure to ‘check the box’ since the competition touts it as a Windows-only feature,” he said.
But will Apple entering this long established market have a big impact and make touch-screen laptops cool?
Maybe for diehard Apple enthusiasts. But for other consumers, DePaoli is skeptical.
“I don’t think you are going to move a lot of units by saying, ‘Hey, that thing you’ve been trying to do for ten years, you can actually do it now,” he said.

coreStoryFacts.text: "We make the world's best touch computer on an iPad," Ternus, then Apple's senior VP of hardware engineering, told The Wall Street Journal in 2021.
And the Mac is totally optimized for indirect input.
We haven't really felt a reason to change that."
"Yes, for the very first time, we are bringing touch to the Mac," Ternus said in live remarks to media and analysts in Los Angeles.
The launch signifies the growing strategic importance of the Mac to Apple, despite it generating less revenue than the iPhone.
In the most recent quarter, Apple reported $10.35 billion in Mac sales, or just under 10% of the company's total revenue.

Hardware technology hasn't been the limiting factor for Apple merging its desktop and mobile interfaces, he added, and Apple could have been waiting to launch a touchscreen laptop until it could present a good user experience and perfect its software after attempts to make its iPad more like a laptop.
Apple has had a historical resistance to touchscreen laptops.
Software chief Craig Federighi said in 2018 that the ergonomics would fatigue users.
Apple on Wednesday announced its first laptop with a touchscreen, which it's calling MacBook Pro with ProLED XDR Display.
This is Apple's third major product launch under new CEO John Ternus, signaling a faster cadence for hardware releases.
It's also a major reversal for Apple, which has resisted putting touchscreens on its laptops for decades as some Windows machines gained the feature.
Apple also introduced new iMac and MacBook Pro models with M6 chips this week, after price hikes to the lineup totaling several hundred dollars in June.
Apple introduced an iPad Mini on Monday that starts at $699, $100 more than its predecessor.
But many software developers swear by the Mac, and it remains the only supported platform to develop iPhone apps.
And in recent months, Apple has highlighted its chips and memory architecture to make the case that its computers are the best fit for local or edge AI that runs on a device, instead of the cloud.
Apple's own shipments fell 11% during the quarter, according to the estimate.
Ternus has been working on Macs since he joined the company and was credited along with silicon chief Johny Srouji as the leader of Apple's effort to get Macs running on Apple's chips, not Intel's.
Apple credited Ternus' work on Mac in its official CEO transition statement .
Apple said the laptop has a new display, using OLED technology, that offers more brightness, better colors and wider viewing angles.
It's using Apple's M5 Pro or Max chips, and Apple said Wednesday that it's lighter than Apple's current Pro laptops.
In a video, Apple showed users swiping on the screen to manipulate videos or images.
In September, Apple released new iPhones, including its first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo.
It also revealed a new smart speaker with a display called HomeView that uses a redesigned version of Siri to answer a broader range of questions.

extraction.body: Apple on Wednesday announced its first laptop with a touchscreen, which it's calling MacBook Pro with ProLED XDR Display. Apple said the laptop has a new display, using OLED technology, that offers more brightness, better colors and wider viewing angles. It's using Apple's M5 Pro or Max chips, and Apple said Wednesday that it's lighter than Apple's current Pro laptops. It's still an Apple laptop, and is running MacOS, not a version of the iPhone or iPad operating system. In a video, Apple showed users swiping on the screen to manipulate videos or images. It also has a glowing Apple logo on the laptop's lid. The new laptop will go on sale Nov. 6 and the 14-inch version will start at $2,899. The 16-inch version will cost at least $3,399. Both are notable price increases from existing models. This is Apple's third major product launch under new CEO John Ternus, signaling a faster cadence for hardware releases. It's also a major reversal for Apple, which has resisted putting touchscreens on its laptops for decades as some Windows machines gained the feature. "Yes, for the very first time, we are bringing touch to the Mac," Ternus said in live remarks to media and analysts in Los Angeles. The laptop market has been going through one of its worst slumps ever. Overall shipments are expected to be down 11% this year. Analysts say the AI-driven global market shortage of memory has contributed to higher laptop prices, which has hurt sales and demand. In the third quarter, total PC shipments dropped 20% on a year-over-year basis, according to market researcher IDC. Apple's own shipments fell 11% during the quarter, according to the estimate. Even Apple's not immune to rising memory prices, after then-CEO Tim Cook warned this summer that the situation around memory prices was "unsustainable." Nearly all Macs got price hikes this year. Mac Minis introduced in August got a $300 bump, for example. The announcement caps a busy two months of product launches under Ternus. Apple also introduced new iMac and MacBook Pro models with M6 chips this week, after price hikes to the lineup totaling several hundred dollars in June. Apple introduced an iPad Mini on Monday that starts at $699, $100 more than its predecessor. In September, Apple released new iPhones, including its first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo. It also revealed a new smart speaker with a display called HomeView that uses a redesigned version of Siri to answer a broader range of questions. The launch signifies the growing strategic importance of the Mac to Apple, despite it generating less revenue than the iPhone. In the most recent quarter, Apple reported $10.35 billion in Mac sales, or just under 10% of the company's total revenue. But many software developers swear by the Mac, and it remains the only supported platform to develop iPhone apps. And in recent months, Apple has highlighted its chips and memory architecture to make the case that its computers are the best fit for local or edge AI that runs on a device, instead of the cloud. Meta's AI model developer team bought hundreds of Mac Minis this year to test agents, for example. And Apple notably teamed up with Meta earlier this month to make an announcement that large, nearly frontier models can run on clusters of Macs connected with high-speed cabling, allowing developers to run agentic code without paying Anthropic or OpenAI. Apple has had a historical resistance to touchscreen laptops. Software chief Craig Federighi said in 2018 that the ergonomics would fatigue users. "We make the world's best touch computer on an iPad," Ternus, then Apple's senior VP of hardware engineering, told The Wall Street Journal in 2021. "It's totally optimized for that. And the Mac is totally optimized for indirect input. We haven't really felt a reason to change that." Ternus has been working on Macs since he joined the company and was credited along with silicon chief Johny Srouji as the leader of Apple's effort to get Macs running on Apple's chips, not Intel's. Apple credited Ternus' work on Mac in its official CEO transition statement . passages: Now it appears ready to prove itself wrong.Apple is holding a product event in Los Angeles on October 28, dubbed “Pro and tell,” where it is expected to debut its first touchscreen MacBook.
Also read: Apple launches new iMac in India at ₹1.75 lakh with faster AI performance Why now?Apple hasn’t explained itself, but the reasons aren’t hard to find.The first is money.
Apple has discussed charging $400 more for the touch model, starting the 14-inch at $2,899.
The Mac has been a growth engine since Apple moved to its own chips, bringing in $40.1 billion in fiscal 2022.
For more than a decade, Apple argued that touchscreens and laptops don’t mix.
Windows laptops have offered touchscreens as a standard feature for years, even as Apple insisted they were ergonomically inferior.
Apple has long held that the iPad is the best touchscreen computer, so it has to keep a clear line between the tablet and the laptop.
Apple appears to be betting that Pro users will pay a real premium for a touch-enabled OLED laptop, which would lift what the average Mac sells for.The second is competition.
Apple’s pro customers have long had a touch-capable alternative at the other end of the aisle.The third is timing.
Software chief Craig Federighi once called touchscreen PCs “experiments” and said he was “not into touchscreens.” The idea has circulated for years.
Expect Apple to pitch touch as a complement to the keyboard and trackpad, not a replacement for them.

The new MacBook Pro, code-named K114 and K116, is expected to arrive with thinner, lighter frames. Other details expected alongside it include a reinforced hinge designed to keep the screen steady when touched, a new cooling system, and software changes built for finger input. The chips are likely to be M5 Pro and M5 Max.Apple is also expected to launch a new iPad mini and M6 versions of the 14-inch MacBook Pro and the iMac at the same event. Today’s non-touch models start at $2,499 and $2,999 and are expected to stay on sale. That makes touch a premium tier rather than a change for every buyer, and the figures aren’t final. extraction.body: A new MARADMIN swaps AI for SI across Total Force products; but statutes, contracts and old titles stay put. The Marine Corps just told the Total Force to swap the term "Artificial Intelligence" for “Super Intelligence” in official writing. MARADMIN 521/26, signed Oct. 23, directs commands to use "Super Intelligence" and the abbreviation SI in place of Artificial Intelligence and AI "to the maximum extent permitted by law." The order covers official correspondence, public communications, websites, reports, policy documents, briefing and training materials, and other non-statutory products. Content owners must update current websites and reusable templates as they revise them. The change implements Executive Order 14434, signed Sept. 29, which told the executive branch to adopt SI terminology. Stars and Stripes covered the Navy and Marine memos as a dual-service rename. The Marine message is narrower and more useful for Marines who write for a living: who owns the policy, what products move first, and what is explicitly left alone. SI, for purposes of the guidance, means the same technologies already covered by the statutory definition of AI in Title 15, U.S. Code, Section 9401(3), except where law says otherwise. Generative systems and other machine-learning applications under that definition are included. Security, privacy, acquisition and responsible-use rules do not change with the name. Commanders and directors are responsible for making sure military and civilian personnel who prepare, review or publish those products understand the guidance. The message applies to the Marine Corps Total Force. Implementation that touches contractor performance will be coordinated through the appropriate contracting authority and the contract requirements already in force. The Deputy Commandant for Information's Chief Data and Super Intelligence Office, or CDSO, remains the Service lead for strategy, policy, governance and oversight. The message cites MCO 5231.4, still titled Marine Corps Data and Artificial Intelligence, as the governing order. The reference titles in 521/26 keep their published wording on purpose. The executive order does not require Marines to alter previously issued regulations, presidential actions, contracts, grants or other historical documents. Issued records stay as issued under records-management rules. Statutory wording, accurate direct quotations and official source titles stay as written when Marines cite or reproduce them. Organization, program and product names stay current unless the responsible authority changes them. In practice, that means a Marine quoting Title 15, pasting a contract clause that says AI, or citing MCO 5231.4 by its published title is not out of step with 521/26. That carve-out matters for contracting officers, requirements writers, and schoolhouse staff who work with citation-heavy products. The rewrite burden falls on forward-looking writing, not on scrubbing every existing document. A historical after-action report that used AI in 2024 does not need a red pen. A new public affairs release written next week does. PAOs, web managers, doctrine writers, schoolhouses and anyone who owns a briefing template will feel this first. Every slide deck that still says AI, every public affairs release, every course syllabus that introduces the Basic AI Course by that name will need a judgment call: Is this a non-statutory product being issued or revised, or is it a quotation of a statutory title? The Corps has spent the last year teaching Marines to use these tools under the old label. Military.com covered how the service framed AI as a warfighting edge in its implementation plan, and Marines are already running competitive wargames against machine opponents under MCU's Humans vs. Machine tournament. MARADMIN 214/26 still requires every active-duty and reserve Marine to finish the Basic AI Course by Dec. 31. MARADMIN 467/26 and its update list additional AI and data courses available through Marine Corps eLearning, Joint Knowledge Online and Navy Community College pathways. Those course titles and syllabus citations will not vanish overnight. Expect mixed language in the near term: SI in new command correspondence, AI in materials that quote statutes or older MARADMINs by title. That is not Marines ignoring the order. It is the order working as written. Nothing in 521/26 changes the systems Marines buy or the security rules that govern them. The same models, the same data pipelines and the same human-on-the-loop requirements apply. The message is terminology policy, not a new capability fielding plan and not a change to how Marines employ machine learning at the edge. MCU's extracurricular Fight Club wargaming program and the new SI vocabulary will have to share a language for a while. The practical application for any Marine writing an operations order, a public affairs release or a schoolhouse handout tomorrow: Use Super Intelligence and SI in new official products unless law, a quotation or an official title forces the older words. extraction.body: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Nearly all industries have been impacted by Artificial Intelligence. Goldman Sachs estimates 300 million jobs will be impacted by the emerging technology by 2030. AI is reshaping industries by the day, resulting in jobs being transformed or erased. The changes are bringing a greater need for AI oversight. “People need to understand that there still needs to be human involvement,” Barry Jones, a Vice President at X2X said. X2X is an AI governance company. Jones said there’s not enough oversight AI oversight right now. “Imagine an AI assistant preparing financial reports,” Jones said. “That’s a potentially productive tool. But just imagine if that AI system provided that critical financial information outside of the company’s internal workings.” Before Congress left Capitol Hill for the midterms, several congressmembers made clear where they stood on what role the government should play on regulation. “Well, look, anytime you can give the federal government out of it, I think we’re better off,” Rep. Buddy Carter (R-GA) said. “We don’t want to stifle innovation. But at the same time, we got to get this right. That’s the key. We got to get a right. I can be a very useful tool, unbelievably useful tool. But there are some concerns and there are some dangers there.” “First, the United States needs to address the very real risks created by increasingly powerful AI systems, and these decisions need to be made by the American people through their representatives,” Senator Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) said. Jones said big picture, self-governance isn’t enough. “But to say that something is self-governing is like having the fox watching the henhouse,” Jones said. “You really need to have a third party, layer in some cases, even the government saying these are the things that I can do and I cannot do.” Jones said that private oversight is creating roles that have been replaced by technology. Microsoft recently announced they offered 60,000 employees buyouts due to AI. Jones has advice for people looking for a career pivot due to AI. “Start learning AI,” Jones said. “Understand how it applies to your profession. Also understand that judgement, experience, trust and accountability matter. The goal shouldn’t be to compete with the machine. The goal should be to become someone who knows the useful power of the technology and using it responsibly.” Efforts to regulate Artificial Intelligence are stalled on Capitol Hill but the 120 th Congress could take up the rapidly evolving technology in January.

sources.title: Microsoft recorded $10 billion in revenue from OpenAI
passages: Microsoft generated $10 billion in revenue from commercial arrangements with OpenAI, including revenue-sharing payments, in the quarter ended September 30, the company said in a regulatory filing on Wednesday.

That represents nearly 11% of Microsoft’s total quarterly revenue of $92.3 billion, highlighting the enormous financial ties that remain between the two companies even as they increasingly compete for the same customers .
For the full 2026 fiscal year, revenue from OpenAI hit $24.1 billion.
At its latest quarterly pace, Microsoft would pull in $40 billion annually from OpenAI-related arrangements.
Microsoft also reported $7.2 billion in outstanding receivables from OpenAI at the end of September, up from $6 billion at the end of June.
That money represents amounts OpenAI owes for previous transactions, not additional revenue.
TechCrunch has reached out for more information.

The companies began loosening the ties of their once-exclusive partnership in October 2025, when Microsoft relinquished its hold on OpenAI to give the startup more freedom to partner with other cloud providers.
In exchange, OpenAI committed to buying an additional $250 billion in Azure services as part of an October 2025 agreement.
Microsoft’s ownership stake in OpenAI has also declined slightly from about 25% in June to 24% in September.
That continues a gradual decline from roughly 27% following the October 2025 recapitalization.
Microsoft did not specify what caused the dilution.

This investment is aimed at preparing the company to deliver on its future revenue commitments under existing contracts with AI labs, further solidifying Microsoft's position as a leader in the tech industry.

facts.text: Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ: MSFT ) quietly disclosed a number that changes the scale of its OpenAI relationship.
In its fiscal 2026 10-K, Microsoft said it recorded $24.1 billion of revenue from commercial arrangements with OpenAI, including revenue-sharing payments.
It also had $6.0 billion of accounts receivable from OpenAI at June 30.
The missing number may be even more consequential.

For investors trying to decide whether the AI buildout is producing returns or merely moving cash among strategic partners, the distinction between revenue scale and margin quality is the whole story.
Microsoft does not separately disclose the profit generated by those OpenAI commercial arrangements.
Insider Monkey's database showed 273 hedge funds holding MSFT as of Q2, down from 282 in Q1.
Those filings precede the annual report's full-year disclosure.
As of August 14, roughly 68.54 million Microsoft shares were sold short, about 0.92% of the public float, with 2.1 days to cover.
It does not answer the more important valuation question: how much incremental profit Microsoft keeps after paying for the infrastructure and capital required to produce it.

But the 10-K also shows why investors should resist treating every OpenAI dollar as high-margin software revenue.
The OpenAI relationship can be extraordinarily valuable while still carrying economics that differ sharply from Microsoft's traditional software franchise.
OpenAI has hit $10 billion in annual recurring revenue, or ARR, less than three years after launching its popular ChatGPT chatbot.

For all of last year, OpenAI had around $5.5 billion in ARR.
Reaching its meteoric growth rates requires a substantial amount of cash.
OpenAI is also targeting $125 billion in revenue by 2029, according to a person familiar with the matter who asked not to be named because the details are confidential.
The Information first reported on OpenAI's revenue ambitions.

OpenAI closed a $40 billion funding round in March, marking the largest private tech deal on record.
At today's metrics, OpenAI is valued at about 30 times revenue, which highlights the hyper growth expectations by some of its largest investors.
OpenAI is backed by Japan's SoftBank , Microsoft , Coatue, Altimeter, Thrive and others.
The figure includes sales from the company's consumer products; ChatGPT business products; and its application programming interface, or API.
It excludes licensing revenue from Microsoft and large one-time deals, according to an OpenAI spokesperson.

(NYSE: ADT) (“ADT” or the “Company”), a leading provider of security, interactive and smart home solutions serving residential and small business customers in the U.S., and Thrive Holdings, a permanent capital holding company focused on investing in established businesses and advancing their capabilities through technology, today announced a definitive agreement under which Thrive Holdings will acquire ADT in an all-cash transaction. The agreement values ADT at approximately $7.6 billion in equity value and $15.3 billion in enterprise value. Under the terms of the agreement, which ADT’s Board of Directors unanimously approved, ADT stockholders will receive $10.00 per share in cash upon completion. The per share price represents a premium of 45.6% to ADT’s unaffected closing share price on October 27, 2026, and 52.1% to its 30-day volume-weighted average share price ending on October 27, 2026. The transaction would combine ADT’s more than 150 years of security experience, nationwide service network and customer trust with Thrive Holdings’ long-term capital and engineering capabilities. Thrive Holdings is a permanent capital holding company, which enables it to own and operate businesses over a long-term horizon. This ownership structure will provide ADT with greater flexibility to invest in its people and the development of new products and services. “ADT is pleased to enter into this transaction, which recognizes the value built by our more than 12,000 employees and delivers an attractive cash premium to our stockholders,” said Jim DeVries, Chairman, President and Chief Executive Officer of ADT. “Our leadership in security is based on a legacy of trust, longstanding customer relationships and the dedication of our employees. With Thrive Holdings’ long-term capital and technology expertise, ADT will gain new opportunities to accelerate innovation, enhance the customer experience and bring greater peace of mind to even more homes and businesses.” “ADT has spent generations showing up for people when it matters most,” said Kareem Zaki, Partner at Thrive Holdings. “We intend to build on that foundation by strengthening ADT’s technology and product capabilities, with the capital and patience to invest over decades. Our ambition is to help ADT’s teams better serve customers and offer a seamless service with more actionable information for the professionals responding.” Currently, more than 75 businesses across accounting, IT services and the built environment are part of Thrive Holdings. Following the closing of the transaction, ADT will form the foundation of Thrive Holdings’ smart home security business. Thrive Holdings intends to support ADT’s management in pursuing long-term growth through continued investment in the Company’s people, products and services. Thrive Holdings’ engineering teams will work alongside ADT’s professionals to identify opportunities for technology to enhance the Company’s products and services and help its teams support customers more effectively. ADT’s data and privacy policies will remain unchanged, and no new data sharing will occur without customer permission. “Protecting customers’ homes also means protecting their data. Thrive Holdings is committed to upholding the highest standards of privacy and cybersecurity to protect the information that customers entrust to ADT,” said Anuj Mehndiratta, Partner at Thrive Holdings. As previously announced, ADT’s third quarter 2026 results will be issued on November 3, 2026, prior to market opening. The Company will share a summary of its results on a 10 a.m. ET conference call. BOCA RATON, Fla. and NEW YORK, Oct. 29, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- ADT Inc. (NYSE: ADT) (“ADT” or the “Company”), a leading provider of security, interactive and smart home solutions serving residential and small business customers in the U.S., and Thrive Holdings, a permanent capital holding company focused on investing in established businesses and advancing their capabilities through technology, today announced a definitive agreement under which Thrive Holdings will acquire ADT in an all-cash transaction. The agreement values ADT at approximately $7.6 billion in equity value and $15.3 billion in enterprise value.

Under the terms of the agreement, which ADT’s Board of Directors unanimously approved, ADT stockholders will receive $10.00 per share in cash upon completion. The per share price represents a premium of 45.6% to ADT’s unaffected closing share price on October 27, 2026, and 52.1% to its 30-day volume-weighted average share price ending on October 27, 2026.

The transaction would combine ADT’s more than 150 years of security experience, nationwide service network and customer trust with Thrive Holdings’ long-term capital and engineering capabilities. Thrive Holdings is a permanent capital holding company, which enables it to own and operate businesses over a long-term horizon. This ownership structure will provide ADT with greater flexibility to invest in its people and the development of new products and services.

“ADT is pleased to enter into this transaction, which recognizes the value built by our more than 12,000 employees and delivers an attractive cash premium to our stockholders,” said Jim DeVries, Chairman, President and Chief Executive Officer of ADT. “Our leadership in security is based on a legacy of trust, longstanding customer relationships and the dedication of our employees. With Thrive Holdings’ long-term capital and technology expertise, ADT will gain new opportunities to accelerate innovation, enhance the customer experience and bring greater peace of mind to even more homes and businesses.”

“ADT has spent generations showing up for people when it matters most,” said Kareem Zaki, Partner at Thrive Holdings. “We intend to build on that foundation by strengthening ADT’s technology and product capabilities, with the capital and patience to invest over decades. Our ambition is to help ADT’s teams better serve customers and offer a seamless service with more actionable information for the professionals responding.”

Currently, more than 75 businesses across accounting, IT services and the built environment are part of Thrive Holdings. Following the closing of the transaction, ADT will form the foundation of Thrive Holdings’ smart home security business.

Thrive Holdings intends to support ADT’s management in pursuing long-term growth through continued investment in the Company’s people, products and services. Thrive Holdings’ engineering teams will work alongside ADT’s professionals to identify opportunities for technology to enhance the Company’s products and services and help its teams support customers more effectively.
ADT’s data and privacy policies will remain unchanged, and no new data sharing will occur without customer permission.

“Protecting customers’ homes also means protecting their data. Thrive Holdings is committed to upholding the highest standards of privacy and cybersecurity to protect the information that customers entrust to ADT,” said Anuj Mehndiratta, Partner at Thrive Holdings.

As previously announced, ADT’s third quarter 2026 results will be issued on November 3, 2026, prior to market opening. The Company will share a summary of its results on a 10 a.m. ET conference call. In consideration of the announced transaction, the Company will not be taking questions on the call. The Company’s third quarter press release and investor presentation will be available on its investor relations website at investor.adt.com.

Citi and Goldman Sachs & Co. LLC are serving as financial advisors to ADT, with Cravath, Swaine & Moore LLP serving as legal counsel. Edelman Smithfield is serving as strategic communications advisor to ADT. Evercore is serving as exclusive financial advisor to Thrive Holdings, with Kirkland & Ellis LLP serving as legal counsel.

Thrive Holdings owns and operates businesses in critical industries. Its engineers and operators work directly with industry specialists to develop and deploy proprietary technology products within the businesses it owns. Thrive Holdings takes a long-term approach to ownership and reinvestment. Its businesses include Current in accounting and Shield in IT services. For more information, visit thriveholdings.com.

(NASDAQ: GOOG ) (NASDAQ: GOOGL ) is seeing record growth in Google Search queries, but weaker monetization in AI-powered search experiences is weighing on revenue growth. During Alphabet's third-quarter earnings call Wednesday, J.P. Morgan analyst Doug Anmuth asked why Search revenue growth slowed even as queries rose at their fastest pace in five years. Philipp Schindler , Google's chief business officer, said Search revenue rose 12% year over year to $63 billion during the quarter. Foreign exchange was the biggest factor behind the slowdown in growth compared with the second quarter, Schindler said. He also cited retail advertising challenges linked to the EU's elimination of its de minimis exemption and normalized media and entertainment spending following an unusually strong second quarter driven by the FIFA Club World Cup. However, AI-powered search experiences also played a role. "The strong growth in AI Overviews had an impact because of the lower monetization we were seeing in AI Mode," Schindler said. Earlier on the call, Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai said Google's AI investments are boosting Search usage and overall query growth, including commercial searches. "In fact, our year over year query growth rate is the highest it's been in the last five years," Pichai stated. Read Also: Google CEO Admits Cloud Business Is Sacrificing Revenue to Win AI Race Google is working to improve advertising revenue from its AI search products as users increasingly turn to AI-generated answers. Schindler said advertising experiments had produced promising results, with Google expanding ads in AI Overviews and AI Mode to more users and queries. The tech giant is also extending these efforts into international markets and testing multi-turn ads in the U.S., which could integrate advertising into longer, conversational search experiences. "To be clear, we feel very good about our trajectory here," Schindler said. Separately, Pichai said increasingly capable AI models could significantly improve Google's internal productivity and accelerate product development. He highlighted improvements in software engineering, including higher-quality code submissions and fewer rollbacks, along with opportunities to tackle bigger problems and improve consumer experiences. Pichai said Google was rolling out a newer internal AI model, Carbon, which he described as a significant improvement over Argon. As access expands and more computing resources become available, Pichai said he expects 2027 to be a "golden year" for productivity and innovation at Google. Alphabet reported third-quarter revenue of about $127.58 billion, below analysts' estimates of $128.20 billion. The company reported earnings of $2.12 per share, compared with estimates of $3.02. Looking ahead, Alphabet expects foreign exchange headwinds to weigh more heavily on fourth-quarter revenue than in the previous quarter, primarily affecting Google Search and YouTube advertising. The company also expects tougher year-over-year comparisons as it faces the impact of Search's accelerated growth in the same quarter last year.
