It is manufactured with 45 percent renewable electricity, such as wind and solar, across the supply chain.
As with all Apple products, its paper packaging is 100 percent fiber-based 10 and designed to be recycled.
Both deliver phenomenal single- and multithreaded CPU performance, along with faster unified memory, giving users blazing speed for the most demanding workflows.

M5 Pro offers game-changing performance for scientists, engineers, software developers, and creative pros tackling intensive projects, accelerating everything from compiling code and running AI tasks to sequencing DNA and editing multiple streams of 8K ProRes video.
M5 Max is built for users who want to push the limits even further, including 3D VFX artists, AI developers, and film composers.

With M5 Max, pros can run LLMs with hundreds of billions of parameters entirely on device and accelerate intense workflows across detailed visual effects, 3D animation projects, film scores, and 8K video post-production.

passages: The 14-inch MacBook Pro with Apple’s PROLED XDR tandem OLED display starts at $2,899 in the US, according to MacRumors , and ships from Friday 6 November 2026.
Apple announced the laptop in a press release on 28 October 2026 and said it brings Touch to the Mac for the first time.
Thinner display borders take the screens to 14.2 and 16.3 inches.
The M5 Pro version drives up to three external displays and the M5 Max up to four.
Fast charging takes the battery to 50 per cent in 30 minutes, and the six-speaker sound system has a new woofer design that Apple said gives 50 per cent deeper bass.
Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 run on an Apple-designed N1 wireless chip.
The panel covers both the P3 and Adobe RGB colour spaces, with more than 80 per cent coverage of Rec.
A nano-texture option etched into the cover glass cuts reflections and glare.
Apple said the display reaches up to 2000 nits of peak brightness for HDR and SDR content, a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio and a refresh rate that varies between 10Hz and 120Hz.
Users can scroll a webpage with a swipe, pinch to zoom in on a photo, drag slides from one presentation to another and double-tap a window to fill the screen.
macOS translates touches into clicks, so many existing apps work with Touch at launch, Apple said.

Apps that Apple lists as taking advantage of Touch include Notion, Canva, Zoom, Microsoft Word, Excel, PowerPoint and Outlook, along with Adobe Lightroom, DaVinci Resolve, Blender, Maxon Cinema 4D, Maxon ZBrush, Shapr3D and Algoriddim djay Pro.
Pixelmator Pro, Logic Pro and Final Cut Pro gain Touch controls through Apple Creator Studio.
Apple said a redesigned hinge adds stability when the screen is touched, and video stabilisation smooths the camera feed when Touch is used during a video call.
The laptops run macOS 27 with Apple Intelligence and Siri AI.

Both deliver phenomenal single- and multithreaded CPU performance, along with faster unified memory, giving users blazing speed for the most demanding workflows.

passages: The 14-inch MacBook Pro with Apple’s PROLED XDR tandem OLED display starts at $2,899 in the US, according to MacRumors , and ships from Friday 6 November 2026.
Apple announced the laptop in a press release on 28 October 2026 and said it brings Touch to the Mac for the first time.
Thinner display borders take the screens to 14.2 and 16.3 inches.
The M5 Pro version drives up to three external displays and the M5 Max up to four.
Fast charging takes the battery to 50 per cent in 30 minutes, and the six-speaker sound system has a new woofer design that Apple said gives 50 per cent deeper bass.
Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 run on an Apple-designed N1 wireless chip.
The panel covers both the P3 and Adobe RGB colour spaces, with more than 80 per cent coverage of Rec.
A nano-texture option etched into the cover glass cuts reflections and glare.
Apple said the display reaches up to 2000 nits of peak brightness for HDR and SDR content, a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio and a refresh rate that varies between 10Hz and 120Hz.
Users can scroll a webpage with a swipe, pinch to zoom in on a photo, drag slides from one presentation to another and double-tap a window to fill the screen.
macOS translates touches into clicks, so many existing apps work with Touch at launch, Apple said.

Apps that Apple lists as taking advantage of Touch include Notion, Canva, Zoom, Microsoft Word, Excel, PowerPoint and Outlook, along with Adobe Lightroom, DaVinci Resolve, Blender, Maxon Cinema 4D, Maxon ZBrush, Shapr3D and Algoriddim djay Pro.
Pixelmator Pro, Logic Pro and Final Cut Pro gain Touch controls through Apple Creator Studio.
Apple said a redesigned hinge adds stability when the screen is touched, and video stabilisation smooths the camera feed when Touch is used during a video call.
The laptops run macOS 27 with Apple Intelligence and Siri AI.

sources.title: Amazon overhauls aging devices lineup with higher-priced Alexa tablet, dumping the budget Fire - CNBC
passages: Amazon on Thursday debuted a set of new, pricier Alexa tablets and said it's ditching its budget-friendly Fire lineup, marking a significant shift in the e-commerce juggernaut's devices strategy.
Amazon denied that rising memory costs played a role in its decision to charge more for the Alexa tablet.
But Panos Panay, the company's devices boss, acknowledged that the shortage made it "quite tricky" to build a premium tablet at a reasonable price without making any "trade-offs."
Alexa is front and center in the new tablets, via a "dynamic tab" on the home screen that offers recommendations and lets users quickly pick up where they left off reading or watching a TV show.
Users can say "Alexa" or tap the "Ask Alexa" button to ask questions.
The Fire lineup includes a 10-inch and 8-inch model as well as two versions targeted for kids.
The $550 Alexa Tablet 12 Pro costs more than double the price of the $155 Fire HD 10, Amazon's base model, and puts it more in line with Apple 's iPad, which runs from $449 to $1,199.
Amazon added a sleeker, sturdier aluminum backing, higher resolution display and faster processors.
The launch comes as Amazon and other device makers are grappling with a historic surge in memory prices .
Amazon in August boosted prices on Echos, Kindles, Fire TVs and other hardware, citing the memory crunch.
In a demo, Panay showed how users could watch a TikTok clip of someone cooking on a grill and ask Alexa to shop for a burger press used in the video.
Users can also pull up a game schedule and add every date to their calendar, Amazon said.

Amazon has historically sold its devices at or near the cost of manufacturing them, partly to undercut competitors with extremely cheap prices, but also with the goal of promoting its other products and services.
It's hoped that for every $80 Echo smart speaker it sells, users will purchase movies, audiobook subscriptions or items from its sprawling webstore, which tend to have higher margins.
The company has recently taken steps to make more money from its devices business under CEO Andy Jassy , who succeeded founder Jeff Bezos in 2021.
Last year, it introduced pricier versions of its Echo smart speakers and began charging non-Prime members a subscription for Alexa+ , the souped-up version of its digital assistant.
"I think the team did a good job designing without making that trade," Panay told CNBC in an interview.
"They gave you the full craftsmanship of a product, but are able to keep it at that price point."

Last year, it introduced pricier versions of its Echo smart speakers and began charging non-Prime members a subscription for Alexa+ , the souped-up version of its digital assistant. The $550 Alexa Tablet 12 Pro costs more than double the price of the $155 Fire HD 10, Amazon's base model, and puts it more in line with Apple 's iPad, which runs from $449 to $1,199. The launch comes as Amazon and other device makers are grappling with a historic surge in memory prices . Amazon in August boosted prices on Echos, Kindles, Fire TVs and other hardware, citing the memory crunch. And earlier this year, Apple raised its prices on MacBooks and iPads, while Nintendo hiked the price of its Switch 2 console. Amazon denied that rising memory costs played a role in its decision to charge more for the Alexa tablet. But Panos Panay, the company's devices boss, acknowledged that the shortage made it "quite tricky" to build a premium tablet at a reasonable price without making any "trade-offs." "I think the team did a good job designing without making that trade," Panay told CNBC in an interview. "They gave you the full craftsmanship of a product, but are able to keep it at that price point." The company said the Alexa tablet's improved speed and performance, artificial intelligence features, and upgraded design warrant a higher price tag and put the devices on par with "the best tablets on the market." Amazon added a sleeker, sturdier aluminum backing, higher resolution display and faster processors. On the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, the highest-end model, it incorporated "Nanomatte" display technology that was developed in partnership with Corning to "dramatically reduce screen glare." One of the most notable upgrades is that all of the devices run Google 's Android operating system, a major departure from earlier models, which relied on a custom Android version dubbed Fire OS and used Amazon's own app store, limiting the number of apps that were available. It's also the first time Amazon has attached a set of devices to the Alexa brand, the company's automated assistant first launched in 2014 via the Echo smart speaker. Users can say "Alexa" or tap the "Ask Alexa" button to ask questions. The company also introduced a new feature called "On-Screen Intelligence," where users can ask Alexa to look at what's on their screen and make suggestions or take actions. In a demo, Panay showed how users could watch a TikTok clip of someone cooking on a grill and ask Alexa to shop for a burger press used in the video. Users can also pull up a game schedule and add every date to their calendar, Amazon said. "She'll do the homework, and if things work out, she's going to bring up a shopping list where I can just hit buy now," Panay said. Amazon said it will continue to support the Fire lineup for four years after the final shipment and consumers can continue using their devices as they do today, but it is no longer manufacturing new units. sources.title: Amazon unveils its newest lineup of Alexa+ devices - About Amazon Australia
passages: Today, Amazon announced the latest generation of Alexa devices , each designed for Alexa+ and purpose-built for the moments and tasks customers turn to Alexa for most.
The next-generation Echo Dot is designed for everywhere you can imagine and packs even more into its compact form factor.

For the first time, it includes a built-in smart home hub, so Alexa connects to hundreds of compatible devices such as lights, locks, thermostats right out of the box, plus a built-in eero Wi-Fi extender that adds up to 93 square metres of coverage to your existing network.
At its core is Amazon’s custom AZ3 silicon, with a new AI Accelerator built for on-device AI that sharpens conversational detection and filters out background noise.
Music, audiobooks, and podcasts sound great on the new Echo Dot, with crisp vocals and 50% more bass than its predecessor.
Echo Studio with Home Camera takes Amazon's best-sounding speaker and gives it a richer understanding of the room around it, making Alexa even more useful.
The camera enables a new Adaptive Volume feature that optimises playback as you move throughout the room.

What's new is context: with more awareness of its surroundings, Alexa can help in real time —explaining the rules on a board game box you hold up, recognizing a box of cereal to help you reorder it, or letting you check in on the room from the Alexa app while you're away.
Privacy is built into every Echo device from the ground up, and customers are in control of their experience.
There are clear visual indicators when Alexa is listening, and a dedicated privacy button turns the microphones off completely.

coreStoryFacts.text: Amazon on Thursday debuted a set of new, pricier Alexa tablets and said it's ditching its budget-friendly Fire lineup, marking a significant shift in the e-commerce juggernaut's devices strategy.
Amazon denied that rising memory costs played a role in its decision to charge more for the Alexa tablet.
But Panos Panay, the company's devices boss, acknowledged that the shortage made it "quite tricky" to build a premium tablet at a reasonable price without making any "trade-offs."
Alexa is front and center in the new tablets, via a "dynamic tab" on the home screen that offers recommendations and lets users quickly pick up where they left off reading or watching a TV show.
Users can say "Alexa" or tap the "Ask Alexa" button to ask questions.
The Fire lineup includes a 10-inch and 8-inch model as well as two versions targeted for kids.
The $550 Alexa Tablet 12 Pro costs more than double the price of the $155 Fire HD 10, Amazon's base model, and puts it more in line with Apple 's iPad, which runs from $449 to $1,199.
Amazon added a sleeker, sturdier aluminum backing, higher resolution display and faster processors.
The launch comes as Amazon and other device makers are grappling with a historic surge in memory prices .
Amazon in August boosted prices on Echos, Kindles, Fire TVs and other hardware, citing the memory crunch.
In a demo, Panay showed how users could watch a TikTok clip of someone cooking on a grill and ask Alexa to shop for a burger press used in the video.
Users can also pull up a game schedule and add every date to their calendar, Amazon said.

Amazon has historically sold its devices at or near the cost of manufacturing them, partly to undercut competitors with extremely cheap prices, but also with the goal of promoting its other products and services.
It's hoped that for every $80 Echo smart speaker it sells, users will purchase movies, audiobook subscriptions or items from its sprawling webstore, which tend to have higher margins.
The company has recently taken steps to make more money from its devices business under CEO Andy Jassy , who succeeded founder Jeff Bezos in 2021.
Last year, it introduced pricier versions of its Echo smart speakers and began charging non-Prime members a subscription for Alexa+ , the souped-up version of its digital assistant.
"I think the team did a good job designing without making that trade," Panay told CNBC in an interview.
"They gave you the full craftsmanship of a product, but are able to keep it at that price point."
Today, Amazon announced the latest generation of Alexa devices , each designed for Alexa+ and purpose-built for the moments and tasks customers turn to Alexa for most.
The next-generation Echo Dot is designed for everywhere you can imagine and packs even more into its compact form factor.

For the first time, it includes a built-in smart home hub, so Alexa connects to hundreds of compatible devices such as lights, locks, thermostats right out of the box, plus a built-in eero Wi-Fi extender that adds up to 93 square metres of coverage to your existing network.
At its core is Amazon’s custom AZ3 silicon, with a new AI Accelerator built for on-device AI that sharpens conversational detection and filters out background noise.
Music, audiobooks, and podcasts sound great on the new Echo Dot, with crisp vocals and 50% more bass than its predecessor.
Echo Studio with Home Camera takes Amazon's best-sounding speaker and gives it a richer understanding of the room around it, making Alexa even more useful.

extraction.body: Amazon on Thursday debuted a set of new, pricier Alexa tablets and said it's ditching its budget-friendly Fire lineup, marking a significant shift in the e-commerce juggernaut's devices strategy. The company unveiled 8-inch, 11-inch and 12-inch models, which start at $230 and run up to $550. All devices are available for preorder on Thursday and will begin shipping Oct. 14. Amazon has historically sold its devices at or near the cost of manufacturing them, partly to undercut competitors with extremely cheap prices, but also with the goal of promoting its other products and services. It's hoped that for every $80 Echo smart speaker it sells, users will purchase movies, audiobook subscriptions or items from its sprawling webstore, which tend to have higher margins. The company has recently taken steps to make more money from its devices business under CEO Andy Jassy , who succeeded founder Jeff Bezos in 2021. Last year, it introduced pricier versions of its Echo smart speakers and began charging non-Prime members a subscription for Alexa+ , the souped-up version of its digital assistant. The $550 Alexa Tablet 12 Pro costs more than double the price of the $155 Fire HD 10, Amazon's base model, and puts it more in line with Apple 's iPad, which runs from $449 to $1,199. The launch comes as Amazon and other device makers are grappling with a historic surge in memory prices . Amazon in August boosted prices on Echos, Kindles, Fire TVs and other hardware, citing the memory crunch. And earlier this year, Apple raised its prices on MacBooks and iPads, while Nintendo hiked the price of its Switch 2 console. Amazon denied that rising memory costs played a role in its decision to charge more for the Alexa tablet. But Panos Panay, the company's devices boss, acknowledged that the shortage made it "quite tricky" to build a premium tablet at a reasonable price without making any "trade-offs." "I think the team did a good job designing without making that trade," Panay told CNBC in an interview. "They gave you the full craftsmanship of a product, but are able to keep it at that price point." The company said the Alexa tablet's improved speed and performance, artificial intelligence features, and upgraded design warrant a higher price tag and put the devices on par with "the best tablets on the market." Amazon added a sleeker, sturdier aluminum backing, higher resolution display and faster processors. On the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, the highest-end model, it incorporated "Nanomatte" display technology that was developed in partnership with Corning to "dramatically reduce screen glare." One of the most notable upgrades is that all of the devices run Google 's Android operating system, a major departure from earlier models, which relied on a custom Android version dubbed Fire OS and used Amazon's own app store, limiting the number of apps that were available. It's also the first time Amazon has attached a set of devices to the Alexa brand, the company's automated assistant first launched in 2014 via the Echo smart speaker. Alexa is front and center in the new tablets, via a "dynamic tab" on the home screen that offers recommendations and lets users quickly pick up where they left off reading or watching a TV show. Users can say "Alexa" or tap the "Ask Alexa" button to ask questions. The company also introduced a new feature called "On-Screen Intelligence," where users can ask Alexa to look at what's on their screen and make suggestions or take actions. In a demo, Panay showed how users could watch a TikTok clip of someone cooking on a grill and ask Alexa to shop for a burger press used in the video. Users can also pull up a game schedule and add every date to their calendar, Amazon said. "She'll do the homework, and if things work out, she's going to bring up a shopping list where I can just hit buy now," Panay said. Amazon said it will continue to support the Fire lineup for four years after the final shipment and consumers can continue using their devices as they do today, but it is no longer manufacturing new units. facts.text: Amazon on Thursday debuted a set of new, pricier Alexa tablets and said it's ditching its budget-friendly Fire lineup, marking a significant shift in the e-commerce juggernaut's devices strategy.
Amazon denied that rising memory costs played a role in its decision to charge more for the Alexa tablet.
But Panos Panay, the company's devices boss, acknowledged that the shortage made it "quite tricky" to build a premium tablet at a reasonable price without making any "trade-offs."
Alexa is front and center in the new tablets, via a "dynamic tab" on the home screen that offers recommendations and lets users quickly pick up where they left off reading or watching a TV show.
Users can say "Alexa" or tap the "Ask Alexa" button to ask questions.
The Fire lineup includes a 10-inch and 8-inch model as well as two versions targeted for kids.
The $550 Alexa Tablet 12 Pro costs more than double the price of the $155 Fire HD 10, Amazon's base model, and puts it more in line with Apple 's iPad, which runs from $449 to $1,199.
Amazon added a sleeker, sturdier aluminum backing, higher resolution display and faster processors.
The launch comes as Amazon and other device makers are grappling with a historic surge in memory prices .
Amazon in August boosted prices on Echos, Kindles, Fire TVs and other hardware, citing the memory crunch.
In a demo, Panay showed how users could watch a TikTok clip of someone cooking on a grill and ask Alexa to shop for a burger press used in the video.
Users can also pull up a game schedule and add every date to their calendar, Amazon said.

Amazon has historically sold its devices at or near the cost of manufacturing them, partly to undercut competitors with extremely cheap prices, but also with the goal of promoting its other products and services.
It's hoped that for every $80 Echo smart speaker it sells, users will purchase movies, audiobook subscriptions or items from its sprawling webstore, which tend to have higher margins.
The company has recently taken steps to make more money from its devices business under CEO Andy Jassy , who succeeded founder Jeff Bezos in 2021.
Last year, it introduced pricier versions of its Echo smart speakers and began charging non-Prime members a subscription for Alexa+ , the souped-up version of its digital assistant.
"I think the team did a good job designing without making that trade," Panay told CNBC in an interview.
"They gave you the full craftsmanship of a product, but are able to keep it at that price point."
Today, Amazon announced the latest generation of Alexa devices , each designed for Alexa+ and purpose-built for the moments and tasks customers turn to Alexa for most.

Echo Studio with Home Camera takes Amazon's best-sounding speaker and gives it a richer understanding of the room around it, making Alexa even more useful.
The camera enables a new Adaptive Volume feature that optimises playback as you move throughout the room.

What's new is context: with more awareness of its surroundings, Alexa can help in real time —explaining the rules on a board game box you hold up, recognizing a box of cereal to help you reorder it, or letting you check in on the room from the Alexa app while you're away.
Privacy is built into every Echo device from the ground up, and customers are in control of their experience.

extraction.body: Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman and senior executive at Singapore -based data center company Megaspeed, has emerged at the center of an alleged Chinese intelligence operation involving advanced artificial intelligence chips and U.S. national security concerns. U.S. intelligence agencies reportedly assessed that she was working as an intelligence asset for Beijing, according to The New York Times, drawing scrutiny to her professional connections and the company's potential role in providing access to restricted computing technology. The allegations have also raised questions about Washington's response to intelligence concerns involving an executive reportedly connected to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. However, key details about Alice Huang's alleged activities remain unclear. Alice Huang, also identified as Huang Le, is a Chinese citizen who held a senior executive position at Megaspeed, a data center company based in Singapore. Her professional background has attracted attention because of the company's potential role in providing access to advanced computing infrastructure. According to the report, U.S. officials suspected Megaspeed of helping Chinese businesses access advanced Nvidia chips despite American export restrictions. These chips are essential to developing and operating sophisticated artificial intelligence systems, making their potential transfer to China a national security concern for Washington. Huang's position at Megaspeed placed her within an industry facing increased scrutiny over whether data centers and intermediary companies could be used to circumvent restrictions on advanced technology. Publicly available information about her education, personal background and wider career history remains limited. Reporting on the case has focused primarily on her alleged intelligence connections and professional associations. U.S. intelligence agencies reportedly concluded that Huang was gathering information for Beijing. However, the specific information she allegedly handled and the extent of her suspected activities have not been publicly established. The investigation into Megaspeed reportedly expanded after a Commerce Department official visited a data center in Malaysia in late 2024 and found Nvidia equipment still packed in boxes. Investigators examined whether the company's operations could have helped Chinese businesses access restricted computing technology. Singaporean authorities questioned Huang in 2025 and later released her, according to the report. The circumstances surrounding the questioning and the full scope of the allegations remain unclear. Reported Association With Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Alice Huang's case has attracted further attention because of her reported close relationship with Jensen Huang, the chief executive of Nvidia, a leading supplier of advanced AI chips. U.S. officials initially reportedly did not believe Jensen Huang knew about Alice Huang's alleged intelligence activities. Some senior administration officials later questioned whether he could have remained unaware, although the report did not establish that he knowingly participated in any wrongdoing. Nvidia rejected suggestions that the relationship involved anything improper. Company spokesman John Rizzo said, "Jensen's contacts with Huang are neither unusual nor unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job." Rizzo added that customers such as Megaspeed receive ordinary business information rather than sensitive trade secrets or national security information. The allegations have drawn attention to the intersection of business relationships and national security. Jensen Huang has lobbied the Trump administration to ease restrictions on Nvidia chip sales to China, while U.S. officials have sought to prevent advanced technology from reaching strategic rivals. President Donald Trump was reportedly briefed on intelligence concerns about Alice Huang approximately a year before its publication but did not take action at the time. Megaspeed said it takes the allegations seriously, has retained outside counsel and intends to cooperate with the U.S. government. China's Embassy in Washington rejected the accusations as "groundless smears and slanders."

NORTH KOREAN HACKERS USE AI TO FORGE MILITARY IDS The conspiracy allegedly involved four separate exports of Nvidia GPUs to China.

The Department of Justice said in a news release that Hon Ning "Mathew" Ho, 34, a U.S. citizen born in Hong Kong and living in Tampa, Florida; Brian Curtis Raymond, 46, of Huntsville, Alabama; Cham "Tony" Li, 38, a Chinese national living in San Leandro, California; and Jing "Harry" Chen, 45, a Chinese national living in Tampa on a student visa, face multiple counts, including conspiracy to violate the Export Control Reform Act, smuggling and money laundering.

The Department of Justice said in a news release that Hon Ning "Mathew" Ho, 34, a U.S. citizen born in Hong Kong and living in Tampa, Florida; Brian Curtis Raymond, 46, of Huntsville, Alabama; Cham "Tony" Li, 38, a Chinese national living in San Leandro, California; and Jing "Harry" Chen, 45, a Chinese national living in Tampa on a student visa, face multiple counts, including conspiracy to violate the Export Control Reform Act, smuggling and money laundering. "The indictment unsealed yesterday alleges a deliberate and deceptive effort to transship controlled Nvidia GPUs to China by falsifying paperwork, creating fake contracts and misleading U.S. authorities," Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg said.  "The National Security Division is committed to disrupting these kinds of black markets of sensitive U.S. technologies and holding accountable those who participate in this illicit trade." CHINESE HACKERS WEAPONIZE ANTHROPIC'S AI IN FIRST AUTONOMOUS CYBERATTACK TARGETING GLOBAL ORGANIZATIONS Prosecutors allege the defendants used a Tampa-based company called Janford Realtor LLC as a front to purchase and export restricted Nvidia GPUs. Despite its name, Janford Realtor never engaged in any real estate business and was allegedly created to conceal shipments of high-end processors bound for China. The group conspired from September 2023 through November 2025 to illegally export the advanced chips through third countries, including Malaysia and Thailand, to avoid U.S. export controls, the indictment states. Investigators said the defendants falsified documents, created fake contracts and misled authorities about the final destination of the technology. NORTH KOREAN HACKERS USE AI TO FORGE MILITARY IDS The conspiracy allegedly involved four separate exports of Nvidia GPUs to China. The first two shipments, sent between October 2024 and January 2025, included roughly 400 Nvidia A100 processors. Law enforcement disrupted two additional shipments before they were completed, which involved 10 Hewlett Packard Enterprise supercomputers containing Nvidia H100 GPUs and 50 separate H200 GPUs. Investigators said the defendants received more than $3.8 million in wire transfers from China to fund the operation. None of the defendants obtained the licenses required to export the technology, and authorities said they knowingly lied about the final destination of the processors to evade U.S. export laws. FORMER GOOGLE CEO WARNS AI SYSTEMS CAN BE HACKED TO BECOME EXTREMELY DANGEROUS WEAPONS The People’s Republic of China, the indictment noted, seeks to become the world leader in AI by 2030 and aims to use AI for military modernization, including the design and testing of weapons of mass destruction. Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Florida is firmly committed to safeguarding our country’s national security," U.S. "Thanks to the dedicated investigative work by our law enforcement partners, these defendants who wrongfully exported this sensitive technology are facing justice."

coreStoryFacts.text: A top executive of a Singapore AI cloud firm that was accused of illegally selling Nvidia chips to China could also have been a Chinese spy, anonymous sources told the New York Times .

In 2025, the Times reported that the Commerce Department had investigated Megaspeed over concerns that it was helping Chinese companies sidestep AI chip export regulations by reselling restricted chips to them.

Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman and senior executive at Singapore -based data center company Megaspeed, has emerged at the center of an alleged Chinese intelligence operation involving advanced artificial intelligence chips and U.S. national security concerns.
The allegations have also raised questions about Washington's response to intelligence concerns involving an executive reportedly connected to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
However, key details about Alice Huang's alleged activities remain unclear.
Jensen Huang has lobbied the Trump administration to ease restrictions on Nvidia chip sales to China, while U.S. officials have sought to prevent advanced technology from reaching strategic rivals.
Nvidia rejected suggestions that the relationship involved anything improper.
The investigation into Megaspeed reportedly expanded after a Commerce Department official visited a data center in Malaysia in late 2024 and found Nvidia equipment still packed in boxes.

The Department of Justice said in a news release that Hon Ning "Mathew" Ho, 34, a U.S. citizen born in Hong Kong and living in Tampa, Florida; Brian Curtis Raymond, 46, of Huntsville, Alabama; Cham "Tony" Li, 38, a Chinese national living in San Leandro, California; and Jing "Harry" Chen, 45, a Chinese national living in Tampa on a student visa, face multiple counts, including conspiracy to violate the Export Control Reform Act, smuggling and money laundering.

passages: Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman and senior executive at Singapore -based data center company Megaspeed, has emerged at the center of an alleged Chinese intelligence operation involving advanced artificial intelligence chips and U.S. national security concerns.
The allegations have also raised questions about Washington's response to intelligence concerns involving an executive reportedly connected to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
However, key details about Alice Huang's alleged activities remain unclear.
Jensen Huang has lobbied the Trump administration to ease restrictions on Nvidia chip sales to China, while U.S. officials have sought to prevent advanced technology from reaching strategic rivals.
Nvidia rejected suggestions that the relationship involved anything improper.

extraction.body: Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman and senior executive at Singapore -based data center company Megaspeed, has emerged at the center of an alleged Chinese intelligence operation involving advanced artificial intelligence chips and U.S. national security concerns. U.S. intelligence agencies reportedly assessed that she was working as an intelligence asset for Beijing, according to The New York Times, drawing scrutiny to her professional connections and the company's potential role in providing access to restricted computing technology. The allegations have also raised questions about Washington's response to intelligence concerns involving an executive reportedly connected to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. However, key details about Alice Huang's alleged activities remain unclear. Alice Huang, also identified as Huang Le, is a Chinese citizen who held a senior executive position at Megaspeed, a data center company based in Singapore. Her professional background has attracted attention because of the company's potential role in providing access to advanced computing infrastructure. According to the report, U.S. officials suspected Megaspeed of helping Chinese businesses access advanced Nvidia chips despite American export restrictions. These chips are essential to developing and operating sophisticated artificial intelligence systems, making their potential transfer to China a national security concern for Washington. Huang's position at Megaspeed placed her within an industry facing increased scrutiny over whether data centers and intermediary companies could be used to circumvent restrictions on advanced technology. Publicly available information about her education, personal background and wider career history remains limited. Reporting on the case has focused primarily on her alleged intelligence connections and professional associations. U.S. intelligence agencies reportedly concluded that Huang was gathering information for Beijing. However, the specific information she allegedly handled and the extent of her suspected activities have not been publicly established. The investigation into Megaspeed reportedly expanded after a Commerce Department official visited a data center in Malaysia in late 2024 and found Nvidia equipment still packed in boxes. Investigators examined whether the company's operations could have helped Chinese businesses access restricted computing technology. Singaporean authorities questioned Huang in 2025 and later released her, according to the report. The circumstances surrounding the questioning and the full scope of the allegations remain unclear. Reported Association With Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Alice Huang's case has attracted further attention because of her reported close relationship with Jensen Huang, the chief executive of Nvidia, a leading supplier of advanced AI chips. U.S. officials initially reportedly did not believe Jensen Huang knew about Alice Huang's alleged intelligence activities. Some senior administration officials later questioned whether he could have remained unaware, although the report did not establish that he knowingly participated in any wrongdoing. Nvidia rejected suggestions that the relationship involved anything improper. Company spokesman John Rizzo said, "Jensen's contacts with Huang are neither unusual nor unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job." Rizzo added that customers such as Megaspeed receive ordinary business information rather than sensitive trade secrets or national security information. The allegations have drawn attention to the intersection of business relationships and national security. Jensen Huang has lobbied the Trump administration to ease restrictions on Nvidia chip sales to China, while U.S. officials have sought to prevent advanced technology from reaching strategic rivals. President Donald Trump was reportedly briefed on intelligence concerns about Alice Huang approximately a year before its publication but did not take action at the time. Megaspeed said it takes the allegations seriously, has retained outside counsel and intends to cooperate with the U.S. government. China's Embassy in Washington rejected the accusations as "groundless smears and slanders."

passages: Two Americans and two Chinese nationals are accused of secretly funneling advanced Nvidia artificial intelligence (AI) chips to China, a plot prosecutors say threatened U.S. national security and violated strict export controls.
NORTH KOREAN HACKERS USE AI TO FORGE MILITARY IDS The conspiracy allegedly involved four separate exports of Nvidia GPUs to China.

The Department of Justice said in a news release that Hon Ning "Mathew" Ho, 34, a U.S. citizen born in Hong Kong and living in Tampa, Florida; Brian Curtis Raymond, 46, of Huntsville, Alabama; Cham "Tony" Li, 38, a Chinese national living in San Leandro, California; and Jing "Harry" Chen, 45, a Chinese national living in Tampa on a student visa, face multiple counts, including conspiracy to violate the Export Control Reform Act, smuggling and money laundering.
GET FOX BUSINESS ON THE GO BY CLICKING HERE The indictment also alleged that the PRC is pursuing cutting-edge U.S. technology in furtherance of that goal, including Nvidia GPUs.
Investigators said the defendants received more than $3.8 million in wire transfers from China to fund the operation.

Law enforcement disrupted two additional shipments before they were completed, which involved 10 Hewlett Packard Enterprise supercomputers containing Nvidia H100 GPUs and 50 separate H200 GPUs.
Despite its name, Janford Realtor never engaged in any real estate business and was allegedly created to conceal shipments of high-end processors bound for China.

extraction.body: Two Americans and two Chinese nationals are accused of secretly funneling advanced Nvidia artificial intelligence (AI) chips to China, a plot prosecutors say threatened U.S. national security and violated strict export controls. The Department of Justice said in a news release that Hon Ning "Mathew" Ho, 34, a U.S. citizen born in Hong Kong and living in Tampa, Florida; Brian Curtis Raymond, 46, of Huntsville, Alabama; Cham "Tony" Li, 38, a Chinese national living in San Leandro, California; and Jing "Harry" Chen, 45, a Chinese national living in Tampa on a student visa, face multiple counts, including conspiracy to violate the Export Control Reform Act, smuggling and money laundering. "The indictment unsealed yesterday alleges a deliberate and deceptive effort to transship controlled Nvidia GPUs to China by falsifying paperwork, creating fake contracts and misleading U.S. authorities," Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg said.  "The National Security Division is committed to disrupting these kinds of black markets of sensitive U.S. technologies and holding accountable those who participate in this illicit trade." CHINESE HACKERS WEAPONIZE ANTHROPIC'S AI IN FIRST AUTONOMOUS CYBERATTACK TARGETING GLOBAL ORGANIZATIONS Prosecutors allege the defendants used a Tampa-based company called Janford Realtor LLC as a front to purchase and export restricted Nvidia GPUs. Despite its name, Janford Realtor never engaged in any real estate business and was allegedly created to conceal shipments of high-end processors bound for China. The group conspired from September 2023 through November 2025 to illegally export the advanced chips through third countries, including Malaysia and Thailand, to avoid U.S. export controls, the indictment states. Investigators said the defendants falsified documents, created fake contracts and misled authorities about the final destination of the technology. NORTH KOREAN HACKERS USE AI TO FORGE MILITARY IDS The conspiracy allegedly involved four separate exports of Nvidia GPUs to China. The first two shipments, sent between October 2024 and January 2025, included roughly 400 Nvidia A100 processors. Law enforcement disrupted two additional shipments before they were completed, which involved 10 Hewlett Packard Enterprise supercomputers containing Nvidia H100 GPUs and 50 separate H200 GPUs. Investigators said the defendants received more than $3.8 million in wire transfers from China to fund the operation. None of the defendants obtained the licenses required to export the technology, and authorities said they knowingly lied about the final destination of the processors to evade U.S. export laws. FORMER GOOGLE CEO WARNS AI SYSTEMS CAN BE HACKED TO BECOME EXTREMELY DANGEROUS WEAPONS The People’s Republic of China, the indictment noted, seeks to become the world leader in AI by 2030 and aims to use AI for military modernization, including the design and testing of weapons of mass destruction. Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Florida is firmly committed to safeguarding our country’s national security," U.S. "Thanks to the dedicated investigative work by our law enforcement partners, these defendants who wrongfully exported this sensitive technology are facing justice."

extraction.body: After years of resisting, Apple today launched a MacBook Pro with a touchscreen starting at $2,899. The release comes nearly 10 years after the company first tried integrating touchscreens on its laptops, with its Touch Bar on a MacBook Pro , which it later went on to remove . The new MacBook Pro more fully embraces the touchscreen, offering a new PROLED XDR Display in both 14-inch and 16-inch screen sizes. The device is powered by M5 Pro and M5 Max chips as options to choose from, along with up to 128GB of unified memory and up to 16TB of storage. The display has 2,000 nits peak HDR and SDR brightness and a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio. To make the new MacBook easy to use, Apple designed a hinge that stabilizes the screen when users touch it. This also helps to stabilize the camera when you are on a video call and trying to access content on the display. In addition, the screen will include a Dynamic Island-style cutout instead of the notch that’s present on most of the current MacBooks. Plus, the new MacBook features a six-speaker array with a new woofer design for better sound. The 14-inch Pro weighs 3.0 pounds (1.38 kg), and the 16-inch Pro weighs 4.0 pounds (1.82 kg) — lighter than its non-touch predecessors. Both feature three Thunderbolt 5 ports, an HDMI port, an SDXC card slot, MagSafe, and a headphone jack. Users can hook up three external displays on the M5 Pro variant and up to four displays on the M5 Max variant. The Touchscreen MacBook Pro 14-inch starts at $2,899, and the 16-inch version starts at $3,399. Consumers can place a preorder for the new touchscreen MacBook Pro from October 30, and the device will be available starting November 6. The new Touchscreen MacBook marks two marquee product launches for new CEO John Ternus, who also introduced the company’s first foldable, the iPhone Duo, in September . Various Apple executives, including Steve Jobs and Tim Cook, have scoffed at the idea of a touchscreen Mac in the past. Jobs famously called the idea “ergonomically terrible” at one point. However, rumors of the company working on such a variant started circulating nearly three years before today’s introduction . The launch follows yesterday’s unveiling of a new standard MacBook Pro with the M6 chip in 14-inch size starting from $1,999 . extraction.body: After years of resisting, Apple today launched a MacBook Pro with a touchscreen starting at $2,899. The release comes nearly 10 years after the company first tried integrating touchscreens on its laptops, with its Touch Bar on a MacBook Pro , which it later went on to remove . The new MacBook Pro more fully embraces the touchscreen, offering a new PROLED XDR Display in both 14-inch and 16-inch screen sizes. The device is powered by M5 Pro and M5 Max chips as options to choose from, along with up to 128GB of unified memory and up to 16TB of storage. The display has 2,000 nits peak HDR and SDR brightness and a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio. To make the new MacBook easy to use, Apple designed a hinge that stabilizes the screen when users touch it. This also helps to stabilize the camera when you are on a video call and trying to access content on the display. In addition, the screen will include a Dynamic Island-style cutout instead of the notch that’s present on most of the current MacBooks. Plus, the new MacBook features a six-speaker array with a new woofer design for better sound. The 14-inch Pro weighs 3.0 pounds (1.38 kg), and the 16-inch Pro weighs 4.0 pounds (1.82 kg) — lighter than its non-touch predecessors. Both feature three Thunderbolt 5 ports, an HDMI port, an SDXC card slot, MagSafe, and a headphone jack. Users can hook up three external displays on the M5 Pro variant and up to four displays on the M5 Max variant. The Touchscreen MacBook Pro 14-inch starts at $2,899, and the 16-inch version starts at $3,399. Consumers can place a preorder for the new touchscreen MacBook Pro from October 30, and the device will be available starting November 6. The new Touchscreen MacBook marks two marquee product launches for new CEO John Ternus, who also introduced the company’s first foldable, the iPhone Duo, in September . Various Apple executives, including Steve Jobs and Tim Cook, have scoffed at the idea of a touchscreen Mac in the past. Jobs famously called the idea “ergonomically terrible” at one point. However, rumors of the company working on such a variant started circulating nearly three years before today’s introduction . The launch follows yesterday’s unveiling of a new standard MacBook Pro with the M6 chip in 14-inch size starting from $1,999 . extraction.body: Personally identifiable information belonging to thousands of U.S. Department of Homeland Security employees has been published online after a hacker stole reams of data in a previously undisclosed breach at the government department earlier this year. The breach includes names, job titles, and work contact information, such as email addresses, cell phone numbers, and office locations, of more than 40,000 people who work for the federal department, including border and immigration agents, cybersecurity staffers, and senior department officials. A hacker who goes by the handle Department of Peace claimed they obtained the data from an Okta single sign-on system used by Homeland Security to allow employees and contractors across its various agencies to log in to its central network. The Okta system also contains IT and log-in records associated with the employees’ user account, including details about which systems and internal apps they are permitted to access. More than half of the dataset — some 21,000 records — relate to employees with U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), who work at airports and other ports of entry. The data also contains records associated with another 10,000 employees of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and its Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) unit, and just under a 1,000 employees who work at U.S. cybersecurity defense agency CISA. Thousands of additional records relate to staff who work at the department’s headquarters and its other agencies, including U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services and the Federal Protective Service. “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs,” said Department of Peace in a note left with the data, which TechCrunch has seen. The hacker did not respond to TechCrunch’s email requesting comment and with questions about how the breach was carried out. This is the latest data breach to hit the U.S. government in recent months, following earlier hacks involving the theft of thousands of FBI agents’ personnel records and the personal information of millions of serving and former military service personnel from the Pentagon’s human resources unit . It’s also the second breach involving Homeland Security this year, after the same hacker claimed to have taken thousands of contracts between the department and the private sector, including defense contractors and surveillance vendors. The latest batch of breached data, which appears authentic, offers a rare — albeit incomplete — view into the scale and operations of Homeland Security, whose deportations, arbitrary detentions, and killings of U.S. citizens under its leadership have become a key issue for voters ahead of the upcoming U.S. midterm elections. The stolen Homeland Security data was provided to journalist and hacker maia arson crimew, who then shared a copy with DDoSecrets , a nonprofit collective that hosts leaked datasets in the public interest. TechCrunch verified a portion of the data as authentic by matching the names of several known Homeland Security employees against an offline copy of the database. The thousands of employee directory records appear to have been exfiltrated around mid-August, according to the timestamps on each person’s record. The number of leaked records is equivalent to about one-fifth of Homeland Security’s workforce, which totals around 220,000 staff . It’s unclear whether the vulnerability that allowed the breach has been fixed or if Homeland Security is aware of the data theft. A spokesperson for Homeland Security told TechCrunch after publication: “DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively. We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected. We will update the public when more information is available.” When reached, Okta said it was aware of this report. “Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised,” a spokesperson said. While the leaked data includes identifiable information about agents and officers, the dataset also reveals more about the surveillance technologies and cybersecurity tools that Homeland Security employees may be able to access. Critics have called for investigations into tech companies that fund or provide their technology to ICE. The leaked data contains information about employees’ membership in user groups within the department’s Active Directory, a system that controls access to the department’s internal tools, services, and third-party offerings used for work. Most of the Homeland Security employees in the dataset were members of the user group that had access to Microsoft 365, the tech giant’s cloud service that hosts the agency’s emails and files, as well as user groups for accessing Adobe Acrobat, Citrix, and other typical desktop software. The data also shows that around 4,500 users, including ICE agents and deportation officers, are members of a group called “Headspace_users.” Online therapy provider Headspace previously had an $82,500 federal contract with ICE that ended in 2023 to fund “mental health software required for ERO employees,” a reference to ICE’s deportation unit. A spokesperson for Headspace said the company has not provided any services to DHS or ICE since 2023. Dozens of other user groups reference Penlink , a web surveillance company that makes technology it claims can track the location data of hundreds of millions of mobile devices. Penlink has had a contract with ICE for years. The user groups vary in size, from a handful of users in local Homeland Security offices around the country to more than 2,000 users across ICE’s HSI unit nationally. One group specifically references Penlink PLX, which the company says is used to capture and analyze “real-time intelligence” from phone calls, texts, web activity, and social media. A spokesperson for Penlink did not respond to a request for comment. One user group also includes more than 200 CBP users associated with Mobile Fortify, a facial-recognition app used by both CBP and ICE agents to identify people and verify their information and immigration status . The user groups also include several employees associated with ChatGPT access, including senior DHS officials, as well as other groups associated with investigations into the China-backed hacking groups known as Salt Typhoon and Volt Typhoon. Researchers and public information advocates say that the exposed data could provide valuable leads for investigations into alleged abuses by the Trump administration, such as identifying email addresses of agents that can be used in public records requests under the Freedom of Information Act. “Email addresses and phone numbers are indispensable tools for FOIA researchers, often making the difference between a vague records request that gets stonewalled and one that gets results,” said Ryan Shapiro, the executive director of transparency nonprofit Property of the People. “Given the Trump administration’s contempt for even basic transparency, the need for such tools is urgent,” said Shapiro. DDoSecrets co-founder and journalist Emma Best said that the exposed Homeland Security data will be a “catalyst for investigations, empowering journalists, Congressional inquiries, legal challenges, community action and Freedom of Information Act requests.” Zack Whittaker is the security editor at TechCrunch. He also authors the weekly cybersecurity newsletter, this week in security . He can be reached via encrypted message at zackwhittaker.1337 on Signal. extraction.body: Personally identifiable information belonging to thousands of U.S. Department of Homeland Security employees has been published online after a hacker stole reams of data in a previously undisclosed breach at the government department earlier this year. The breach includes names, job titles, and work contact information, such as email addresses, cell phone numbers, and office locations, of more than 40,000 people who work for the federal department, including border and immigration agents, cybersecurity staffers, and senior department officials. A hacker who goes by the handle Department of Peace claimed they obtained the data from an Okta single sign-on system used by Homeland Security to allow employees and contractors across its various agencies to log in to its central network. The Okta system also contains IT and log-in records associated with the employees’ user account, including details about which systems and internal apps they are permitted to access. More than half of the dataset — some 21,000 records — relate to employees with U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), who work at airports and other ports of entry. The data also contains records associated with another 10,000 employees of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and its Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) unit, and just under a 1,000 employees who work at U.S. cybersecurity defense agency CISA. Thousands of additional records relate to staff who work at the department’s headquarters and its other agencies, including U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services and the Federal Protective Service. “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs,” said Department of Peace in a note left with the data, which TechCrunch has seen. The hacker did not respond to TechCrunch’s email requesting comment and with questions about how the breach was carried out. This is the latest data breach to hit the U.S. government in recent months, following earlier hacks involving the theft of thousands of FBI agents’ personnel records and the personal information of millions of serving and former military service personnel from the Pentagon’s human resources unit . It’s also the second breach involving Homeland Security this year, after the same hacker claimed to have taken thousands of contracts between the department and the private sector, including defense contractors and surveillance vendors. The latest batch of breached data, which appears authentic, offers a rare — albeit incomplete — view into the scale and operations of Homeland Security, whose deportations, arbitrary detentions, and killings of U.S. citizens under its leadership have become a key issue for voters ahead of the upcoming U.S. midterm elections. The stolen Homeland Security data was provided to journalist and hacker maia arson crimew, who then shared a copy with DDoSecrets , a nonprofit collective that hosts leaked datasets in the public interest. TechCrunch verified a portion of the data as authentic by matching the names of several known Homeland Security employees against an offline copy of the database. The thousands of employee directory records appear to have been exfiltrated around mid-August, according to the timestamps on each person’s record. The number of leaked records is equivalent to about one-fifth of Homeland Security’s workforce, which totals around 220,000 staff . It’s unclear whether the vulnerability that allowed the breach has been fixed or if Homeland Security is aware of the data theft. A spokesperson for Homeland Security told TechCrunch after publication: “DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively. We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected. We will update the public when more information is available.” When reached, Okta said it was aware of this report. “Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised,” a spokesperson said. While the leaked data includes identifiable information about agents and officers, the dataset also reveals more about the surveillance technologies and cybersecurity tools that Homeland Security employees may be able to access. Critics have called for investigations into tech companies that fund or provide their technology to ICE. The leaked data contains information about employees’ membership in user groups within the department’s Active Directory, a system that controls access to the department’s internal tools, services, and third-party offerings used for work. Most of the Homeland Security employees in the dataset were members of the user group that had access to Microsoft 365, the tech giant’s cloud service that hosts the agency’s emails and files, as well as user groups for accessing Adobe Acrobat, Citrix, and other typical desktop software. The data also shows that around 4,500 users, including ICE agents and deportation officers, are members of a group called “Headspace_users.” Online therapy provider Headspace previously had an $82,500 federal contract with ICE that ended in 2023 to fund “mental health software required for ERO employees,” a reference to ICE’s deportation unit. A spokesperson for Headspace said the company has not provided any services to DHS or ICE since 2023. Dozens of other user groups reference Penlink , a web surveillance company that makes technology it claims can track the location data of hundreds of millions of mobile devices. Penlink has had a contract with ICE for years. The user groups vary in size, from a handful of users in local Homeland Security offices around the country to more than 2,000 users across ICE’s HSI unit nationally. One group specifically references Penlink PLX, which the company says is used to capture and analyze “real-time intelligence” from phone calls, texts, web activity, and social media. A spokesperson for Penlink did not respond to a request for comment. One user group also includes more than 200 CBP users associated with Mobile Fortify, a facial-recognition app used by both CBP and ICE agents to identify people and verify their information and immigration status . The user groups also include several employees associated with ChatGPT access, including senior DHS officials, as well as other groups associated with investigations into the China-backed hacking groups known as Salt Typhoon and Volt Typhoon. Researchers and public information advocates say that the exposed data could provide valuable leads for investigations into alleged abuses by the Trump administration, such as identifying email addresses of agents that can be used in public records requests under the Freedom of Information Act. “Email addresses and phone numbers are indispensable tools for FOIA researchers, often making the difference between a vague records request that gets stonewalled and one that gets results,” said Ryan Shapiro, the executive director of transparency nonprofit Property of the People. “Given the Trump administration’s contempt for even basic transparency, the need for such tools is urgent,” said Shapiro. DDoSecrets co-founder and journalist Emma Best said that the exposed Homeland Security data will be a “catalyst for investigations, empowering journalists, Congressional inquiries, legal challenges, community action and Freedom of Information Act requests.” Zack Whittaker is the security editor at TechCrunch. He also authors the weekly cybersecurity newsletter, this week in security . He can be reached via encrypted message at zackwhittaker.1337 on Signal. You can also contact him by email, or to verify outreach, at [email protected] .

sources.title: The NYT Cooking app is testing AI recipe modifications
passages: The New York Times is testing a new AI feature for its Cooking app that helps users to modify recipes, and it has sparked some drama among users.

Last Friday, NYT Cooking senior editor Genevieve Ko announced the feature, which can be used to recommend substitutions for ingredients and cooking equipment, scale recipes to any number of servings, and “generally make our recipes work for what a cook needs at that moment.” One of the examples given in the article shows a user asking to use baby spinach instead of kale, with the Cooking app feature advising that because baby spinach wilts faster, it should be added during a later step of the recipe.

The AI modification feature is being rolled out gradually while the NYT monitors how it performs — it’s currently available to all Cooking subscribers on the iOS app, and it will be more broadly available “soon.” Some NYT readers have pushed back against the feature, citing concerns in the article’s comment section around the environmental impact of widespread AI adoption and the general impact that AI features may have on the user experience.

extraction.body: The New York Times is testing a new AI feature for its Cooking app that helps users to modify recipes, and it has sparked some drama among users. Last Friday, NYT Cooking senior editor Genevieve Ko announced the feature, which can be used to recommend substitutions for ingredients and cooking equipment, scale recipes to any number of servings, and “generally make our recipes work for what a cook needs at that moment.” One of the examples given in the article shows a user asking to use baby spinach instead of kale, with the Cooking app feature advising that because baby spinach wilts faster, it should be added during a later step of the recipe. Ko says it can also change the recipes around different pans and tools. Customized recipes are private and can’t be published or shared through the app. The AI modification feature is being rolled out gradually while the NYT monitors how it performs — it’s currently available to all Cooking subscribers on the iOS app, and it will be more broadly available “soon.” Some NYT readers have pushed back against the feature, citing concerns in the article’s comment section around the environmental impact of widespread AI adoption and the general impact that AI features may have on the user experience. “I’ve always loved NYT Cooking and it pains me that the AI mandate has reached what used to be a wonderful and simple collection of recipes and notes from all sorts of different people.” This isn’t the first time that AI has been used by the NYT Cooking app. Ko says it was used to convert imperial volume measurements to metric weight measurements in recipes two years ago, and a feature was added last year that converts recipes to halve or double the original serving size. The comments on the new AI feature announcement post have since been closed, but NYT spokesperson Jordan Cohen tells The Verge that this is standard practice: “Comments on this article remained open for four days, with editors from Cooking taking care to answer questions, address concerns and engage directly with readers. We kept that conversation open to give readers a meaningful opportunity to share feedback and hear from the team. Closing comments on older articles is standard practice at The Times so that our moderators can focus on new discussions. We’re pleased to see that many members of our Cooking community are interested in exploring this tool and are already trying it out on our iOS app; they’re reporting good results.”

extraction.body: Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit The New York Times is trying out a new way to boost subscriptions and engagement to its paywalled NYT Cooking recipe platform. With a simple text featuring an emoji, the publisher is dishing out 150 recipes for free. From June 21 through August 15, people in the U.S. can text one fruit or vegetable emoji — like a strawberry, tomato, coconut or corn on the cob — to “361-COOK-NYT” and receive a link to a recipe for free featuring that food item. They will also get early access to special NYT Cooking events starting this July, such as cherry picking in Michigan. Normally, it would cost a subscriber $5 a month to access these features. Once readers get a recipe, they can text that same emoji up to five times to get different recipes featuring that same ingredient. The recipes come from a pool of them that the Times team deemed popular, are easy to make and highlighted summer produce, said Camilla Velasquez, general manager of New York Times Cooking. The Times hopes that giving away recipes for free via text message will help people who are familiar with the NYT Cooking product but aren’t paying subscribers to see the value of a subscription. The Times is not providing any additional special subscription offer or messaging to texters. “It’s [for] people who are curious about [NYT Cooking], but haven’t really been able to take the plunge because they haven’t been able to experience enough of the recipes and this is their opportunity to do so,” Velasquez said. Why emojis? Velasquez said it’s a “fast” and “playful” way to communicate with NYT Cooking and to simplify the process of finding summer recipes. It’s also a way to appeal to the younger audiences NYT Cooking is trying to target, such as millennials. For the text line, The New York Times is working with text messaging platform Subtext, which also works with other publishers like Condé Nast and USA Today Network. This text line is part of a broader strategy at NYT Cooking. The focus for NYT Cooking’s team this year has been “easy to find, easy to make,” Velasquez said. The team was hearing from readers that Cooking recipes were too hard to make and had inaccessible ingredients, Velasquez explained, so it became clear that they had to highlight easier recipes to both draw new subscribers in and retain those who are already paying. There are a couple of ways NYT Cooking is responding. The overarching goal is to “simplify [NYT Cooking] as much as we can,” Velasquez said. The team is working on cutting down the number of ingredients and steps in some recipes. And they want to get more free and simple recipes in front of readers — such as with free seven-day and 14-day trials, and now with the emoji text line. The hope is to ultimately convert newly introduced readers into paid subscribers, who pay $5 a month or $40 a year for a subscription to NYT Cooking. “If a user voluntarily texts NYT Cooking, this is a strong signal of propensity to engage [and or] pay and reduces friction for the user getting the recipe they are after,” said Arvid Tchivzhel, svp of product at subscription management and customer data analytics firm Mather Economics. However, it will also require “significant outreach” to introduce audiences to this initiative, he added. The New York Times is marketing its new emoji text line with billboards in states like Michigan and Washington (for in-season cherries and corn, respectively), events and posts on its social accounts. Despite recent reports that subscriptions to news organizations have stalled in the past year, The New York Times Company has continued to grow its subscriber base, adding 190,000 digital-only subscribers in the first quarter of this year. The company now has over 9 million digital-only subscribers, though it does not break out data on how many subscribers are specifically subscribed to Cooking. In Q1 2023, The New York Times Company surpassed 3 million subscribers who were paying for a bundle (which includes access to the Times’ core news and standalone Cooking, Games, Wirecutter and The Athletic products) or multi-product subscription plan, thanks to about 520,000 new digital-only bundle and multi-product subscribers in the quarter. Velasquez said the main drivers of subscriber conversions are NYT Cooking app usage, videos on social media and newsletters. She declined to share how many NYT Cooking subscribers there are, or how many are converting through these platforms. Texting as an audience engagement channel historically hasn’t been successful in driving subscriber acquisitions, according Tchivzhel, based on his experience working with publishers at Mather Economics. “But it is perhaps a deeper level of engagement that can drive more meaningful connections between [the] audience and the Cooking product,” he said in an email. Other companies are also using text messaging as a marketing tactic, such as KBP Brands, a KFC franchisee , which recently expanded SMS marketing across its 847 U.S. locations. The Times has a plan for readers who don’t want to subscribe. “It’s [for] people who are curious about [NYT Cooking], but haven’t really been able to take the plunge because they haven’t been able to experience enough of the recipes and this is their opportunity to do so,” Velasquez said.

Why emojis? Velasquez said it’s a “fast” and “playful” way to communicate with NYT Cooking and to simplify the process of finding summer recipes. It’s also a way to appeal to the younger audiences NYT Cooking is trying to target, such as millennials. For the text line, The New York Times is working with text messaging platform Subtext, which also works with other publishers like Condé Nast and USA Today Network.

This text line is part of a broader strategy at NYT Cooking. The focus for NYT Cooking’s team this year has been “easy to find, easy to make,” Velasquez said. The team was hearing from readers that Cooking recipes were too hard to make and had inaccessible ingredients, Velasquez explained, so it became clear that they had to highlight easier recipes to both draw new subscribers in and retain those who are already paying.

There are a couple of ways NYT Cooking is responding. The overarching goal is to “simplify [NYT Cooking] as much as we can,” Velasquez said. The team is working on cutting down the number of ingredients and steps in some recipes. And they want to get more free and simple recipes in front of readers — such as with free seven-day and 14-day trials, and now with the emoji text line. The hope is to ultimately convert newly introduced readers into paid subscribers, who pay $5 a month or $40 a year for a subscription to NYT Cooking.

“If a user voluntarily texts NYT Cooking, this is a strong signal of propensity to engage [and or] pay and reduces friction for the user getting the recipe they are after,” said Arvid Tchivzhel, svp of product at subscription management and customer data analytics firm Mather Economics.

However, it will also require “significant outreach” to introduce audiences to this initiative, he added. The New York Times is marketing its new emoji text line with billboards in states like Michigan and Washington (for in-season cherries and corn, respectively), events and posts on its social accounts.

Despite recent reports that subscriptions to news organizations have stalled in the past year, The New York Times Company has continued to grow its subscriber base, adding 190,000 digital-only subscribers in the first quarter of this year. The company now has over 9 million digital-only subscribers, though it does not break out data on how many subscribers are specifically subscribed to Cooking.

In Q1 2023, The New York Times Company surpassed 3 million subscribers who were paying for a bundle (which includes access to the Times’ core news and standalone Cooking, Games, Wirecutter and The Athletic products) or multi-product subscription plan, thanks to about 520,000 new digital-only bundle and multi-product subscribers in the quarter.

Velasquez said the main drivers of subscriber conversions are NYT Cooking app usage, videos on social media and newsletters. She declined to share how many NYT Cooking subscribers there are, or how many are converting through these platforms.

Texting as an audience engagement channel historically hasn’t been successful in driving subscriber acquisitions, according Tchivzhel, based on his experience working with publishers at Mather Economics. “But it is perhaps a deeper level of engagement that can drive more meaningful connections between [the] audience and the Cooking product,” he said in an email.
Other companies are also using text messaging as a marketing tactic, such as KBP Brands, a KFC franchisee , which recently expanded SMS marketing across its 847 U.S. locations.
The Times has a plan for readers who don’t want to subscribe.

Ko says it can also change the recipes around different pans and tools. Customized recipes are private and can’t be published or shared through the app. The AI modification feature is being rolled out gradually while the NYT monitors how it performs — it’s currently available to all Cooking subscribers on the iOS app, and it will be more broadly available “soon.” Some NYT readers have pushed back against the feature, citing concerns in the article’s comment section around the environmental impact of widespread AI adoption and the general impact that AI features may have on the user experience. “I’ve always loved NYT Cooking and it pains me that the AI mandate has reached what used to be a wonderful and simple collection of recipes and notes from all sorts of different people.” This isn’t the first time that AI has been used by the NYT Cooking app. Ko says it was used to convert imperial volume measurements to metric weight measurements in recipes two years ago, and a feature was added last year that converts recipes to halve or double the original serving size. The comments on the new AI feature announcement post have since been closed, but NYT spokesperson Jordan Cohen tells The Verge that this is standard practice: “Comments on this article remained open for four days, with editors from Cooking taking care to answer questions, address concerns and engage directly with readers. We kept that conversation open to give readers a meaningful opportunity to share feedback and hear from the team. Closing comments on older articles is standard practice at The Times so that our moderators can focus on new discussions. We’re pleased to see that many members of our Cooking community are interested in exploring this tool and are already trying it out on our iOS app; they’re reporting good results.”

story.title: The NYT Cooking app is testing AI recipe modifications

facts.text: The most-watched YouTube video for the New York Times’ Cooking channel features chef and cookbook author Claire Saffitz carefully walking viewers through the steps of making the perfect croissant.
After launching 10 years ago, NYT Cooking has succeeded in a crowded field with its blend of sleek videos, massive recipe catalog and an active community of home chefs.
The New York Times is testing a new AI feature for its Cooking app that helps users to modify recipes, and it has sparked some drama among users.

Last Friday, NYT Cooking senior editor Genevieve Ko announced the feature, which can be used to recommend substitutions for ingredients and cooking equipment, scale recipes to any number of servings, and “generally make our recipes work for what a cook needs at that moment.” One of the examples given in the article shows a user asking to use baby spinach instead of kale, with the Cooking app feature advising that because baby spinach wilts faster, it should be added during a later step of the recipe.
