story.title: Google Updates Spam Guide For Shared Pages, Generated Content & Apps - Search Engine Journal

facts.text: Google today revised its Search Central guide on preventing user-generated spam , widening it beyond comment forms and hosting services to "tools that let users publish shared pages, generated content, or web apps." The page gains a new section, "Only index content meant for Search," which says pages created for direct sharing, collaboration or utility should carry a noindex rule or be blocked from crawling by default, and it adds Search Console alerts and platform-level metrics to its monitoring checklist.
The change is logged in an entry posted today on Google's documentation changelog , and the page carries a "Last updated 2026-10-26 UTC" stamp.
Marketing teams use many of the kinds of services the guide now describes.
Campaign microsites, prototype landing pages, hosted forms, interactive calculators, AI-generated reports and shared chat outputs are often built on third-party platforms and passed around by link.
Google's guidance does not describe what that opt-in should look like.

When DuckDuckGo launched share links for its Duck.ai assistant on October 7, 2026, it said that shared conversations from ChatGPT and Claude had appeared in search results over the previous year, sometimes with names and personal details attached.

Security firm Claroc has cited 2025 cases in which more than 370,000 Grok conversations were indexed, figures it gave when Meta paused sharing in its Muse AI agent on October 20 after more than 6,800 share hostnames surfaced in passive DNS records.
Claroc said that exposure did not involve search engines, and that Muse's robots.txt asked crawlers to stay off its share paths.
It is filed as an update to a guide, not as a change to Google's spam policies, which live in a separate document.
That distinction carries particular weight for link-shared content.

A share link exists to be pasted elsewhere - into social posts, forums, messaging apps and emails - which is precisely the kind of external linking that can lead Google to index a blocked URL without its content.
The new section does not discuss the interaction.
Google's own products fall within the categories as well.
Neither product's coverage establishes whether its shared pages are indexed by search engines.
Google has not said whether enforcement will follow, and the guide describes no consequence for a platform that leaves shared pages indexable.

What the page does say is that spammers "may create a large number of pages or sites that violate our spam policies." Those policies include scaled content abuse , which covers mass-produced pages that add little value for users, and Google stated in May 2026 that its spam policies apply to AI Overviews and AI Mode as well as to traditional results.
Those pages can end up in Google Search even when they were only meant for the few people holding the link, which lets spammers fill results with junk hosted on someone else's trusted website.
Google names no products, companies or technologies.
The words "artificial intelligence" appear nowhere on the page.
A robots.txt disallow rule works at a different stage.
It stops a crawler from fetching a URL but does not, on its own, keep that URL out of the index.
The two methods therefore do not stack, and combining them can defeat the noindex rule.
Google does not say which services prompted the change.
PPC Land's coverage over the past year has documented several types of product that match the guide's new language.
The change also concerns publishers, SEO teams and marketers who build on those platforms or compete with pages hosted on them.
RedAccess located the apps by searching Google and Bing for the platforms' default domains.
The UGC Fresh Data Program offers a contrast with today's change.

Within one month, then, Google has documented a faster route into its systems for moderated public discussion, and a default route out of its index for user-created pages that were never meant to be searched.
For platform operators, the monitoring additions carry a cost.

Verifying subdomains, watching Page Indexing reports for unexplained growth, and building internal alerts for concentrated URL creation by a handful of accounts all require engineering and moderation time.
The guide acknowledges this kind of trade-off elsewhere, noting that moderation "adds overhead" to daily workflows.
It does not quantify what Google expects of smaller services.
The "Monitor your service for abuse" list gained two items, both placed at the top.
The first asks operators to verify their site or subdomain in Search Console so that Google can email them if it issues a manual action against the site or detects security issues.

It also names two Search Console reports, Page Indexing and Search performance, to be checked regularly for "unexpected spikes in indexed pages, impressions, or queries" that do not match what the platform is for.
According to Search Engine Roundtable, consultant Marie Haynes asked on X whether the update means new manual actions are coming for AI tools and app-building platforms.

Another clue from Google about new types of spam they are dealing with (likely at a big enough scale to warrant changing their documentation) and ... another clue about what they'll be targeting in the future?"
The question of manual actions has been live for weeks.
The evidence was anecdotal, and Google did not comment.
That update was the fourth spam update of the year, following rollouts on March 24, June 24 and August 18 .

It still suggests applying a noindex robots meta tag to posts from new users who have no reputation on a platform, lifting it once they earn one, and adding a "nofollow or ugc rel attribute" to links in untrusted content.
Pages published on trusted platform domains can compete in results with original sites, and since May those same spam policies have applied to the AI answers that sit above the links.
Platforms that tighten indexing defaults reduce one source of that competition.
Those signals remain, now from third place down.
Will those platforms switch their indexing defaults?
The timing matters because the traffic data is already moving.

Over the past month I've watched websites with heavy concentrations of AI-generated content, the kind Ahrefs now flags as "Very high" on its AI Content Level metric, begin sliding in Google organic search.
This also lines up with the rollout of Google’s latest June 2026 spam update that recently finished rolling out.
But when declines cluster around a specific site profile right as Google publishes both an algorithm update and research on detecting that exact profile, it deserves attention.
Google's 2023 guidance rewards content for quality regardless of production method; enforcement targets scaled content abuse, meaning high-volume, low-value pages built mainly to manipulate rankings.
A content classifier scans for repetitive, templated narratives and for high-frequency publishing behavior that no human schedule produces.
An infrastructure component ties accounts back to a common source.
When enough accounts in a cluster show the same AI-generated templates, Google removes the whole cluster at once rather than penalizing individual pages.
Automation has been part of publishing for decades, from sports scores to weather forecasts.
The risk calculus for AI-heavy SEO & AEO has changed shape.
The question used to be whether a single page looked low quality.
The question now includes whether your templates, publishing cadence, infrastructure and content similarities make your operation resemble a coordinated spam network.
Gabe's read: Google will not let companies spam their way into AI search , and marketers should expect stronger automated systems plus manual actions.
Traditional quality filters evaluate one piece of content at a time.
Google's researchers acknowledge that generative AI broke that model.
Spammers can now produce endless variations of what the paper calls functionally identical content: every page technically unique, every page effectively the same.
At volume, that flood is built to swamp content-level filters.
SBERT has existed since 2019, and Montti points out the SEO industry has rarely discussed it as a spam-detection mechanism.
Its appearance in a Google paper about catching synthetic spam suggests it may have been put to that use only recently.
One more detail worth knowing: speed of adaptation.
The paper describes using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and Automatic Prompt Optimization (APO) to retune classifiers when spammers move to new generative models.
That means days of adjustment instead of months of retraining.
When the next model ships and spam operations migrate, Google can follow almost immediately.
The paper, covered by Roger Montti at Search Engine Journal and shared widely by Glenn Gabe on X , describes the Scalable Cluster Termination System.

extraction.body: The identities of over 41,000 officials from the Department of Homeland Security have allegedly been exposed in a massive data breach by a hacktivist group calling itself the Department of Peace. The new laptop will go on sale Nov. 6 and the 14-inch version will start at $2,899. The 16-inch version will cost at least $3,399. Both are notable price increases from existing models.

passages: It marks a turning point for the company, which for years said it would not develop a touch-screen laptop.
But will Apple entering this long established market have a big impact and make touch-screen laptops cool?
More than a decade after touch-screen Windows laptops first hit the market, Apple has taken the wraps off its first touch-screen Macbook Pro.
The company has flirted with adding touch inputs on its laptops before.
It is targeted at graphic designers, photographers, musicians and other creative types.
Cesareo Contreras is a Northeastern Global News reporter.
Follow him on X/Twitter @cesareo_r and Threads @cesareor .
The Cupertino-based company announced the new laptop on Wednesday during its “Pro and Tell” in Los Angeles, a special event to launch the new product.

Apple never acknowledged why it removed the Touch Bar, but the feature had poor software support from outside developers, and many Mac users prefer traditional function row keys, according to tech industry experts.
“Apple has made itself the go-to brand for people who do drawing and drafting as part of their work,” he said.
Some users have reported that their phone’s inner folding displays are already breaking under normal use.
Apple issued a statement acknowledging the defect was “impacting a small number of iPhone units” and that anyone who is experiencing the issue should contact the company for a replacement.
“This is a technology that is not going to surprise or delight people,” he said.
“It’s going to confuse people that Apple didn’t already offer this.”
“No doubt Apple feels some pressure to ‘check the box’ since the competition touts it as a Windows-only feature,” he said.
Apple wasn’t the first to enter the folding phone market, but early reception of the device has been positive.
Analysts at Counterpoint Research , a marketing research firm, estimated that by the end of the year the company is expected to sell more than six million units.
But for other consumers, DePaoli is skeptical.

extraction.body: Apple has revealed its first touch screen Macbook. It is targeted at graphic designers, photographers, musicians and other creative types. More than a decade after touch-screen Windows laptops first hit the market, Apple has taken the wraps off its first touch-screen Macbook Pro. The Cupertino-based company announced the new laptop on Wednesday during its “Pro and Tell” in Los Angeles, a special event to launch the new product. It marks a turning point for the company, which for years said it would not develop a touch-screen laptop. Apple users interested in a touch-first device should buy an iPad instead, the company has long argued. In fact, Apple co-founder and former CEO Steve Jobs once famously said that touch-screen laptops were “ergonomically terrible ” during a keynote in 2010 promoting the Macbook Air, the company’s light and ultraportable laptop. Alex DePaoli, a marketing professor in the D’Amore-McKim School of Business said the company likely has pivoted on its stance against making a totally touch-friendly Mac out of the desire to entice the higher end market and creative professionals. “Apple has made itself the go-to brand for people who do drawing and drafting as part of their work,” he said. That is how the company is marketing it. In a press release announcing the laptop, the company touted its new features, specifically to that crowd. Graphic designers no longer have to rely on the computer’s trackpad to move and orient their 3D models or sketches, musicians can use their hands to play keys on a virtual piano, and photographers can easily pinch and zoom on images using their fingers, it highlighted. And it is certainly high end. The computer, which comes in 14-inch and 16-inch variants, starts at $2,899. Customers can pre-order the device now. It launches on Nov. 6. DePaoli said Apple is following its signature playbook with the touch-screen Macbook, as the company has a habit of entering established consumer electronic categories with its own premium line of products. It waits for others to work out the kinks with the underlying technology and then introduces its own more “polished” device, he said. A great example is the iPhone Duo, the company’s first folding phone that hit store shelves last week, he said. Apple wasn’t the first to enter the folding phone market, but early reception of the device has been positive. Analysts at Counterpoint Research , a marketing research firm, estimated that by the end of the year the company is expected to sell more than six million units. It hasn’t been completely rosey, however. Some users have reported that their phone’s inner folding displays are already breaking under normal use. Apple issued a statement acknowledging the defect was “impacting a small number of iPhone units” and that anyone who is experiencing the issue should contact the company for a replacement. The launch of the Macbook Pro is likely to bring less fanfare than Duo as many users likely assumed Apple already offered a touch-screen Macbook, DePaoli said. “This is a technology that is not going to surprise or delight people,” he said. “It’s going to confuse people that Apple didn’t already offer this.” The company has flirted with adding touch inputs on its laptops before. In 2016, it introduced the Touch Bar to the Macbook Pro, a touch-screen display that replaced the laptop’s function key row. But it was phased out a few years later. Apple never acknowledged why it removed the Touch Bar, but the feature had poor software support from outside developers, and many Mac users prefer traditional function row keys, according to tech industry experts. Mark Miller, a computer science professor in Northeastern’s Silicon Valley campus and a former Apple employee, believes the company is adding a touch screen to the Macbook as a way to stand out in a sea of touch-screen Windows laptops. “No doubt Apple feels some pressure to ‘check the box’ since the competition touts it as a Windows-only feature,” he said. But will Apple entering this long established market have a big impact and make touch-screen laptops cool? Maybe for diehard Apple enthusiasts. But for other consumers, DePaoli is skeptical. “I don’t think you are going to move a lot of units by saying, ‘Hey, that thing you’ve been trying to do for ten years, you can actually do it now,” he said. Cesareo Contreras is a Northeastern Global News reporter. Email him at c.contreras@northeastern.edu . Follow him on X/Twitter @cesareo_r and Threads @cesareor .

Also read: Apple launches new iMac in India at ₹1.75 lakh with faster AI performance Why now?Apple hasn’t explained itself, but the reasons aren’t hard to find.The first is money.
Apple has discussed charging $400 more for the touch model, starting the 14-inch at $2,899.
The Mac has been a growth engine since Apple moved to its own chips, bringing in $40.1 billion in fiscal 2022.
For more than a decade, Apple argued that touchscreens and laptops don’t mix.
Windows laptops have offered touchscreens as a standard feature for years, even as Apple insisted they were ergonomically inferior.
Apple has long held that the iPad is the best touchscreen computer, so it has to keep a clear line between the tablet and the laptop.
Apple appears to be betting that Pro users will pay a real premium for a touch-enabled OLED laptop, which would lift what the average Mac sells for.The second is competition.
Apple’s pro customers have long had a touch-capable alternative at the other end of the aisle.The third is timing.
Software chief Craig Federighi once called touchscreen PCs “experiments” and said he was “not into touchscreens.” The idea has circulated for years.
Expect Apple to pitch touch as a complement to the keyboard and trackpad, not a replacement for them.

extraction.body: A new MARADMIN swaps AI for SI across Total Force products; but statutes, contracts and old titles stay put. The Marine Corps just told the Total Force to swap the term "Artificial Intelligence" for “Super Intelligence” in official writing. MARADMIN 521/26, signed Oct. 23, directs commands to use "Super Intelligence" and the abbreviation SI in place of Artificial Intelligence and AI "to the maximum extent permitted by law." The order covers official correspondence, public communications, websites, reports, policy documents, briefing and training materials, and other non-statutory products. Content owners must update current websites and reusable templates as they revise them. The change implements Executive Order 14434, signed Sept. 29, which told the executive branch to adopt SI terminology. Stars and Stripes covered the Navy and Marine memos as a dual-service rename. The Marine message is narrower and more useful for Marines who write for a living: who owns the policy, what products move first, and what is explicitly left alone. SI, for purposes of the guidance, means the same technologies already covered by the statutory definition of AI in Title 15, U.S. Code, Section 9401(3), except where law says otherwise. Generative systems and other machine-learning applications under that definition are included. Security, privacy, acquisition and responsible-use rules do not change with the name. Commanders and directors are responsible for making sure military and civilian personnel who prepare, review or publish those products understand the guidance. The message applies to the Marine Corps Total Force. Implementation that touches contractor performance will be coordinated through the appropriate contracting authority and the contract requirements already in force. The Deputy Commandant for Information's Chief Data and Super Intelligence Office, or CDSO, remains the Service lead for strategy, policy, governance and oversight. The message cites MCO 5231.4, still titled Marine Corps Data and Artificial Intelligence, as the governing order. The reference titles in 521/26 keep their published wording on purpose. The executive order does not require Marines to alter previously issued regulations, presidential actions, contracts, grants or other historical documents. Issued records stay as issued under records-management rules. Statutory wording, accurate direct quotations and official source titles stay as written when Marines cite or reproduce them. Organization, program and product names stay current unless the responsible authority changes them. In practice, that means a Marine quoting Title 15, pasting a contract clause that says AI, or citing MCO 5231.4 by its published title is not out of step with 521/26. That carve-out matters for contracting officers, requirements writers, and schoolhouse staff who work with citation-heavy products. The rewrite burden falls on forward-looking writing, not on scrubbing every existing document. A historical after-action report that used AI in 2024 does not need a red pen. A new public affairs release written next week does. PAOs, web managers, doctrine writers, schoolhouses and anyone who owns a briefing template will feel this first. Content owners must update current websites and reusable templates as they revise them. The change implements Executive Order 14434, signed Sept. 29, which told the executive branch to adopt SI terminology. Stars and Stripes covered the Navy and Marine memos as a dual-service rename. The Marine message is narrower and more useful for Marines who write for a living: who owns the policy, what products move first, and what is explicitly left alone. SI, for purposes of the guidance, means the same technologies already covered by the statutory definition of AI in Title 15, U.S. Code, Section 9401(3), except where law says otherwise. Generative systems and other machine-learning applications under that definition are included. Security, privacy, acquisition and responsible-use rules do not change with the name. Commanders and directors are responsible for making sure military and civilian personnel who prepare, review or publish those products understand the guidance. The message applies to the Marine Corps Total Force. Implementation that touches contractor performance will be coordinated through the appropriate contracting authority and the contract requirements already in force. The Deputy Commandant for Information's Chief Data and Super Intelligence Office, or CDSO, remains the Service lead for strategy, policy, governance and oversight. The message cites MCO 5231.4, still titled Marine Corps Data and Artificial Intelligence, as the governing order. The reference titles in 521/26 keep their published wording on purpose. The executive order does not require Marines to alter previously issued regulations, presidential actions, contracts, grants or other historical documents. Issued records stay as issued under records-management rules. Statutory wording, accurate direct quotations and official source titles stay as written when Marines cite or reproduce them. Organization, program and product names stay current unless the responsible authority changes them. In practice, that means a Marine quoting Title 15, pasting a contract clause that says AI, or citing MCO 5231.4 by its published title is not out of step with 521/26. That carve-out matters for contracting officers, requirements writers, and schoolhouse staff who work with citation-heavy products. The rewrite burden falls on forward-looking writing, not on scrubbing every existing document. A historical after-action report that used AI in 2024 does not need a red pen. A new public affairs release written next week does. PAOs, web managers, doctrine writers, schoolhouses and anyone who owns a briefing template will feel this first. Every slide deck that still says AI, every public affairs release, every course syllabus that introduces the Basic AI Course by that name will need a judgment call: Is this a non-statutory product being issued or revised, or is it a quotation of a statutory title? The Corps has spent the last year teaching Marines to use these tools under the old label. Military.com covered how the service framed AI as a warfighting edge in its implementation plan, and Marines are already running competitive wargames against machine opponents under MCU's Humans vs. Machine tournament. MARADMIN 214/26 still requires every active-duty and reserve Marine to finish the Basic AI Course by Dec. 31. MARADMIN 467/26 and its update list additional AI and data courses available through Marine Corps eLearning, Joint Knowledge Online and Navy Community College pathways. Those course titles and syllabus citations will not vanish overnight. Expect mixed language in the near term: SI in new command correspondence, AI in materials that quote statutes or older MARADMINs by title. That is not Marines ignoring the order. It is the order working as written. Nothing in 521/26 changes the systems Marines buy or the security rules that govern them. The same models, the same data pipelines and the same human-on-the-loop requirements apply. The message is terminology policy, not a new capability fielding plan and not a change to how Marines employ machine learning at the edge. MCU's extracurricular Fight Club wargaming program and the new SI vocabulary will have to share a language for a while. The practical application for any Marine writing an operations order, a public affairs release or a schoolhouse handout tomorrow: Use Super Intelligence and SI in new official products unless law, a quotation or an official title forces the older words. extraction.body: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Nearly all industries have been impacted by Artificial Intelligence. Goldman Sachs estimates 300 million jobs will be impacted by the emerging technology by 2030. AI is reshaping industries by the day, resulting in jobs being transformed or erased. The changes are bringing a greater need for AI oversight. “People need to understand that there still needs to be human involvement,” Barry Jones, a Vice President at X2X said. X2X is an AI governance company. Jones said there’s not enough oversight AI oversight right now. “Imagine an AI assistant preparing financial reports,” Jones said. “That’s a potentially productive tool. But just imagine if that AI system provided that critical financial information outside of the company’s internal workings.” Before Congress left Capitol Hill for the midterms, several congressmembers made clear where they stood on what role the government should play on regulation. “Well, look, anytime you can give the federal government out of it, I think we’re better off,” Rep. Buddy Carter (R-GA) said. “We don’t want to stifle innovation. But at the same time, we got to get this right. That’s the key. We got to get a right. I can be a very useful tool, unbelievably useful tool. But there are some concerns and there are some dangers there.” “First, the United States needs to address the very real risks created by increasingly powerful AI systems, and these decisions need to be made by the American people through their representatives,” Senator Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) said. Jones said big picture, self-governance isn’t enough. “But to say that something is self-governing is like having the fox watching the henhouse,” Jones said. “You really need to have a third party, layer in some cases, even the government saying these are the things that I can do and I cannot do.” Jones said that private oversight is creating roles that have been replaced by technology. Microsoft recently announced they offered 60,000 employees buyouts due to AI. Jones has advice for people looking for a career pivot due to AI. “Start learning AI,” Jones said. “Understand how it applies to your profession. Also understand that judgement, experience, trust and accountability matter. The goal shouldn’t be to compete with the machine. The goal should be to become someone who knows the useful power of the technology and using it responsibly.” Efforts to regulate Artificial Intelligence are stalled on Capitol Hill but the 120 th Congress could take up the rapidly evolving technology in January.
